title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
When to use regex



Regex works well when

the text follows a format: IDs, dates, amounts, codes
the wording repeats, as in the Fed’s sentence that states the target range
you can list the variants and test each one
you need the same answer every time the code runs
the corpus is large: a pattern runs on millions of documents in seconds, for free




Use a parser or a model when

the meaning depends on context or on negation: the Fed’s “might not be strong enough” (13 Sep 2012) scores as positive
the same idea is written in more ways than you can list
the text is a web page (HTML) or data from an API (JSON), where parts sit inside other parts
the variable is a judgment call, such as whether a sentence signals that the Fed will raise its rate





Parser: a function that reads a structured format into its parts, such as jsonlite::fromJSON() for JSON or rvest::read_html() for a web page. Model: a language model, the kind of program behind a chatbot, asked to read each text and return a label, or a statistical classifier trained on texts that people labeled by hand.


A pattern gives NA or a wrong number, with no error message, when the wording or a character changes. A chatbot can write the pattern. You still read it, test it on strings from your documents, and compare its output with a second source such as FRED.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
What net tone misses

The target range has a second source, FRED, and 170 of 171 values now equal it. Net tone has no second source, so its errors show only when you read the sentences it scored. The finance word list scores each word on its own:




R Console; needs fomc

s <- str_extract(fomc$text[fomc$date == "2012-09-13"], "economic growth might not[^.]*")
str_view(s, "\\b(not|strong|improvement)\\b")


#> [1] │ economic growth might <not> be <strong> enough to generate sustained <improvement> in labor market conditions




Negation. 13 Sep 2012 (also 24 Oct and 12 Dec 2012): “strong” and “improvement” count as positive. Each word is scored on its own, so the “not” before them changes nothing.
Context. 25 Apr 2012, “the unemployment rate has declined but remains elevated”: “unemployment” and “declined” count as negative, although a falling unemployment rate is good news.
The event behind the words. 3 Mar 2020, a cut in the target range between scheduled meetings as the coronavirus spread, is the 8th most positive of 171 statements. “strong”, “achieving” and “stability” count as positive. “coronavirus” and “risks” are on neither list.


Words the finance list misreads in Fed statements.










Word
List
Times
In a Fed statement




unemployment
negative
154
a statistic: “unemployment rate” (141)


against
negative
86
the vote: “Voting against” (75)


impede
negative
46
one set phrase about risks to the committee’s goals


declined
negative
45
good news in “the unemployment rate declined” (18 statements)


stability
positive
223
the goal: “price stability” (218)


exceptionally
positive
56
always “exceptionally low”, about the rate





Dropping unemployment, against, stability and exceptionally leaves the lowest statement unchanged and makes 12 Jun 2024 the highest (Practice 8).

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Practice
Task 7 uses the word lists of Baker, Bloom & Davis (QJE, 2016).

# Practice. Run in the 16-text-regex folder with stringr loaded, after the
# slides' code has built fomc (with the three changes), tokens, pos, neg
# and the FRED columns.

# Patterns and numbers
#  1. Label each statement by its opening with ^: "Information received",
#     "Recent indicators", or "other". Count them by year with table().
#  2. Run str_match(fomc$text, "(\\d+) basis points") and table() column 2.
#     Read each matching sentence. Which matches are not the committee's
#     decision? Change the pattern so only decisions match.
#  3. The 2026 statements give the vote ("by a 12 – 0 vote"). Extract the
#     two numbers as numeric columns. Why does "by a (\\d+) - (\\d+) vote"
#     fail? Use utf8ToInt() on the character between the numbers.
#  4. Validate the url column: every address should look like
#     https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetaryYYYYMMDDa.htm
#     Write the pattern with ^, \d{8} and $. Which addresses fail, and why?
# Base R
#  5. Rewrite the three changes with gsub(), regmatches() with regexpr(),
#     and regexec(). Do the same 170 statements equal FRED?
# Word counts
#  6. For each statement, compute the share of its tokens that are
#     "inflation". Average it by year with tapply(share, fomc$year, mean),
#     which applies mean() within each year, and plot it. Which year is
#     highest, which lowest?
#  7. Apply the core words of the three lists of Baker, Bloom & Davis
#     (QJE, 2016) to the statements with \\b and |. How many statements
#     match each list, and all three, and in which years?
# Tone
#  8. Recompute net tone after removing "unemployment" and "against" from
#     neg, and "stability" and "exceptionally" from pos. Which statements
#     are now lowest and highest? Where does 3 Mar 2020 land?
#  9. List the word after every "not" with str_match_all(), which returns
#     str_match()'s matrix for every match in each statement. How many are
#     on the positive list, and how many on the negative list?
# Characters
# 10. List every character with a code point above 127, with its code
#     point, its count, and the statements it appears in. Which would you
#     replace before matching?







NoteSolutions








R Console; needs fomc, tokens, pos, neg, num, to_num() and fred

# 1. Openings by year
op <- ifelse(str_detect(fomc$text, "^Information received"), "Information received",
      ifelse(str_detect(fomc$text, "^Recent indicators"), "Recent indicators", "other"))
table(op)


#> op
#> Information received                other    Recent indicators 
#>                   88                   60                   23

table(fomc$year, op)[c("2009", "2019", "2020", "2022", "2026"), ]

#>       op
#>        Information received other Recent indicators
#>   2009                    7     1                 0
#>   2019                    8     0                 0
#>   2020                    1     9                 0
#>   2022                    0     4                 4
#>   2026                    0     5                 1

# 2. Basis points: 20 matches, 7 of them in dissents
bp <- str_match(fomc$text, "(\\d+) basis points")
table(bp[, 2])

#> 
#> 25 50 75 
#> 14  4  2

dec <- str_match(fomc$text, "decided[^.]*?(\\d+) basis points")
table(dec[, 2])

#> 
#> 25 50 75 
#>  7  4  2

# 3. The vote: the character between the numbers is an en dash, 8211
vt <- str_match(fomc$text, "by a (\\d+) (.) (\\d+) vote")
vt[!is.na(vt[, 1]), ]

#>      [,1]               [,2] [,3] [,4]
#> [1,] "by a 12 – 0 vote" "12" "–"  "0" 
#> [2,] "by a 9 – 3 vote"  "9"  "–"  "3" 
#> [3,] "by a 12 – 0 vote" "12" "–"  "0"

utf8ToInt(vt[!is.na(vt[, 1]), 3][1])

#> [1] 8211

# 4. Statement addresses: three end in "b.htm", a second release that day
url_ok <- str_detect(fomc$url,
  "^https://www\\.federalreserve\\.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary\\d{8}a\\.htm$")
fomc$url[!url_ok]

#> [1] "https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20070817b.htm"
#> [2] "https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20080122b.htm"
#> [3] "https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20081216b.htm"

# 5. The three changes in base R
tx  <- gsub("\u2011", "-", fomc$text)
sg  <- regmatches(tx, regexpr("(?:decided|maintain|reaffirmed)[^.]*?percent\\b", tx,
                              ignore.case = TRUE, perl = TRUE))
has <- grepl("(?:decided|maintain|reaffirmed)[^.]*?percent\\b", tx,
             ignore.case = TRUE, perl = TRUE)
seg_b <- rep(NA_character_, length(tx))
seg_b[has] <- sg
mb <- regmatches(seg_b, regexec(paste0("(", num, ")(?:\\s+to\\s+(", num, "))?\\s+percent\\b"),
                                seg_b, perl = TRUE))
lo <- sapply(mb, function(v) if (length(v)) to_num(v[2]) else NA)
hi <- sapply(mb, function(v) if (length(v) && v[3] != "") to_num(v[3]) else NA)
hi <- ifelse(is.na(hi), lo, hi)
table(lo == fomc$fred_lower & hi == fomc$fred_upper, useNA = "ifany")

#> 
#> TRUE <NA> 
#>  170    1

# 6. "inflation" as a share of tokens, by year
share <- sapply(tokens, function(w) mean(w == "inflation"))
by_year <- tapply(share, fomc$year, mean)
round(100 * by_year[c(which.max(by_year), which.min(by_year))], 2)

#> 2018 2009 
#> 2.82 0.49

plot(as.numeric(names(by_year)), 100 * by_year, type = "b", xlab = "",
     ylab = "\"inflation\", percent of tokens", las = 1)
# 7. The three word lists of Baker, Bloom & Davis
E <- str_detect(fomc$text, regex("\\beconom(y|ic)\\b", ignore_case = TRUE))
U <- str_detect(fomc$text, regex("\\buncertain(ty)?\\b", ignore_case = TRUE))
P <- str_detect(fomc$text, "\\b(Congress|deficit|Federal Reserve|legislation|regulation|White House)\\b")
c(economy = sum(E), uncertainty = sum(U), policy = sum(P), all_three = sum(E & U & P))

#>     economy uncertainty      policy   all_three 
#>         171          41          53           8

table(fomc$year[E & U & P])

#> 
#> 2007 2008 2022 2026 
#>    2    2    1    3

# 8. Tone without the four misread words
pos2 <- setdiff(pos, c("stability", "exceptionally"))
neg2 <- setdiff(neg, c("unemployment", "against"))
tone2 <- sapply(tokens, function(w) 100 * (sum(w %in% pos2) - sum(w %in% neg2)) / length(w))
round(cor(fomc$tone, tone2), 2)

#> [1] 0.92

fomc$date[c(which.min(tone2), which.max(tone2))]

#> [1] "2008-09-16" "2024-06-12"

match(which(fomc$date == "2020-03-03"), order(-tone2))     # its rank, most positive first

#> [1] 43

# 9. The word after "not"
nm <- str_match_all(str_to_lower(fomc$text), "\\bnot ([a-z]+)")
after_not <- unlist(lapply(nm, function(x) x[, 2]))
length(after_not)

#> [1] 38

c(positive = sum(after_not %in% pos), negative = sum(after_not %in% neg))

#> positive negative 
#>        4        1

# 10. Characters above code point 127
ch <- unlist(strsplit(read.csv("fomc_statements.csv")$text, ""))
odd <- ch[sapply(ch, utf8ToInt) > 127]
sort(table(sapply(odd, utf8ToInt)), decreasing = TRUE)

#> 
#> 8209 8217 8211 8212 8195 
#>   50   25    3    2    1

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Quick reference
Pattern pieces: . any character · \\. a period · \\d a digit · \\s a space or line break · [ ] one of a set · [^ ] one not in the set · + one or more · * zero or more · ? zero or one · {n} exactly n · .*? as few as possible · ^ start · $ end · \\b a word boundary · ( ) a capture group · (?: ) a group with no column · | either side · regex(p, ignore_case = TRUE, dotall = TRUE).
Functions: str_detect, str_count, str_view, str_extract, str_extract_all, str_match, str_replace_all, str_sub, str_c, str_to_lower, regex, utf8ToInt, match, table, sort, unlist, which, is.na, %in%, sapply, which.min, which.max.
The word list. The shipped file keeps the words whose Positive or Negative flag in the master dictionary is a year above 0, because a negative year marks a word removed from the list. It leaves out 17 removed words, so it has 347 positive and 2,345 negative words; Shapiro and Wilson used an earlier version. The master dictionary has five more lists (uncertainty, litigious, strong modal, weak modal, constraining).
Sources. Baker, Bloom & Davis (QJE, 2016); Shapiro & Wilson (REStud, 2022), “Taking the Fed at its Word: A New Approach to Estimating Central Bank Objectives using Text Analysis” (method details from FRBSF Working Paper 2019-02); Djourelova (AER, 2023); Loughran & McDonald (JF, 2011) and their master dictionary. FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis: DFEDTAR, DFEDTARL, DFEDTARU. Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, federalreserve.gov (public domain; disclaimer).
The statements were collected from federalreserve.gov in October 2026, FRED’s series were downloaded the same month, and the word list is the authors’ March 2026 update.
Links: slides · stringr · Syllabus

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
From text to variables



The Federal Open Market Committee decided today to establish a target range for the federal funds rate of 0 to 1/4 percent.
Since the Committee’s last meeting, labor market conditions have deteriorated, and the available data indicate that consumer spending, business investment, and industrial production have declined. Financial markets remain quite strained and credit conditions tight. Overall, the outlook for economic activity has weakened further.




A pattern finds 0 to 1/4 percent → lower = 0 and upper = 0.25 (percent).
A count of words on a finance word list: the statement has 403 words. 8 are negative (the 4 in red are in these two paragraphs) and 2 are positive.
Net tone = 100 × (positive − negative) / words = 100 × (2 − 8) / 403 = −1.49.
Run on all 171 statements from 2006 to 2026, each method gives a column you can plot and compare with other data.




The Federal Reserve (the Fed) is the US central bank. Its policy committee, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), sets a target range for the federal funds rate (the interest rate banks charge each other on overnight loans). It publishes a statement after each meeting.

Paragraphs 1 and 2 of the FOMC statement of 16 December 2008, during the financial crisis.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Three papers that count words




Paper
Text
What they counted
Finding




Baker, Bloom & Davis (QJE, 2016)
articles in 10 US newspapers, each month
share of articles with a word from each of three lists: economy, policy, uncertainty (an uncertainty index)
the index rises near close elections, wars, 9/11, the failure of Lehman Brothers and the 2011 debt-ceiling fight


Shapiro & Wilson (REStud, 2022)
transcripts of Fed policy meetings, 2000–2011
negative and positive words from a finance word list
the committee aimed at about 1.5 percent inflation, below the 2 percent usually assumed


Djourelova (AER, 2023)
more than 2,000 US news outlets
the phrase “illegal immigrant”, before and after the Associated Press told its reporters to stop using it in April 2013
readers of papers that relied on AP stories became less supportive of restrictive immigration policy





Lehman Brothers: a large US investment bank that failed in September 2008. Debt ceiling: the legal limit on US federal borrowing. Associated Press (AP): a US news agency whose stories many local papers reprint.
Takeaway: each paper turns text into a variable by counting words or a phrase. In the first two, people read a random sample by hand to confirm the count measures what the authors claim. Details and figures are on the session page.


Lehman Brothers: a large US investment bank that failed in September 2008. The debt ceiling: the legal limit on federal borrowing. The Associated Press is a news agency whose stories many local papers reprint.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Terms for text as data


Corpus: the 171 Fed statements, 2006–2026. Example document: the statement of 22 March 2023 (target range 4-3/4 to 5 percent).

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
What a regular expression is


A regular expression (regex) is a pattern, written as a string, that describes a set of texts. A function reads the pattern and finds the stretches of text that fit it, called matches.
Most characters match themselves: the pattern "rate" finds the letters r, a, t, e in that order. These are literals.
A few characters have a special meaning, such as ?, which makes the piece before it optional. These are metacharacters.
The same syntax works in most programming languages and text editors.





R Console; needs stringr

# install.packages(c("stringr", "stopwords"))   # once
library(stringr)               # text functions; every name starts with str_
words <- c("color", "colour", "colr", "Colour")
str_detect(words, "colou?r")   # TRUE if the string contains a match; ? makes the u optional


#> [1]  TRUE  TRUE FALSE FALSE

str_view(words, "colou?r")     # the strings that match, each match in < >

#> [1] │ <color>
#> [2] │ <colour>

str_detect(words, regex("colou?r", ignore_case = TRUE))   # upper and lower case match alike

#> [1]  TRUE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE



Matching is case-sensitive, so “Colour” does not match until ignore_case = TRUE inside regex() turns that off.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Metacharacters










Symbol
Means
Pattern
Example match




.
any one character
r.te
rate, rite


[ ]
one character from the set
[0-9]
4


[^ ]
one character not in the set
[^0-9]
the - and / in 4-3/4


?
the piece before, zero or one time
rates?
rate, rates


*
the piece before, zero or more times
10*
1, 10, 100


+
the piece before, one or more times
[0-9]+
2026


{n}
the piece before, exactly n times
[0-9]{4}
2026


^ $
the start, the end of the text
^The
“The” at the start


|
the piece on either side
raise|lower
raise, lower


( )
a group, whose match R can return alone
([0-9]+)%
4% (group: 4)


\\
the next character is plain (in R, typed twice)
\\.
a period





Shortcuts: \\d a digit, \\s a space or line break, \\w a letter, digit or underscore, \\b the edge of a word. In R each backslash is written twice: you type "\\d" and the pattern receives \d. A piece is one character, a class in brackets, or a group.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Character classes [ ] and \\d



R Console; needs stringr

# a sentence from the Fed's policy statement of 22 March 2023
x <- "the Committee decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate to 4-3/4 to 5 percent."
str_view(x, "\\d")


#> [1] │ the Committee decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate to <4>-<3>/<4> to <5> percent.

str_view(x, "[0-9/-]")

#> [1] │ the Committee decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate to <4><-><3></><4> to <5> percent.

str_view(x, "[^a-z ]")      # ^ inside brackets: any character NOT in the set

#> [1] │ the <C>ommittee decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate to <4><-><3></><4> to <5> percent<.>




Character class: characters in brackets. It matches any one of them.
Inside brackets, 0-9 means any digit and a-z any lowercase letter. A hyphen placed last, as in [0-9/-], is a plain hyphen.
[^ ] matches any one character NOT in the set. The set in [^a-z ] is the lowercase letters and the space, so it catches the capital C, the digits, the - and the /, and the final period.
\\d: one digit, the same as [0-9].
The Fed writes rates as a whole number and a fraction: “4-3/4 percent” is 4.75 percent.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
The dot and the escape



R Console; needs stringr and x

str_view(c("rate", "rite", "r8te", "rte"), "r.te")   # . : any one character


#> [1] │ <rate>
#> [2] │ <rite>
#> [3] │ <r8te>

str_view(x, "\\.")           # \\. : a period

#> [1] │ the Committee decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate to 4-3/4 to 5 percent<.>

c(str_count(x, "."), str_count(x, "\\."))

#> [1] 97  1




The dot .: any one character.
The dot needs exactly one character, so “rte” does not match. str_count() counts the matches in each string.
Escape: a backslash that turns a metacharacter back into a plain character: \\. a period, \\$ a dollar sign, \\? a question mark, \\( a parenthesis.
x has 97 characters. "." matches each of them, and "\\." only the period.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Quantifiers



R Console; needs x

str_extract_all(x, "[0-9/-]+")            # + : one or more of the piece before


#> [[1]]
#> [1] "4-3/4" "5"

str_extract(x, "\\d+-\\d+/\\d+")           # a whole number, a hyphen, a fraction

#> [1] "4-3/4"

str_detect(c("1/4 percentage point", "1/2 percentage points"), "percentage points?")

#> [1] TRUE TRUE

str_extract(c("year 2026", "26"), "\\d{4}")   # {4} : exactly four digits

#> [1] "2026" NA




Quantifier: a mark after a piece (one character, a class in brackets, or a group) saying how many times it may repeat: + one or more, * zero or more, ? zero or one, {4} exactly four.
str_extract() returns the first match in each string, or NA. str_extract_all() returns every match, as a list with one element per string (the [[1]]).

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Anchors and word boundaries



R Console; needs stringr

s <- c("rate", "the rate rose", "moderate", "rates")
str_detect(s, "rate")             # the literal also matches inside other words


#> [1] TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE

str_detect(s, "\\brate\\b")       # \\b : the edge of a word

#> [1]  TRUE  TRUE FALSE FALSE

str_detect(s, "^rate$")           # ^ : start of the text; $ : end of the text

#> [1]  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE




Anchor: ^ pins the pattern to the start of the text and $ to the end. With both, the whole string must match. Inside brackets, ^ means NOT.
Word boundary \\b: the edge between a letter, digit or underscore and anything else: a space, a punctuation mark, or the start or end of the text.
False positive: text the pattern catches but should skip, such as “moderate” when you want the word “rate”. False negative: text it misses but should catch, such as “rates” under \\brate\\b.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Capture groups ( )



R Console; needs stringr

rates <- c("4-3/4", "1-1/2", "5")             # rates as the Fed writes them
m <- str_match(rates, "(\\d+)-(\\d+)/(\\d+)")  # whole number, numerator, denominator
m


#>      [,1]    [,2] [,3] [,4]
#> [1,] "4-3/4" "4"  "3"  "4" 
#> [2,] "1-1/2" "1"  "1"  "2" 
#> [3,] NA      NA   NA   NA

as.numeric(m[, 2]) + as.numeric(m[, 3]) / as.numeric(m[, 4])   # 4 + 3/4 = 4.75

#> [1] 4.75 1.50   NA




Capture group: a part of the pattern inside ( ). str_match() returns the whole match in column 1, then one column per group, in the order the groups open.
The groups split “4-3/4” into 4, 3 and 4, so the last line can compute 4 + 3/4 = 4.75.
“5” has no fraction, so the pattern finds no match and the whole row is NA.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Alternatives |



R Console; needs stringr

# phrases from the Fed statements of 8 Aug 2006, 22 Mar 2023 and 16 Dec 2008
phrases <- c("keep its target for the federal funds rate at 5-1/4 percent",
             "raise the target range for the federal funds rate to 4-3/4 to 5 percent",
             "establish a target range for the federal funds rate of 0 to 1/4 percent")
str_match(phrases, "(?:at|to|of) ([0-9/-]+) percent")


#>      [,1]               [,2]   
#> [1,] "at 5-1/4 percent" "5-1/4"
#> [2,] "to 5 percent"     "5"    
#> [3,] "to 1/4 percent"   "1/4"




at|to|of matches at, to or of. (?: ) groups the three words without adding a column, so the number lands in column 2.
Rows 2 and 3 return only the upper end of the range:

The pattern needs a space and “percent” right after the number.
After “to 4-3/4” comes “to 5”, so the search moves on and matches “to 5 percent”.
Getting both ends takes a second number group.




The same constructions come back in the chatbot’s pattern in Part 5.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
The functions for each task









Task and result
stringr
base R




find, validateTRUE or FALSE
str_detect(x, p)
grepl(p, x)


counta number per string
str_count(x, p)
lengths(regmatches(x, gregexpr(p, x)))


extractfirst match, or NA
str_extract(x, p)
regmatches(x, regexpr(p, x))


groupsmatch, then groups
str_match(x, p)
regmatches(x, regexec(p, x))


extract alla list of matches
str_extract_all(x, p)
regmatches(x, gregexpr(p, x))


replacethe new strings
str_replace_all(x, p, r)
gsub(p, r, x)





Result: what the stringr function returns. x is the text, p the pattern and r the replacement. Base R puts the pattern first, and its extract functions drop strings with no match. Chatbots write either style.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Validating a format



R Console; needs stringr

fips <- c("06037", "6037", "36109", "3610A", " 36109")   # US county codes
str_detect(fips, "^\\d{5}$")         # exactly five digits, nothing before or after


#> [1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE

str_detect(fips, "\\d{5}")           # without the anchors, " 36109" passes

#> [1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE

fips[!str_detect(fips, "^\\d{5}$")]  # the values that fail

#> [1] "6037"   "3610A"  " 36109"

dates <- c("2026-10-22", "10/22/2026", "2026-1-5")
str_detect(dates, "^\\d{4}-\\d{2}-\\d{2}$")   # year-month-day, two digits each

#> [1]  TRUE FALSE FALSE




Validation: checking that every value has the format it should, before you merge or analyze the data.
A FIPS code is the US government’s five-digit code for each US county: two digits for the state, three for the county. Read as a number, “06037” (Los Angeles County, California) becomes 6037, and a merge on it fails.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Extracting numbers



R Console; needs stringr

prices <- c("$1,250", "price: $99.99", "free", "$52,000")
str_extract(prices, "[0-9,.]+")             # digits, commas and periods


#> [1] "1,250"  "99.99"  NA       "52,000"

ages <- c("<1", "1-5", "5-10", "15+")        # age groups in a mortality table
str_match(ages, "(\\d+)(?:-(\\d+))?")         # group 1: the first number; group 2: the second

#>      [,1]   [,2] [,3]
#> [1,] "1"    "1"  NA  
#> [2,] "1-5"  "1"  "5" 
#> [3,] "5-10" "5"  "10"
#> [4,] "15"   "15" NA




Extraction: keeping only the part of each string that matches.
str_extract() returns the match as text.
str_match() returns one column per group, so “5-10” splits into “5” and “10”. (?:-(\\d+))? makes the hyphen and the second number optional together; when they are missing, group 2 is NA.
The pattern returns 1 for “<1” and 15 for “15+”. You code by hand that “<1” starts at 0 and that “15+” has no upper end.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Replacing and cleaning text



R Console; needs prices

amount <- str_extract(prices, "[0-9,.]+")       # "free" has no digits, so NA
as.numeric(str_replace_all(amount, ",", ""))    # drop the commas, then convert


#> [1]  1250.00    99.99       NA 52000.00

str_squish("  Federal   Reserve \n Board ")     # \n: a line break; result: one space between words

#> [1] "Federal Reserve Board"

# month/day/year becomes year-month-day
str_replace(c("10/22/2026", "01/05/2026"), "(\\d{2})/(\\d{2})/(\\d{4})", "\\3-\\1-\\2")

#> [1] "2026-10-22" "2026-01-05"




Replacement: rewriting what the pattern matches. str_replace() changes the first match, str_replace_all() every match.
Backreference: \\1, \\2 and \\3 in the replacement stand for what groups 1, 2 and 3 matched. The US writes dates month/day/year (10/22/2026), so the replacement puts the year first: 2026-10-22.
as.numeric("1,250") gives NA, which is why the commas go first.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Testing a pattern



R Console; needs stringr

should_match <- c("the federal funds rate", "longer-term interest rates")
should_skip  <- c("at a moderate pace", "to generate sustained improvement")
str_detect(should_match, "\\brate\\b")


#> [1]  TRUE FALSE

str_detect(should_skip, "\\brate\\b")

#> [1] FALSE FALSE

str_detect(should_match, "\\brates?\\b")      # ? makes the "s" optional

#> [1] TRUE TRUE

str_detect(should_skip, "\\brates?\\b")

#> [1] FALSE FALSE

str_detect(should_skip, "rate")               # without \\b, "moderate" and "generate" match

#> [1] TRUE TRUE




Test a pattern on strings with a known answer first. Goal here: the word “rate” or “rates”, and not “moderate” or “generate”.
Should-match and should-skip tests: short vectors of real strings the pattern must catch and must leave alone, rerun after every change.
\\brate\\b misses “rates” (false negative); "rate" catches both skip strings (false positives); \\brates?\\b passes both.
Copy test strings from the documents. When the corpus shows a case the pattern gets wrong, add that string to one of the two vectors.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Exercise 1

ExerciseSolution




# Exercise 1 (5 minutes). R Console; needs stringr. Answers to a survey
# question on yearly income:
income <- c("$52,000", "48500", "Income: $61,250.00", "N/A", "about 40k",
            "$1,000,000")
# 1. Validation: write ok_pat, a pattern for an answer that is only an
#    amount: an optional $, then digits and commas, then optional cents
#    (.00). Run str_detect(income, ok_pat). Alone, $ means the end of the
#    text, so write \\$ for a dollar sign.
# 2. Extraction: pull the number out of every answer with str_extract().
# 3. Replacement: drop the commas with str_replace_all(), then as.numeric().
# 4. Read the result next to income. Which answers give NA or a wrong number?
#
# Two answers to compare with the room: how many answers pass step 1, and
# what "about 40k" becomes.







R Console; needs stringr

income <- c("$52,000", "48500", "Income: $61,250.00", "N/A", "about 40k",
            "$1,000,000")
ok_pat <- "^\\$?[0-9,]+(\\.\\d{2})?$"
str_detect(income, ok_pat)


#> [1]  TRUE  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE

n <- str_extract(income, "[0-9,.]+")
as.numeric(str_replace_all(n, ",", ""))

#> [1]   52000   48500   61250      NA      40 1000000


Three answers pass: “$52,000”, “48500” and “$1,000,000”. “about 40k” becomes 40, a thousand times too small, with no warning. It fails step 1, which is how you find it.




Uses only the functions of this part. The $ needs an escape because, on its own, $ is the end anchor. Without ^ and $, “Income: $61,250.00” passes step 1. “N/A” gives NA in step 2, which is the right answer for a missing value.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
The Fed’s policy statements










The Federal Reserve (“the Fed”) is the US central bank.
Its Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) sets the policy interest rate. It meets eight times a year and publishes a statement after each meeting. A few statements follow unscheduled meetings.
The federal funds rate is the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans. The Fed steers it.
The target range is the band the FOMC announces for that rate. “4-3/4 to 5 percent” means 4.75 to 5. Before 16 December 2008 the FOMC announced a single number.
The file fomc_statements.csv has one row per statement: 171 statements, 31 Jan 2006 to 16 Sep 2026, 165 of them after scheduled meetings.



Screenshot: federalreserve.gov, statement of 22 March 2023 (public domain).

This is the file the scraping session built. The meeting came 12 days after Silicon Valley Bank failed, which is why paragraph 2 opens “The U.S. banking system is sound and resilient.”

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Finding a word in 171 statements



R Console, in the 16-text-regex folder; needs stringr; reads fomc_statements.csv (date, url, words, text, scheduled)

fomc <- read.csv("fomc_statements.csv")
dim(fomc)


#> [1] 171   5

c(inflation = sum(str_detect(fomc$text, "inflation")),
  Inflation = sum(str_detect(fomc$text, "Inflation")),
  either    = sum(str_detect(fomc$text, regex("inflation", ignore_case = TRUE))))

#> inflation Inflation    either 
#>       165        99       168

fomc$n_infl <- str_count(fomc$text, regex("inflation", ignore_case = TRUE))
summary(fomc$n_infl)

#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>   0.000   5.000   8.000   7.795  10.500  17.000

fomc$date[which(fomc$n_infl == 0)]   # which(): the positions where the condition is TRUE

#> [1] "2007-08-17" "2020-03-03" "2020-03-23"




Literal pattern: a pattern with no metacharacters. Matching is case-sensitive: 165 statements contain “inflation”, 99 “Inflation”, 168 either.
str_detect() gives TRUE or FALSE per statement, and sum() counts the TRUEs. str_count() gives the number of matches per statement, a new column n_infl (0 to 17, median 8).
The three statements without “inflation” all followed unscheduled meetings: 17 Aug 2007, and 3 and 23 Mar 2020, as the coronavirus spread.



Paragraphs inside text are separated by a blank line (“”). The three statements with no “inflation” are the unscheduled 17 Aug 2007 and 23 Mar 2020 and the emergency cut of 3 Mar 2020.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
section: False positives in a large text
text:
False positives in a large text



R Console; needs fomc

sum(str_count(fomc$text, "rate"))


#> [1] 982

sum(str_count(fomc$text, "\\brate\\b"))

#> [1] 705

caught <- unlist(str_extract_all(fomc$text, "[a-z]*rate[a-z]*"))   # every word containing "rate"
head(sort(table(caught), decreasing = TRUE), 6)

#> caught
#>       rate   moderate      rates moderately  moderated   generate 
#>        705        144         58         42         21          3




The literal “rate” matches 982 times, the whole word 705 times. The other 277 are 58 “rates”, which you may want (\\brates?\\b keeps them), and 219 inside other words, such as “moderate” (144).
A false positive is text the pattern catches but should skip. In a short test vector you see one at a glance. In 171 statements, a table of everything the pattern caught shows them.
unlist() puts every statement’s matches in one vector, so table() can count them.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Splitting text into words



R Console; needs stringr and fomc

i <- which(fomc$date == "2023-03-22")                         # the row of the 22 Mar 2023 statement
fomc$year <- as.numeric(str_sub(fomc$date, 1, 4))             # the year, used in Exercise 2
tokens <- str_extract_all(str_to_lower(fomc$text), "[a-z]+")  # every run of letters
head(tokens[[i]], 12)


#>  [1] "recent"     "indicators" "point"      "to"         "modest"    
#>  [6] "growth"     "in"         "spending"   "and"        "production"
#> [11] "job"        "gains"

length(tokens[[i]])

#> [1] 364




Token: one unit of text after splitting, here a word in lower case. Extracting every run of letters does the split: spaces, punctuation and numbers are left out.
str_to_lower() comes first so “Inflation” and “inflation” count as one word. tokens is a list with one vector of words per statement, and [[i]] picks one.
The apostrophe is not a letter, so “Committee’s” becomes two tokens, “committee” and “s”.



The file’s words column says 365 for this statement. It counts words differently, which is why the slides say tokens.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Word counts and stop words



R Console; needs tokens and the stopwords package

all_words <- unlist(tokens)
length(all_words)


#> [1] 73839

head(sort(table(all_words), decreasing = TRUE), 8)

#> all_words
#>       the       and        to        of committee        in inflation      will 
#>      5320      2854      2576      2382      1706      1534      1330       950

stop_words <- stopwords::stopwords("en")     # pkg::fun(): a package's function without library()
kept <- all_words[!all_words %in% stop_words & nchar(all_words) > 1]   # !x %in% y: x is not in y
head(sort(table(kept), decreasing = TRUE), 8)

#> kept
#> committee inflation  economic      rate   federal    policy    market   percent 
#>      1706      1330       842       705       686       649       642       619




Stop words: very common words dropped before counting (“the”, “of”, “will”). The package’s default English list (Snowball) has 175.
Term frequency: a word’s count divided by all tokens. “inflation” is 1,330 of 73,839, or 1.8 percent.
nchar() counts characters. nchar(all_words) > 1 drops 1,793 more one-letter tokens: the s of “Committee’s” and “U.S.”, and middle initials such as the H in Jerome H. Powell (each statement ends by naming the members who voted).
The stop list also drops “not” and “no”, which reverse a sentence, and “against”, which is on the negative word list used for tone.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Exercise 2

ExerciseSolution




# Exercise 2 (5 minutes). R Console; needs fomc (with its year column) and
# tokens from the previous slides.
# Which words appear in the statements for the first time in 2022?
#
# 1. Put the words of the 2022 statements in one vector:
#      w22 <- unlist(tokens[fomc$year == 2022])
# 2. Put the words of every statement before 2022 in a second vector
#    called before.
# 3. Keep the 2022 words that are not in the vector before (use %in% and !).
# 4. Count them with table() and sort them, largest first.
#
# Two answers to compare with the room: the most frequent new word, and the
# new words that are people's names.







R Console; needs fomc and tokens

w22    <- unlist(tokens[fomc$year == 2022])
before <- unlist(tokens[fomc$year < 2022])
new    <- w22[!w22 %in% before]
head(sort(table(new), decreasing = TRUE), 16)


#> new
#>       war    russia   ukraine attentive  invasion    issued      cook  creating 
#>         8         7         7         6         6         6         5         5 
#>         d jefferson      lisa         n    philip  weighing      barr   collins 
#>         5         5         5         5         5         5         4         4


“war” (8), then “russia” and “ukraine” (7 each) and “invasion” (6): from 16 Mar 2022 the statements say “The invasion of Ukraine by Russia is causing tremendous human and economic hardship.” The names belong to four new voting members of the committee (Lisa D. Cook, Philip N. Jefferson, Michael S. Barr, Susan M. Collins); d and n are their middle initials.




Each statement lists the members who voted. Lisa D. Cook and Philip N. Jefferson appear from 15 Jun 2022, Michael S. Barr and Susan M. Collins from 27 Jul 2022; “d” and “n” are middle initials. Of the 2,886 words in the 2022 statements, 105 are new, 27 different words. The exercise needs no stop words, so a student whose stopwords install failed can still do it.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
A finance word list



R Console; reads lm_words.csv

lm_words <- read.csv("lm_words.csv")         # word, list: "positive" or "negative"; lower case
table(lm_words$list)


#> 
#> negative positive 
#>     2345      347

pos <- lm_words$word[lm_words$list == "positive"]
neg <- lm_words$word[lm_words$list == "negative"]
c("liability", "tax", "cost") %in% neg      # three words a general-purpose list calls negative

#> [1] FALSE FALSE FALSE




Word list (dictionary): a fixed list of words tied to a category. Counting the words on a positive and a negative list gives a statement’s tone.
Loughran & McDonald (JF, 2011) built the lists for 10-Ks, the yearly report every listed US company files with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the US regulator of stock markets).
Finding. In 10-Ks from 1994 to 2008, a general-purpose list (the Harvard General Inquirer, built for psychology and sociology) flagged many words as negative. Almost three-fourths of them, such as tax, cost and liability, are not negative in financial text.
Takeaway: a word list built for one kind of text misreads another. Shapiro & Wilson (REStud, 2022) used these lists on the Fed’s meeting transcripts, and the next slides apply them to the statements.


Free for use in academic research; commercial licences from the authors (sraf.nd.edu).

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Net tone of each statement

Net tone: positive words minus negative words, per 100 tokens.




R Console; needs fomc, tokens, pos and neg

net_tone <- function(w) 100 * (sum(w %in% pos) - sum(w %in% neg)) / length(w)
j <- which(fomc$date == "2008-12-16")
w <- tokens[[j]]
w[w %in% neg]


#> [1] "deteriorated" "declined"     "strained"     "weakened"     "diminished"  
#> [6] "declines"     "weaker"       "weak"

w[w %in% pos]

#> [1] "stability"     "exceptionally"

net_tone(w)

#> [1] -1.488834

fomc$tone <- sapply(tokens, net_tone)        # sapply(): the function on each statement's words
fomc[c(which.min(fomc$tone), which.max(fomc$tone)), c("date", "tone")]   # lowest, highest

#>           date      tone
#> 24  2008-09-16 -2.727273
#> 130 2021-07-28  2.057613



On 16 Dec 2008, during the financial crisis, the committee cut its target to a range of 0 to 1/4 percent; the statement has 403 tokens. The two positive words come from set phrases: “price stability” and “exceptionally low”.


The lowest, 16 Sep 2008, came the day after Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy. Its 220 tokens contain 1 positive and 7 negative words.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Drawing net tone over time



R Console; needs fomc with its tone column

par(mar = c(2.5, 4.5, 0.8, 0.5))               # margins in lines: bottom, left, top, right
plot(as.Date(fomc$date), fomc$tone, type = "h", ylim = c(-3.4, 2.8),
     xlab = "", ylab = "Net tone per 100 tokens", las = 1)    # "h": one bar per statement
abline(h = 0, col = "grey60")
lab <- which(fomc$date %in% c("2008-09-16", "2020-03-03", "2021-07-28"))
text(as.Date(fomc$date[lab]), fomc$tone[lab], c("16 Sep 2008", "3 Mar 2020", "28 Jul 2021"),
     pos = c(1, 3, 3), cex = 1, xpd = NA)




type = "h" draws one vertical bar from 0 to each statement’s tone.
text() labels three statements: the lowest (16 Sep 2008), the highest (28 Jul 2021) and 3 Mar 2020, a rate cut between scheduled meetings.
pos = 1 puts a label below its bar and pos = 3 above it. xpd = NA lets a label run outside the box.



The plot is on the next slide.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Net tone of 171 statements, 2006–2026






Net tone per 100 tokens (Loughran-McDonald lists), one bar per statement: 103 above zero, 54 below, 14 at zero. Lowest: 16 Sep 2008, the day after the US bank Lehman Brothers failed. Highest: 28 Jul 2021. 3 Mar 2020, a rate cut between scheduled meetings as the coronavirus spread, still ranks 8th most positive.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
The prompt and the reply

I have a data frame in R called fomc with a column text that holds the full text of every FOMC statement since 2006, one statement per row. Each statement says what the Fed decided about its policy rate, for example: “the Committee decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate to 4-3/4 to 5 percent.” Write R code with stringr that extracts the target range from each statement into two numeric columns, lower and upper (here 4.75 and 5).



chat_reply.R in the zip: steps 1 to 3 of the reply's code, unchanged; the lines above them define num and to_num()

# 1. Isolate the part of the statement describing the decision on the funds rate
seg <- str_extract(
  fomc$text,
  regex("decided.*?federal funds rate.*?percent\\b", ignore_case = TRUE, dotall = TRUE)
)
# 2. Pull out "to/at/of X [to Y] percent"
pat <- str_c("\\b(?:to|at|of)\\s+(", num, ")(?:\\s+to\\s+(", num, "))?\\s+percent\\b")
m   <- str_match(seg, pat)
# 3. Convert to numeric
first  <- to_num(m[, 2])
second <- to_num(m[, 3])
fomc$lower <- first
fomc$upper <- ifelse(is.na(second), first, second)


The reply: “For your example, "...to 4-3/4 to 5 percent." gives lower = 4.75 and upper = 5.” The prompt shows one example sentence and gives no other statements to test the code on. What follows reads num, step 1 and step 2 in turn. The full reply is on the session page.

Reply from Claude (claude-sonnet-5-5) through Anthropic’s API, 20 October 2026, to the prompt shown. The same prompt in the chat at claude.ai can return different code.

This is the chatbot the course recommended. Students will get different code if they paste the prompt; the steps that follow apply to any reply.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Reading the number pattern



R Console, in the 16-text-regex folder; needs stringr and fomc

source("chat_reply.R")      # runs the reply's code, unchanged
str_view(c("5", "1/4", "4-3/4", "0.25"), num)


#> [1] │ <5>
#> [2] │ <1/4>
#> [3] │ <4-3/4>
#> [4] │ <0.25>

to_num(c("4-3/4", "1/4", "5", "0"))

#> [1] 4.75 0.25 5.00 0.00





num: the reply’s pattern for one number as the Fed writes it (“5”, “1/4”, “4-3/4”). Step 2 uses it twice, for the lower and the upper limit.
source() runs every line of a script file. chat_reply.R defines num, to_num(), seg and pat, and adds lower and upper to fomc.
Known-answer test: inputs whose right output you know before running. In str_view() all four strings match in full, and to_num() returns 4.75, 0.25, 5 and 0, as expected.
to_num() (in chat_reply.R) splits “4-3/4” into 4, 3 and 4 and returns 4 + 3/4.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Greedy and lazy matching



R Console; needs fomc and seg from chat_reply.R

i <- which(fomc$date == "2023-03-22")
greedy <- str_extract(fomc$text[i], regex("decided.*percent", dotall = TRUE))
lazy   <- str_extract(fomc$text[i], regex("decided.*?percent", dotall = TRUE))
c(nchar(greedy), nchar(lazy))       # nchar() counts characters


#> [1] 926  82

lazy

#> [1] "decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate to 4-3/4 to 5 percent"

identical(lazy, seg[i])             # the reply's step 1 gives the same text

#> [1] TRUE




Step 1 of the reply cuts the decision sentence out of each statement with lazy .*?.
Greedy .* takes as many characters as it can. Here greedy runs 926 characters, to the last “percent” in the statement (“…returning inflation to its 2 percent”).
Lazy .*? takes as few as it can.
dotall = TRUE lets . match a line break (“\n”). Paragraphs in text are separated by line breaks, so with dotall a match can run from one paragraph into the next.
Why the reply stops at the first “percent” after “federal funds rate”: “This keeps it from picking up other numbers in the statement, such as the 2 percent inflation goal, ‘25 basis points’, or the discount rate.” A basis point is 0.01 percentage point; the discount rate is the rate the Fed charges banks that borrow from it.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Reading the range pattern



R Console; needs seg, pat and i

str_match(seg[i], pat)              # the reply's step 2


#>      [,1]                    [,2]    [,3]
#> [1,] "to 4-3/4 to 5 percent" "4-3/4" "5"





str_c() joins strings end to end (base R paste0()). pat pastes in num, the previous slide’s number pattern, once per limit.
On 22 March 2023, group 1 is “4-3/4” (the lower limit) and group 2 is “5” (the upper). to_num() turns them into 4.75 and 5.
The second group is optional. A single target such as “at 5-1/4 percent”, the form used before December 2008, also matches, and the reply then sets upper equal to lower.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
The reply’s tests on 171 statements



R Console; needs fomc after source("chat_reply.R")

sum(is.na(fomc$upper))                         # the reply's test 1 prints these rows; here we count them


#> [1] 32

summary(fomc[, c("lower", "upper")])           # the reply's test 2

#>      lower           upper      
#>  Min.   :0.000   Min.   :0.250  
#>  1st Qu.:0.000   1st Qu.:0.250  
#>  Median :1.000   Median :1.250  
#>  Mean   :1.939   Mean   :2.128  
#>  3rd Qu.:4.250   3rd Qu.:4.500  
#>  Max.   :5.250   Max.   :5.500  
#>  NAs    :32      NAs    :32

sum(fomc$lower > fomc$upper, na.rm = TRUE)     # the reply's test 3: lower <= upper

#> [1] 0




The reply suggests three tests: print the NA rows (fomc[is.na(fomc$upper), "text"]), run summary(), and verify lower <= upper.
It expects NA only for “a few unscheduled statements about liquidity facilities”. There are 32, and reading them shows wordings the pattern misses.
summary() shows values from 0 to 5.5 percent, all plausible for a policy rate, and no row has lower above upper.
The tests cannot say whether the other 139 values are right.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Comparing with FRED



R Console; needs fomc after the reply's code; reads fred_target_range.csv

fred <- read.csv("fred_target_range.csv")                # date, lower, upper: one row per day
k <- match(as.Date(fomc$date) + 1, as.Date(fred$date))    # + 1: the day after each statement
fomc$fred_lower <- fred$lower[k]
fomc$fred_upper <- fred$upper[k]
fomc$agree <- fomc$lower == fomc$fred_lower & fomc$upper == fomc$fred_upper
table(fomc$agree, useNA = "ifany")


#> 
#> FALSE  TRUE  <NA> 
#>     9   130    32

fomc$date[which(!fomc$agree)]

#> [1] "2014-03-19" "2014-04-30" "2014-06-18" "2014-07-30" "2014-09-17"
#> [6] "2014-10-29" "2019-12-11" "2020-01-29" "2022-06-15"




FRED, the free data service of the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, gives the target for every day: DFEDTAR, the single target to 15 Dec 2008 (copied into both columns), then DFEDTARL and DFEDTARU, the lower and upper limits.
match() finds the position of each statement’s next day among FRED’s dates. Adding 1 to a date gives the next day. Since 2017 a new range takes effect the day after the statement, so the next day is the first day FRED shows it.
agree is TRUE for 130 statements (both limits equal FRED’s), FALSE for 9 and NA for 32 (no number found). which() skips NA, so only the nine wrong statements print. In all nine, lower equals upper, so the reply’s lower <= upper test passes on every one.



Since March 2017 a new range takes effect, and appears in FRED, the day after the statement (30 changes). From 2006 to 2016 FRED shows it from the statement date (16 changes). On the statement date itself 106 agree.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Drawing the comparison with FRED



R Console; needs fred, and fomc with the reply's lower and upper and the FRED columns

d <- as.Date(fomc$date) + 1                    # the day after each statement
ok <- fomc$agree %in% TRUE                     # %in% TRUE: NA counts as not TRUE
bad <- fomc$agree %in% FALSE
par(mar = c(2.5, 4.5, 0.5, 0.5))               # margins in lines: bottom, left, top, right
plot(as.Date(fred$date), fred$upper, type = "s", col = "grey60", ylim = c(0, 6),
     xlab = "", ylab = "Target, percent", las = 1)    # "s": steps, flat between decisions
lines(as.Date(fred$date), fred$lower, type = "s", col = "grey60")
points(d[ok], fomc$upper[ok], pch = 16, cex = 0.7)
points(d[bad], fomc$lower[bad], pch = 4, cex = 1.4, lwd = 2, col = "firebrick")
segments(d[bad], fomc$fred_lower[bad], d[bad], fomc$lower[bad], col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)

title: 16 · Text I: regex
section: Two hyphens that look the same
text:
Two hyphens that look the same



R Console; needs fomc, seg and num from chat_reply.R

j <- which(fomc$date == "2025-12-10")
str_view(seg[j], num)


#> [1] │ decided to lower the target range for the federal funds rate by <1/4> percentage point to <3-1/2> to <3>‑<3/4> percent

utf8ToInt(str_extract(seg[j], "3.3/4"))     # . matches either hyphen; utf8ToInt(): each code point

#> [1]   51 8209   51   47   52

utf8ToInt("3-3/4")                           # typed with the hyphen key

#> [1] 51 45 51 47 52

sum(str_detect(fomc$text, "\u2011"))         # statements with character 8209

#> [1] 34



In the str_view() output, “3-1/2” is one match but “3‑3/4” is two, <3> and <3/4>: num stops at the look-alike hyphen, so the row is NA.











Code point: the number a computer stores for each character. Unicode is the standard list of them.
Character 8209: a non-breaking hyphen. Web pages use it to keep “3‑3/4” on one line. In R, "\u2011" writes it: 2011 is 8209 in hexadecimal (base 16), the form Unicode lists use.
The - in a pattern matches only character 45.




The Fed’s pages use character 8209 fifty times, in 34 statements from July 2015 on, and in 12 of them it sits inside a number.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Fixing the reply’s code



R Console; needs fomc, num, to_num() and the FRED columns

# 1. the look-alike hyphen (character 8209) becomes "-"
fomc$text <- str_replace_all(fomc$text, "\u2011", "-")
# 2. stop at the period; 3. three verbs, no "federal funds rate"
seg <- str_extract(fomc$text, regex("(?:decided|maintain|reaffirmed)[^.]*?percent\\b",
                                    ignore_case = TRUE))
# 3. no "to/at/of" before the number
m <- str_match(seg, str_c("(", num, ")(?:\\s+to\\s+(", num, "))?\\s+percent\\b"))
fomc$lower <- to_num(m[, 2])
fomc$upper <- ifelse(is.na(m[, 3]), fomc$lower, to_num(m[, 3]))
fomc$agree <- fomc$lower == fomc$fred_lower & fomc$upper == fomc$fred_upper
table(fomc$agree, useNA = "ifany")


#> 
#> TRUE <NA> 
#>  170    1




Change 1: every look-alike hyphen (character 8209) becomes “-”. This fixes the 12 hyphen rows.
Change 2: [^.]*?, as few characters as possible that are not a period, replaces .*?, and dotall goes. Inside brackets the dot is a plain period, so the match ends with its sentence. The six 2014 rows now give NA in place of a wrong number.
Change 3: step 1 accepts “maintain” and “reaffirmed” and drops “federal funds rate”, which can come after the number (“the current 0 to 1/4 percent target range for the federal funds rate”). Step 2 drops “to|at|of”, since “current 0 to 1/4” has none.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
When to use regex



Regex works well when

the text follows a format: IDs, dates, amounts, codes
the wording repeats, as in the Fed’s sentence that states the target range
you can list the variants and test each one
you need the same answer every time the code runs
the corpus is large: a pattern runs on millions of documents in seconds, for free




Use a parser or a model when

the meaning depends on context or on negation: the Fed’s “might not be strong enough” (13 Sep 2012) scores as positive
the same idea is written in more ways than you can list
the text is a web page (HTML) or data from an API (JSON), where parts sit inside other parts
the variable is a judgment call, such as whether a sentence signals that the Fed will raise its rate




Parser: a function that reads a structured format into its parts, such as jsonlite::fromJSON() for JSON or rvest::read_html() for a web page. Model: a language model, the kind of program behind a chatbot, asked to read each text and return a label, or a statistical classifier trained on texts that people labeled by hand.


A pattern gives NA or a wrong number, with no error message, when the wording or a character changes. A chatbot can write the pattern. You still read it, test it on strings from your documents, and compare its output with a second source such as FRED.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
What net tone misses

The target range has a second source, FRED, and 170 of 171 values now equal it. Net tone has no second source, so its errors show only when you read the sentences it scored. The finance word list scores each word on its own:




R Console; needs fomc

s <- str_extract(fomc$text[fomc$date == "2012-09-13"], "economic growth might not[^.]*")
str_view(s, "\\b(not|strong|improvement)\\b")


#> [1] │ economic growth might <not> be <strong> enough to generate sustained <improvement> in labor market conditions




Negation. 13 Sep 2012 (also 24 Oct and 12 Dec 2012): “strong” and “improvement” count as positive. Each word is scored on its own, so the “not” before them changes nothing.
Context. 25 Apr 2012, “the unemployment rate has declined but remains elevated”: “unemployment” and “declined” count as negative, although a falling unemployment rate is good news.
The event behind the words. 3 Mar 2020, a cut in the target range between scheduled meetings as the coronavirus spread, is the 8th most positive of 171 statements. “strong”, “achieving” and “stability” count as positive. “coronavirus” and “risks” are on neither list.



The full 13 Sep 2012 sentence opens “The Committee is concerned that”, and “concerned” is on the negative list, so the sentence nets +1. Shapiro and Wilson ignored words after “not”, ran their estimates without “unemployment”, and filtered phrases such as “price stability”; their estimates barely moved (working paper version).

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Practice
Ten exercises on the session page, with solutions behind a click. Run them after the slides’ code, which builds fomc, tokens, pos and neg from the files in the 16-text-regex folder. None needs an internet connection.

1–4 Patterns and numbers: the opening phrase by year; rate moves stated in basis points (1 basis point = 0.01 percentage point), and which come from members who voted against; the vote, such as “12 – 0”, in the 2026 statements; validating the web address (url) of each statement
5 Base R: the three fixes to the chatbot’s code, rewritten with gsub(), regmatches() and regexec()
6–7 Word counts: “inflation” as a share of tokens by year; the three word lists of Baker, Bloom & Davis (QJE, 2016) on the statements
8–9 Net tone: recomputed without unemployment, against, stability and exceptionally; the word after each “not”
10 Characters: every character with a code point above 127, such as the dash in “12 – 0”

title: 14 · Channels I: APIs
text:
Slides · Live script · Source · the project
How to get data from an API into R, from the general ideas to the specific. The session starts with what an API is and two studies built on one. It takes one World Bank request apart in the browser, then requests every page of the same series from R: access to electricity by country. With a key, it requests a year of hourly electricity demand on New York’s grid from the EIA and finds the hour of the June 2025 heat-wave peak. It ends by asking a language model, through its API, to label each of the 266 names in the World Bank table as an economy or a group of economies. It compares the labels with the World Bank’s own list, and asks when to call a model from R and when to have a model write R.
The project. Download 14-apis.zip, unzip it, and open 14-apis.Rproj, so that R starts in the project folder. It holds:

title: 14 · Channels I: APIs
text:
Objectives
By the end of this session you can:

Explain what an API is and when to use one instead of downloading a file or scraping a page.
Read a request URL: its endpoint, its query parameters and its key.
Read a reply’s status code and its JSON body.
Send a request from R with httr2.
Turn a JSON reply into a data frame with fromJSON().
Request every page of a long result and compare the rows with the total the API reports.
Save each raw reply with writeLines() and rebuild the table from the saved files.
Store an API key in ~/.Renviron and confirm it loaded without printing it.
Send a prompt to a language model from R.
Read the model’s reply into a data frame.
Measure a model’s labels against a reference list.
Decide when to call a model from R and when to have a model write R.
Keep API keys out of a repository and away from a coding agent.

title: 14 · Channels I: APIs
section: Three ways to get data from someone else’s computer
text:
Three ways to get data from someone else’s computer






API (application programming interface): a service that answers requests sent by a program, with a reply in a fixed structure. Server: the computer that holds the data and answers requests. HTML: the text a web page is written in. JSON: a plain-text format for data.




The same series in the page built for people: the World Bank’s indicator page for access to electricity in India, with its line chart and the Download button.


A download suits a file you need once. An API suits requests you repeat or send many times. It is also the only route to data that has no download, such as a travel time between two points or a model’s reply. Scraping, reading the numbers out of a page built for people, is the route when there is neither a file nor an API.

title: 14 · Channels I: APIs
section: Who offers APIs, and which need a key or a payment
text:
Who offers APIs, and which need a key or a payment










Kind
Source
What you get
Key
Cost




Public statistics
World Bank
indicators by country and year
none
free


Public statistics
EIA

travel times, places

Model provider
a company that runs a language model

World Bank: an international development lender. It publishes indicators (data series, such as access to electricity) for 217 economies (countries and territories). EIA: the US government’s statistics agency for energy (the Energy Information Administration). Platform: a company whose website or app is where people search, post or trade. Language model: the program behind a chat assistant. Key: a private string that identifies you to the service and counts your requests.

Two more statistical sources with APIs, often used in economics: Eurostat, the European Union’s statistics office (no key), and FRED, a database of economic series from the St. Louis branch of the US central bank (a free key).

title: 14 · Channels I: APIs
section: What a script gains over a manual download
text:
What a script gains over a manual download



The script records the request: its web address (URL) names the series, the places and the years.
The script saves each reply as it arrived, so you can rebuild the table without asking again.
When the source revises its numbers, you run the script again.
Some data have no download, such as travel times or a model’s reply. A script can request them.

title: 14 · Channels I: APIs
section: Travel speeds in 180 Indian cities, from Google Maps
text:
Travel speeds in 180 Indian cities, from Google Maps


Akbar, Couture, Duranton & Storeygard (AER, 2023)


Question

How fast can people travel by car within Indian cities, and how much does traffic slow them?

What they did

They sent 57 million requests to Google Maps’ API: 2.7 million car trips in 180 cities, each at about 21 departure times.
One trip in three ended at a business or landmark listed on Google Places; the rest joined random points.
They compared these times with trips people actually took.

Finding

Average travel speed differs widely from one city to another.
Most of that difference comes from how fast cars move on empty roads; congestion, the slowdown from traffic, explains less.
Larger, denser cities are slower, only partly because of congestion.










Takeaway: an API can produce data no agency publishes, and the authors compared it with records of real trips before using it.

title: 14 · Channels I: APIs
section: Early Twitter users by county, from Twitter’s API
text:
Early Twitter users by county, from Twitter’s API


Fujiwara, Müller & Schwarz (JEEA, 2024)


Question

Did Twitter change how people in the US voted?

What they did

Twitter (now X) use grew quickly after South by Southwest (SXSW), a festival in Austin, Texas, in March 2007.
They pulled the profiles of about 658,000 followers of the festival’s account through Twitter’s API.
Join dates and typed locations placed early users in US counties.
Counties with more sign-ups during the 2007 festival had more Twitter users years later.
Those sign-ups are unrelated to how counties voted before Twitter, so the study uses them to compare votes across counties.

Finding

Twitter lowered the vote share of the Republican Party, one of the two main US parties, in the 2016 and 2020 presidential elections, with little effect on elections to Congress (the US legislature).










Takeaway: an API returns what the platform records (here, what users typed in their profiles), and the researcher decides what each field measures.

title: 14 · Channels I: APIs
text:
A request and its reply








GET: the kind of request that asks for data, with everything written in the URL.
Reply, also called a response: what comes back.
Status code: a three-digit number that says if the request worked, such as 200.



Header: a labelled line sent with a request or reply, apart from the data, such as the body’s format (content-type) or how many requests you have left.
Body: the data itself.

title: 14 · Channels I: APIs
section: Requesting India’s access to electricity in your browser
text:
Requesting India’s access to electricity in your browser

The request. Open this address in your browser to send a request to the World Bank’s server: https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/IND/indicator/EG.ELC.ACCS.ZS?date=2023&format=json






The reply. The text on the left is the body of the server’s reply, in JSON. Here the browser indents it (Pretty-print ticked); other browsers show one long line or a tree you can expand. The status code (200, it worked) arrives too but stays out of view.
In JSON (JavaScript Object Notation), names and values come in pairs ("value": 99.5). Braces { } hold one record; square brackets [ ] hold a list.
Hands up: what number do you see, and what does it measure?

title: 14 · Channels I: APIs
section: The parts of the request URL
text:
The parts of the request URL







Endpoint: the web address that answers one kind of request.
Query parameter: a named option after the ? that narrows what comes back. date=2000:2023 asks for a range of years.
Without format=json, the World Bank replies in XML, another text format.
Indicator code: the World Bank’s name for one series. EG.ELC.ACCS.ZS is “Access to electricity (% of population)”.
This API needs no key. The EIA takes its key as one more parameter (api_key=...), and model providers take it in a header.


Documentation: the World Bank’s Indicators API · the EIA’s API

title: 14 · Channels I: APIs
section: Reading the reply in JSON format
text:
Reading the reply in JSON format






The reply to the India request has two parts: page information first, then the records.
The country’s name sits one level down, inside "country".
A CSV holds one flat table, so it cannot carry these two parts or values inside values.

title: 14 · Channels I: APIs
text:
Status codes in every reply








Code
Meaning
Example




200
it worked
the India request


400
the server cannot read the request



401, 403
the key is missing or refused
the EIA with no key: 403, "API_KEY_MISSING"


404
no such address
a misspelled path, /v2/countryy/IND/...


429
more requests than the service allows per minute, hour or day
the EIA’s shared DEMO_KEY, used up: "OVER_RATE_LIMIT"


500 and above
the server failed; try again later
a 5,000-row EIA page: 504 after 61 seconds



httr2, the R package used below, stops with an error at 400 and above. A 200 can still hold an error message in its body.
A browser shows the status of every request in its developer tools: open them (right-click the page, then Inspect), choose the Network tab, and reload the page.

title: 14 · Channels I: APIs
text:
Long results arrive in pages
Replace IND with all in the request to get one row for each of 217 economies and 49 groups of economies, such as regions and income groups. The reply starts "page": 1, "pages": 6, "per_page": 50, "total": 266.

Pagination: a long result split into pages, which you request one after another with page=1, page=2, and so on.
total counts the rows on all pages. pages counts the requests at per_page rows each.
You have every row when your count equals total.

title: 14 · Channels I: APIs
text:
Rate limits on requests

Rate limit: the most requests a service accepts from you per minute, hour or day. Above it, the reply is 429.
The World Bank code in this session waits one second between requests.



Two header lines of an EIA reply sent with DEMO_KEY, a key everyone shares

x-ratelimit-limit: 10
x-ratelimit-remaining: 2


In these two lines the limit is 10 requests, and 2 are left. The headers do not say over what period.
The EIA counts them per internet address, and a classroom shares one, so the class reads the saved replies.

The EIA’s API also accepts api_key=DEMO_KEY, a key shared by everyone. Its replies reported a limit of 10 requests (x-ratelimit-limit: 10), counted per internet address, and a classroom on one network shares a single address, so it is often used up. Register for your own key (Part 4) instead.

title: 14 · Channels I: APIs
section: Terms of use for the data an API returns
text:
Terms of use for the data an API returns
Terms of use: the rules a source sets on what you may do with its data. Read them before you build a dataset on an API.








Source
Terms
What they mean for you




World Bank
Creative Commons Attribution licence
reuse it, with credit to the source


EIA
US government work, in the public domain (no copyright)
use it freely; the EIA asks for a source line


Google Maps Platform
its terms of service
you may not store what it returns, apart from a few short-term exceptions


Twitter (now X)
its developer terms
free research access ended



Sources: World Bank data licences; EIA copyright and reuse; Google Maps Platform terms; X developer terms.
The World Development Indicators carry the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence. The EIA’s data are in the public domain; the EIA asks users to cite it as “Source: U.S. Energy Information Administration (date)”. Google’s terms restrict storing or caching what its Maps services return. Twitter ended its free access for researchers.

title: 14 · Channels I: APIs
section: Sending the request from R with httr2
text:
Sending the request from R with httr2



R Console; needs internet and the httr2 package

# install.packages(c("httr2", "jsonlite"))   # once; jsonlite does not come with httr2
library(httr2)
req <- request("https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/all/indicator/EG.ELC.ACCS.ZS")
req <- req_url_query(req, date = 2023, format = "json", per_page = 100, page = 1)
req
#> <httr2_request>
#> GET https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/all/indicator/EG.ELC.ACCS.ZS?date=2023&format=json&per_page=100&page=1
#> Body: empty
resp <- req_perform(req)
resp_status(resp)
#> [1] 200



The request: access to electricity (% of population) in 2023 for every country and group (country/all), page 1 at 100 rows a page.
httr2: an R package that writes and sends web requests.
request() takes the address. req_url_query() adds the parameters after the ?.
Printing req shows the exact URL. Nothing has been sent yet.
req_perform() sends it and waits for the reply. resp_status() reads the status code.

title: 14 · Channels I: APIs
section: A status 200 whose body holds an error
text:
A status 200 whose body holds an error



R Console, in the 14-apis folder; needs internet and httr2

bad <- request("https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/all/indicator/EG.ELC.ACCS.ZZ")
bad <- req_url_query(bad, date = 2023, format = "json")
resp_bad <- req_perform(bad)
resp_status(resp_bad)
#> [1] 200
writeLines(resp_body_string(resp_bad))
#> [{"message":[{"id":"120","key":"Invalid value","value":"The provided parameter value is not valid"}]}]
# no network? writeLines(readLines("saved/wb_bad_code.json")) shows the same body



The indicator code ends in ZZ instead of ZS.
resp_body_string() returns the reply’s body as text.
"key":"Invalid value" names the error. This "key" is a field of the JSON, unrelated to API keys.
The misspelled path countryy returns status 404, and req_perform() stops R with HTTP 404 Not Found.
This 200 passes req_perform() with no error. The parsing steps below fail on it later with subscript out of bounds, a message that does not name the typo.
Read the body of every reply and count its rows.

title: 14 · Channels I: APIs
section: Reading the JSON reply into R with fromJSON()
text:
Reading the JSON reply into R with fromJSON()



R Console, in the 14-apis folder; needs jsonlite and resp from the httr2 request (or the saved file)

library(jsonlite)
first <- fromJSON(resp_body_string(resp))
# no network? first <- fromJSON("saved/wb_2023_p1.json") gives the same
str(first[[1]])


#> List of 6
#>  $ page       : int 1
#>  $ pages      : int 3
#>  $ per_page   : int 100
#>  $ total      : int 266
#>  $ sourceid   : chr "2"
#>  $ lastupdated: chr "2026-10-08"

d <- first[[2]]
dim(d)

#> [1] 100   8

names(d)

#> [1] "indicator"       "country"         "countryiso3code" "date"           
#> [5] "value"           "unit"            "obs_status"      "decimal"



fromJSON() turns JSON text into R lists and data frames.
first is a list, R’s container for parts of different kinds: first[[1]] holds the page information (3 pages, 266 rows in all), first[[2]] this page’s 100 records.

                  year = d$date, access = d$value)
head(wb1, 3)

#>                       country iso3 year   access

wb1[wb1$iso3 == "IND", ]

Flatten: turn nested fields into plain columns, one value per cell.

title: 14 · Channels I: APIs
section: fetch() to request and save one page, flat() to flatten it
text:
fetch() to request and save one page, flat() to flatten it



wb_functions.R (part), in the 14-apis folder; needs httr2 and jsonlite

dir.create("raw", showWarnings = FALSE)
fetch <- function(p, year, per) {
  req <- request("https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/all/indicator/EG.ELC.ACCS.ZS")
  req <- req_url_query(req, date = year, format = "json", per_page = per, page = p)
  txt <- resp_body_string(req_perform(req))
  writeLines(txt, paste0("raw/wb_", year, "_p", p, ".json"))  # the reply as sent
  Sys.sleep(1)                                                # one request a second
  fromJSON(txt)
}
flat <- function(reply) {
  d <- reply[[2]]
  data.frame(country = d$country$value, iso3 = d$countryiso3code,
             year = d$date, access = d$value)
}



Run source("wb_functions.R") to define both functions. The file ships in the project.
fetch(p, year, per) requests page p of one year at per rows a page, writes the reply to raw/ as sent, waits one second, and returns it parsed.
Raw reply: the reply exactly as the server sent it, saved before any parsing.
flat() turns one parsed reply into the four-column table.

title: 14 · Channels I: APIs
section: Requesting all pages and comparing rows with the total
text:
Requesting all pages and comparing rows with the total



R Console, in the 14-apis folder; needs internet, fetch() and flat(); writes three replies to raw/

first <- fetch(1, 2023, 100)
replies <- lapply(1:first[[1]]$pages, fetch, year = 2023, per = 100)
wb <- do.call(rbind, lapply(replies, flat))
c(rows = nrow(wb), total = first[[1]]$total)
#>  rows total
#>   266   266
wb[wb$iso3 == "IND", ]
#>     country iso3 year access
#> 139   India  IND 2023   99.5



Page 1’s information gives the number of pages (3) and the total (266).
lapply() calls fetch() once per page, passing year and per on to it.
do.call(rbind, ...) stacks the three pages into one table.
The rows received equal the total the API reports.
Rows 1 to 49 are groups of economies (regions, income and lending groups, World). Rows 50 to 266 are the 217 economies.

per_page=300 returns all 266 rows in one page, so this series needs no loop. The loop is for the series that do not fit: most APIs cap the page size, and the EIA caps it at 5,000 rows.
httr2 also has helpers for paging and rate limits. req_perform_iterative() with iterate_with_offset() requests page after page until the last one. req_throttle() spaces the requests, req_retry() sends a request again after a 429 or a 503, and req_timeout() sets how long to wait for a slow reply (a 5,000-row EIA page once returned a 504, a timeout at the server, after 61 seconds). The same table as above, with the helpers:



R Console; needs internet, httr2, jsonlite and flat()

req <- request("https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/all/indicator/EG.ELC.ACCS.ZS")
req <- req_url_query(req, date = 2023, format = "json", per_page = 100)
req <- req_throttle(req, capacity = 1, fill_time_s = 1)  # one request a second
req <- req_retry(req, max_tries = 3)                     # again after a 429 or 503
req <- req_timeout(req, 90)                              # wait up to 90 seconds
resps <- req_perform_iterative(req,
  next_req = iterate_with_offset("page",
    resp_pages = function(resp) fromJSON(resp_body_string(resp))[[1]]$pages),
  max_reqs = Inf)
wb <- do.call(rbind, lapply(resps, function(r) flat(fromJSON(resp_body_string(r)))))
nrow(wb)
