title: HW2 · What was the wind doing?
text: AI assistance is recommended on this one. See the rule near the bottom: use it, disclose it, and write the change note yourself.

title: HW2 · What was the wind doing?
text:
What happened
HW1 ended on a puzzle. The air across the Los Angeles basin was worse in early December than in the week of the fires, on days when nothing was burning anywhere in the state. And the fire’s own smoke, from two fires that burned for three weeks, was gone from the monitors within days.
Both fires were driven by the Santa Ana winds, a dry wind that blows from the desert, over the mountains, and out to sea. On the night of 7 January 2025 it gusted past 100 km/h. The rest of the winter the basin’s air mostly sat still, and Los Angeles in winter is famous for inversions: a lid of warm air that traps whatever is emitted underneath it.
Many of the sites that measure PM2.5 also measure wind, and EPA publishes that record too, every day, for every instrument. This assignment puts the two records side by side and asks: was it the wind?

title: HW2 · What was the wind doing?
text:
What you produce
One figure, and a note.
It is your HW1 figure with one new panel. Panel A is unchanged. Panel B is new: wind speed across the wind monitors, each day, summarised exactly the way panel A summarises PM2.5. Panel C is HW1’s heat map, relettered but otherwise unchanged.



Target figure


Study it before you write a line. The network’s worst days, in early December and at New Year, are days when the wind across the basin averaged under 5 km/h. The fire week is the one stretch where the basin was windy and dirty at the same time.
The note is a short file, CHANGES.md, that says what you changed from your HW1 project and why, what you checked, and how you used AI. The format is below.

title: HW2 · What was the wind doing?
text:
What you get
Your own HW1, already in the repo. Clone hw2-<your username> and your HW1 submission is sitting there as the first commit, with hw1.Rproj renamed hw2.Rproj. Nothing to download, nothing to copy across. Start from what you wrote.
Building on it is required, and it is graded. That first commit is your HW1 exactly as you handed it in, and HW2 is the change you make to it. The grader opens that commit beside your last one. Scripts that still carry your object names, your section headers and your comments read as yours, however heavily you edited them; scripts deleted and replaced by a fresh project do not. How far your HW1 was from the target costs you nothing here. If that first commit holds no R code, because you did not submit HW1 or your HW1 arrived as a zip, say so in the first line of CHANGES.md and nothing is held against you.
The HW1 solution is now posted. If your figure did not match the HW1 target, closing that gap is part of this assignment: the target is still on the HW1 page along with the rules it follows, and CHANGES.md is where you say what you repaired. Open your PNG and the target side by side at the same size and work through the differences. That comparison is the assignment as much as the wind panel is.
The wind data. One file, cut from EPA’s pre-generated annual files (daily_WIND_2024.zip and daily_WIND_2025.zip) to the same area and window as HW1’s file: every wind monitor within 150 km of the Eaton Fire, 1 December 2024 to 28 February 2025. The columns are exactly as EPA ships them.

https://arielortizbobea.github.io/assets/data/epa_wind_la_fires_2024_2025.csv

6,702 rows, 38 sites, 2.2 MB. Two parameters share the file: Parameter Code 61103 is wind speed, 61104 is wind direction. This assignment uses speed; direction waits for HW3.
The layout is not the one HW1’s file used. EPA’s download tool does not offer wind, so this file comes from a different EPA product with its own conventions:

title: HW2 · What was the wind doing?
text:
The rules the figure follows

Everything HW1’s figure encoded still holds: the window, what a monitor is, the 60-of-90-days rule, distance from the Eaton Fire, the row order, EPA’s six colours, the two summaries in panel A, the one red line at 7 January.
A wind monitor is a site plus a POC. Build the key from the three site columns and the POC. It is unique on any given day within parameter 61103, and your script checks that it is. That test is worth more than it looks: drop the 61103 filter and the file still holds a speed row and a direction row for the same instrument on the same day, so the test stops the script.
Keep the wind speed rows only, parameter 61103.
Convert knots to km/h, multiplying by 1.852. The constant lives in the parameters block, with its name.
Keep wind monitors that reported at least 60 of the 90 days, the same rule as for PM2.5.
Panel B: for each day, the mean across the wind monitors that reported, and the 10th and 90th percentile of those same readings. Axis from 0 to 30 km/h. Same lines, same colours, same key as panel A.
Layout: three rows, heights in the ratio 1 : 0.75 : 2.6, one shared set of margins so the three x axes line up. The red line runs from the top of A to the bottom of C.
Output: figures/hw2_target.png, 183 × 270 mm, 300 dpi. The page is taller than HW1’s to make room for the third row.

Panels A and B are the same drawing on two grids. Write it once as a function that takes a grid, a panel letter and an axis label, and call it twice. Session 6 was about this. It is not a rule, but the Coding score looks for it, and the alternative, a copy of panel A with edits, doubles the length of your diff.

title: HW2 · What was the wind doing?
text:
Checking as you go
Panel B draws whether or not the numbers behind it are right. Wind speed left in knots gives you the same shape, the same 7 January peak, a line about half as high, and no error anywhere. Session 10 covered the answer: the script says what it expects and stops when the data disagrees.
Put a check where this week’s data can go wrong, and write it so that it could actually fail. The size of the wind numbers is the one that matters most. The tips below give you the scale: an ordinary day across the network reads 3 to 5 km/h and the Santa Ana reads 13.
  # after the wind grid is built, in code/1_get_clean_data.R
  daily <- apply(grid_wind, 2, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
  stopifnot(median(daily) > 3,    # it is 2.7 if the conversion never ran
            median(daily) < 8)    # it is 9.1 if it ran twice
In km/h that median is 4.9 and the script carries on. Both bounds can fail on a mistake you could actually make, which is what makes the line worth writing. It also catches a parameter code mistyped as 61104, where the median comes out above 300.
Rule 2’s key test is the other one. It costs one line and it stops the script if the 61103 filter never ran. What it cannot see is a filter that ran on the wrong code, which is why the two checks are worth having together.
A check that cannot fail earns nothing. max(grid_wind) < 150 passes on knots and on km/h alike, because the fastest cell in this file is 38 km/h. stopifnot(nrow(w) == 6702) passes today, says nothing about whether what you did to the rows was right, and breaks the week EPA regenerates the file.
Printing the number of rows after each step that can drop rows, and the number of monitors before and after the 60-of-90 rule, is worth doing and worth quoting in CHANGES.md. The check the rubric looks for is one that stops.

Prose, not a diff. “Moved the scripts into code/ so the project matches the layout the assignment asks for” is a sentence; a list of changed line numbers is not.
The grader reads the note first, then compares your HW2 code with your HW1 code. Every change in the code should be in the note, and nothing in the note should be missing from the code.
Write the note yourself. A chatbot will write a flawless one from a diff in ten seconds. The point of the note is that you read the change. Ask AI to explain a line you changed, by all means. The note describes what you did, in your words.

title: HW2 · What was the wind doing?
text:
Tips
Three rows shrink your text. layout() with three or more rows quietly sets par("cex") to 0.66, so every label and every margin is a third smaller than in HW1 and the site names no longer fit. Put par(cex = 1) right after layout().
The red line has further to go. Your HW1 geometry assumed one panel above the heat map. Now there are two. Derive the top of panel A from the three layout heights rather than from the single ratio 2.6.
What “resultant” means. EPA’s daily wind speed is a vector average over the 24 hours: a day when the wind blows one way in the morning and back in the afternoon averages close to zero. That is why an ordinary day reads 3 to 5 km/h and the Santa Ana reads 13. It is the right number for this question, because it measures how far the day’s air actually moved.
The site ID in three pieces. paste0() of the three columns gives HW1’s Site ID. You do not need it this week, but it is how HW3 will match a wind monitor to a PM2.5 monitor at the same site.
Restart and source before you submit. Session > Restart R, then source("code/run_everything.R"). It must run top to bottom and write the figure. Test it the way the grader will: delete the data/ and data_clean/ folders, not just the files inside them. A fresh clone of your repo has neither, so your script has to create them before it downloads or saves anything.

title: HW2 · What was the wind doing?
text:
How to submit
Your repository is hw2-<your github username>, inside the course organization. It is already there, and your HW1 submission is already in it. Find it at https://github.com/aem6850-cornell or in the repositories list on your GitHub home page.
This is the first assignment you submit with git. Three commands, from session 7:
git clone https://github.com/aem6850-cornell/hw2-<your username>.git
# ... work, as often as you like ...
git add -A
git commit -m "what you changed"
git push
Commit in the order you work. The grader reads git log first and grades the last commit pushed before the deadline. A reasonable sequence:

Repair your HW1 figure against the HW1 target. Nothing about wind yet; the project still draws one figure and still runs.
Move the project into the layout above, if it is not already there, and source it from a restarted session.
Add the wind file to code/1_get_clean_data.R: the URL, the three character columns, the speed rows, the conversion, the checks. The figure does not change yet.
Turn panel A’s drawing into a function and call it once for panel A. The figure is identical to the previous commit’s.
Add panel B by calling the same function on the wind grid, with the three-row layout and the longer red line.

Then CHANGES.md, written last, from the history you already have. Messages like “Repair the percentile lines in panel A” and “Add wind to script 1, with the unit and key checks”. The number of commits is yours, and a step that took two tries is two commits. What is graded is that the repair, the data and the drawing are separable and in a sensible order, and that each message names what changed. If your HW1 figure already matched its target, skip step 1 and say so in the note. The whole assignment arriving as one commit costs you under the last dimension even when everything in it is right. If a push problem is what kept you to one commit, say so on the day and it is not counted against you. RStudio’s Git pane and VS Code do the same three steps with buttons; session 7 shows all three ways.
What has to be in that final commit:

code/1_get_clean_data.R
code/2_plot_figure.R
code/run_everything.R
CHANGES.md

Leave data/ and data_clean/ out; the .gitignore in your repo already does that for you. You do not need to commit the figures either. The grader clones your repo fresh, runs code/run_everything.R, which downloads both CSVs and rebuilds everything, and grades the figure your code draws.
Before you push for the last time: Session > Restart R, then source("code/run_everything.R"). If it writes the figure with no errors, you are done.
Stuck on git? Office hours, or ask in the course channel. Do not let a push problem cost you the deadline: a repo that will not push is a problem to raise on the day, not the night before.

title: HW2 · What was the wind doing?
text:
AI on this one
Recommended, from here on. The things it is good at this week, in the chat tier:

Explain the wind file. Paste the header line and the first three rows and ask what each column is. Then check the answer against EPA’s file format page.
Turn panel A into a function. Paste your panel A code and ask for a function that draws it for any grid. Read every line it gives back against the code you pasted.
Debug the shrinking text. Describe what you see. Ask why. Then check the reason in ?layout.
Explain an argument you have not used. Paste your layout() call and ask what heights does to the panels, or why the labels shrank. Then check the answer in ?layout before you believe it.
Ask where it could go wrong quietly. Give it the wind file’s header and the steps your script takes, and ask which mistakes would still draw a figure. Then ask for one line that would catch each. Read them before you keep any: several will pass on this file whatever you did, and one of them will quietly drop rows to make the data agree. Keep the ones that can fail, and say in the disclosure which you asked for and which you wrote.

Three rules, from the syllabus and session 8. Ask for the script, not the answer: a number a chatbot typed is not a result. Verify one claim per conversation, on principle, and say which in the note. Disclose. The disclosure block in your note lists the tools, what you used them for, and what you checked. Disclosed use is never penalised. Undisclosed use is misrepresentation under the syllabus and is treated as an integrity violation.

title: HW2 · What was the wind doing?
text:
Rubric
15 points. Five dimensions, three points each. The grader clones your repo into an empty folder, sources code/run_everything.R in a fresh R session, compares the figure with the target, reads the checks your script makes, and reads your note against your commits, the first of which is your HW1.

Similarity (3 points)







3
The figure is virtually identical to the target. One has to really pay attention to see any difference.


2
One or two clear differences from the target: panel B on the wrong scale or missing a summary, the red line stopping short, labels missing, a panel letter missing. Wind speed left in knots lands here, where the line has the right shape and sits a little over half as high as it should.


1
Three or more clear differences, or a panel missing, or the series does not line up with the calendar, so the wind peak falls on a day other than 7 January.


0
No figure, or a figure of something else.



Similarity is judged on what the figure encodes, not on pixel-level matching. Font sizes, margins and tick placement are not differences. Panel C is judged against the HW1 target: if your heat map was wrong in HW1, repairing it is part of this assignment and you are not scored against your own version.


Reproducibility (3 points)







3
The code runs start to finish, without any edits, and writes the figure. Paths are relative to the project root. Nothing depends on objects left over from an earlier session.


2
The code requires one minor edit to run: a stray absolute path, a folder it expected to exist, a library() call for something base R already does.


1
The code requires several edits to run, or runs with errors, or does not produce the figure.


0
The code does not run.



Two things cost points here every year. Absolute paths: read.csv("/Users/you/Desktop/hw2/data/...") works on your laptop and nowhere else; open the .Rproj and use "data/...". Session leftovers: a script that works because an object is still in your environment from twenty minutes ago is not a script that works. Restart R and source it before you push. Every time.


Coding structure (3 points)







3
The code (1) has clear and logical sections, (2) has a clearly identified parameter section that can be modified to produce slightly different versions of the output, including the new file, the parameter code and the unit conversion, (3) is well annotated, and (4) is concise but spacious: one drawing for panels A and B, not two.


2
The code has at most one of the following: (1) no clear structure, (2) parameters hard-coded within the core of the script, (3) missing key annotations, (4) too dense or too verbose.


1
The code has more than one of those.


0
There is no code, or the code cannot perform the basic steps needed to generate the output.



“A clearly identified parameter section” means the URLs, the file names, the dates, the parameter code, the knots conversion and the layout heights live together at the top of each script, named, and are used by name below.


Verification (3 points)







3
The script says what it expects of the data and stops when the data disagrees, at the places this week’s data can go wrong. At least one check could have failed on a mistake you could actually have made, and CHANGES.md says for each check what it would have caught.


2
Checking is thin: one place covered and the obvious one left open, or a bound so wide that the right answer and the wrong answer both pass, or the note lists the checks without saying what any of them would catch.


1
The only check is the one rule 2 already asks for, or every check is one that cannot fail: a row count compared with a number taken from the same run, a test that the line above ran.


0
The script makes no check of its own data.



“Checking as you go” above names the two places that matter this week and shows one of them written out. A check earns its point by being able to fail.


The note and the history (3 points)







3
The repo’s first commit is still the one the course made, and your HW2 scripts are that code edited: your object names, your section headers and your comments are still in them. The work arrives in separable commits in a sensible order, each message naming what that commit did. CHANGES.md gives every change with its reason, names the files that moved and the layout changes, and discloses the tools, the uses and the checks.


2
One of those falls short: the whole assignment arrives in a single commit, or the messages say only “update”, or the order contradicts the note, or a change in the code is missing from the note, or the file and layout changes are glossed over. A push problem you raised on the day is not counted here.


1
Two or more fall short. Also here, whatever else is true: your HW2 scripts share nothing with the first commit’s, not an object name, not a section header, not a comment, so they did not grow out of your HW1. Files you moved from the repo root into code/ count as moved, not replaced.


0
No note, or you pushed no commit of your own. Also here: the repo’s first commit is no longer the one the course made, because the repository was replaced or the history rewritten. If that first commit holds no R code, because you did not submit HW1 or your HW1 arrived as a zip, say so in the first line of CHANGES.md: you have nothing to build on, and this dimension is then scored on your commits and your note alone.





The one thing that scores below zero
AI use is recommended and must be disclosed. Undisclosed AI use, and code taken from anyone else without saying whose, are misrepresentation under the syllabus and are treated as integrity violations rather than as grading matters.

title: HW1 solution · How bad was the air?
text: This page is the instructor’s solution to HW1. Two R scripts and a master file download EPA’s raw file, clean it, and draw the target figure below. Run from a fresh clone, they write the same PNG that is posted here. The page walks through the approach and the code and lists where submissions went wrong. It then explains a mistake in the target as first posted and ends with the three scripts in full.

title: HW1 solution · How bad was the air?
text:
From download to figure
The work runs in seven steps.

Download the CSV into data/. Later runs find the file there and skip the download.
Read it with Site.ID kept as text, keep the 90 days from 1 December to 28 February, and check that the instrument key is unique on each day.
Measure each instrument’s distance from the Eaton Fire’s ignition point and sort the instruments nearest first. Give each one a row label.
Build two matrices with one row per instrument and one column per day, one of PM2.5 and one of AQI, and drop the instruments that reported on fewer than 60 days.
Save everything the figure needs as one list in data_clean/hw1_clean.rds.
Read that list back, compute the network’s daily mean and percentiles, and put each AQI value in one of EPA’s six categories.
Draw both panels into one PNG, figures/hw1_target.png.

code/1_get_clean_data.R does steps 1 to 5, and code/2_plot_figure.R does steps 6 and 7. The master file, code/run_everything.R, sources the two in order.
Downloading and cleaning happen once, and the figure gets redrawn dozens of times while you adjust margins, labels and the key. With the cleaning in its own script, each redraw runs script 2 alone, in seconds, with no download. The .rds file is the only link between the scripts. Script 2 reads all its data from that file, so it draws the same figure whether script 1 ran a minute ago or last week. A change to the drawing code cannot alter the data.

title: HW1 solution · How bad was the air?
text:
How the code is organised
hw1/
  hw1.Rproj                 open this first
  code/
    run_everything.R        master file: two source() calls
    1_get_clean_data.R      download, clean, save
    2_plot_figure.R         read, summarise, draw
  data/                     the CSV, exactly as downloaded
  data_clean/               hw1_clean.rds
  figures/                  hw1_target.png
hw1.Rproj sits at the project root. Opening it sets the working directory to hw1/, so every path in the code starts from there: "data/...", "figures/...". Raw data stays in data/, and anything the code computed goes to data_clean/.
The parameter block. Each script opens with a list called misc. Script 1’s block has the download URL, the file paths, the start and end dates, the 60-day minimum, the fire’s coordinates and the two km-per-degree constants. The block in script 2 has the file paths, the ignition date, the AQI category bounds, the six colours and their labels, the colour for no reading, and the figure’s size, point size, margins and text size. Each of these values is typed once, at the top, so a change to one of them happens on one line. Script 2 takes the window’s start and end from the .rds file, so the window is set in script 1 only. A few drawing values stay in the body of script 2: the tick dates at lines 87–88, panel A’s upper limit of 80 at lines 105 and 117, and the 2.6 in the panel heights at lines 98 and 173. The 80 and the 2.6 are each typed twice, and the two copies must change together.
The sections. Comment lines ending in ---- divide each script, and RStudio lists them in the document outline. Script 1 has three: Preliminary (parameters and folders), Get the data, and Clean, which ends by saving the list and printing a short report. In script 2 the three are Preliminary (parameters, the figures folder, reading the .rds, and the one small function), Compute daily summaries, and Create the figure. The last one has a sub-section for each panel, also marked with dashes. Each panel’s code sits in its own if (T) { } block, which lets you fold it away or run it as one piece.
Running it. From a fresh clone, open hw1.Rproj and run
source("code/run_everything.R")
or, from a terminal in hw1/, Rscript code/run_everything.R. The master file empties the workspace first, so a script that uses an object no line creates stops with an error. Script 1 creates data/ and data_clean/ and downloads the file if it is missing, and script 2 creates figures/. The code uses base R only, so there is nothing to install. On a fresh clone, script 1 prints:
42 monitors at 33 sites, reporting 60+ of the 90 days
3555 of 3780 cells have a reading (94%)
nearest 21 km, farthest 151 km from the Eaton fire
Saved: data_clean/hw1_clean.rds

title: HW1 solution · How bad was the air?
text:
The code, step by step
Each excerpt is copied from the scripts, with the file name and line numbers.

Reading the file
read.csv() guesses a type for each column. It reads Site.ID as a number, and 060371103 becomes 60371103 with no warning. colClasses keeps that one column as text from the start.


code/1_get_clean_data.R, line 56

  d <- read.csv(misc$file, colClasses = c("Site.ID" = "character"))



The window and the instrument key
The file writes dates as month/day/year text, so as.Date() needs the format spelled out. One logical index then keeps the 90 days. The key pastes site, POC and parameter code together, and stopifnot() halts the script if any instrument appears twice on the same day.


code/1_get_clean_data.R, lines 69–77

  d$date <- as.Date(d$Date, format = "%m/%d/%Y")
  d <- d[d$date >= misc$start & d$date <= misc$end, ]

  # A site is a place; a monitor is one instrument at that place, and a busy
  # site runs several. Site plus POC plus parameter names the instrument.
  # That key is unique on any given day, so every instrument can have its own
  # row in the heat map and nothing is counted twice.
  d$monitor <- paste(d$Site.ID, d$POC, d$AQS.Parameter.Code)
  stopifnot(anyDuplicated(paste(d$monitor, d$date)) == 0)



Distance from the fire and the row order
Each difference in degrees becomes kilometres through its constant, and Pythagoras gives the distance. duplicated() keeps one row per instrument, and order() sorts those rows nearest first. That sort fixes the order of panel B, so the code never names a site.


code/1_get_clean_data.R, lines 82–88

  north <- (d$Site.Latitude  - misc$fire_lat) * misc$km_lat
  east  <- (d$Site.Longitude - misc$fire_lon) * misc$km_lon
  d$km  <- sqrt(north^2 + east^2)

  # One row per monitor, nearest the fire first.
  m <- d[!duplicated(d$monitor), ]
  m <- m[order(m$km), ]



The monitor-by-day grid and the 60-day rule
tapply() builds a matrix with one row per instrument and one column per day. The factor’s levels list all 90 dates, so every day gets a column even if no instrument reported on it. The key allows one reading per instrument per day, so mean returns that reading unchanged. Indexing with [m$monitor, ] puts the rows in distance order. A day an instrument missed stays NA.


code/1_get_clean_data.R, lines 102–105

  cal     <- seq(misc$start, misc$end, by = "day")
  day     <- factor(format(d$date), levels = format(cal))
  grid_pm  <- tapply(d$pm25, list(d$monitor, day), mean)[m$monitor, ]
  grid_aqi <- tapply(d$aqi,  list(d$monitor, day), mean)[m$monitor, ]

The 60-day rule counts the readings in each row and keeps the rows with at least misc$min_days. One logical vector subsets both grids and the monitor table, so the three stay aligned.


code/1_get_clean_data.R, lines 110–113

  enough   <- apply(!is.na(grid_pm), 1, sum) >= misc$min_days
  grid_pm  <- grid_pm[enough, ]
  grid_aqi <- grid_aqi[enough, ]
  m        <- m[enough, ]



Row labels with POC brackets
Each label starts as the site name. The one site with a blank name gets its ID. Where a site has more than one instrument, the POC goes in brackets after the name. This test runs before the 60-day rule, so seven rows in the target keep a bracket although their site’s other instruments were dropped. Reseda’s [3] is the first of them.


code/1_get_clean_data.R, lines 94–98

  m$label <- m$site
  blank <- m$label == ""
  m$label[blank] <- paste("Site", m$Site.ID[blank])
  many <- m$site %in% m$site[duplicated(m$site)]
  m$label[many] <- paste0(m$site[many], " [", m$POC[many], "]")



Panel A’s daily mean and percentiles
pctl() sorts a day’s readings, which also drops the NAs, and picks one value by position. With 40 readings on a day, the 10th percentile is the 4th smallest and the 90th is the 36th.


code/2_plot_figure.R, lines 67–71

  pctl <- function(x, p) {
    x <- sort(x)
    if (length(x) == 0) return(NA)
    x[max(1, round(p * length(x)))]
  }

apply() with 2 runs down each column of the PM2.5 grid, one day at a time. Panel A then draws the two percentiles in grey and the mean in black with lines(), at lines 111–113.


code/2_plot_figure.R, lines 77–79

  avg <- apply(d$grid_pm, 2, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
  p10 <- apply(d$grid_pm, 2, pctl, p = 0.10)
  p90 <- apply(d$grid_pm, 2, pctl, p = 0.90)



Panel B’s colours
findInterval() turns each AQI value into its category number, 1 to 6, using the category lower bounds c(0, 51, 101, 151, 201, 301) from the parameter block. band[] <- keeps the matrix shape and fills it with those numbers.


code/2_plot_figure.R, lines 83–84

  band   <- d$grid_aqi
  band[] <- findInterval(d$grid_aqi, misc$breaks)

image() then gives each number a colour. Left alone, it spreads the six colours over the range of the data. Nothing in this window goes past category 4, so the six colours would stretch over categories 1 to 4, and categories 3 and 4 would come out in colours 4 and 6. A zlim running from 0.5 to 6.5 pins the range to all six categories, and category k gets colour k whatever the data contain. The matrix goes in upside down, band[nrows:1, ], because image() draws row 1 at the bottom, and t() turns it so the days run along the x axis. Cells with no reading are NA. image() leaves them undrawn, and the white background of the PNG shows through. The assignment’s tip paints the panel white with rect() before image(), which gives the same result. Line 144 of code/2_plot_figure.R keeps that call commented out because the PNG already starts white. The comment above it mentions grey because an earlier version painted missing days grey. The dates go in as plain numbers for the reason given further down.


code/2_plot_figure.R, lines 150–151

    image(x = as.numeric(d$cal), y = 1:nrows, z = t(band[nrows:1, ]), add = TRUE,
          col = misc$cols, zlim = c(0.5, length(misc$cols) + 0.5))



One date axis for both panels
The red line runs straight through both panels only if their x axes match exactly. Both panels use the same margins, set once in the parameter block.


code/2_plot_figure.R, lines 53–54

  misc$mar    <- c(2.0, 15.4, 1.4, 3.7)   # shared, so the two x axes line up;
                                          # left fits the longest site name exactly

The two plot() calls share an xlim that runs half a day either side of the window, because each heat-map cell is one day wide and centred on its date. xaxs = "i" stops plot() from adding 4 percent of padding at each end. Panel A’s call at lines 109–110 uses the same xlim and xaxs.


code/2_plot_figure.R, lines 140–141

    plot(NA, xlim = c(d$start - 0.5, d$end + 0.5), ylim = c(0.5, nrows + 0.5),
       axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")



The red line
The line is drawn once, from panel B. It starts at the bottom of B and runs up through the gap to the top of panel A, and xpd = NA lets it leave the plot region. The top end comes from the panel sizes: par("pin") is B’s plot region in inches, par("mai") its margins, and the layout heights make panel A’s figure 1/2.6 the height of B’s. Panel A carries the red “Fire begins” label at the same date, at line 122.


code/2_plot_figure.R, lines 171–176

    per_in   <- nrows / par("pin")[2]                        # B's y units per inch
    fig_b_in <- par("pin")[2] + par("mai")[1] + par("mai")[3] # B's figure height
    fig_a_in <- fig_b_in / 2.6                                # from layout heights
    a_plot   <- fig_a_in - par("mai")[1] - par("mai")[3]      # A's plot height
    y_top    <- nrows + 0.5 + per_in * (par("mai")[3] + par("mai")[1] + a_plot)
    lines(c(misc$ignite, misc$ignite), c(0.5, y_top), col = "red", lwd = 1.5, xpd = NA)



The key
One legend() call draws the key in panel B’s lower right corner. fill gives each label a coloured box. The labels and colours come from the parameter block, which holds all six categories, so the key lists each one whether or not it occurs. “No reading” and white are added at the end.


code/2_plot_figure.R, lines 160–164

      legend("bottomright", inset = 0.01, bg = "white", box.col = "grey45",
           cex = misc$cex * 0.72, y.intersp = 1,
           title = "EPA Air Quality Index (AQI):", title.adj = 0.1,
           legend = c(misc$labs, "No reading"),
           fill   = c(misc$cols, misc$no_data), border = "grey45")



The figure size
png() takes inches here, so the parameter block divides 183 and 247 mm by 25.4. The same call sets the resolution to the 300 dpi the assignment asks for. It also sets the point size, the base text size that every cex in the code scales.


code/2_plot_figure.R, lines 50–52

  misc$width  <- 183 / 25.4                # 7.20 in
  misc$height <- 247 / 25.4                # 9.72 in
  misc$pt     <- 9



code/2_plot_figure.R, lines 96–97

  png(misc$fig, width = misc$width, height = misc$height,
      units = "in", res = 300, pointsize = misc$pt)

title: HW1 solution · How bad was the air?
text:
Where submissions went wrong
Of the 39 students enrolled, 38 submitted. Each project was run from a fresh clone. Twenty-eight ran with no change to the code, some after their uploaded files were moved into the right folders, which cost nothing. Two more ran once their output folders were created, and eight needed a fix to the code before they ran. Of the 38 figures, 21 matched the target on every item the graders checked. The three lists below follow the rubric’s three dimensions, Replicability, Similarity and Coding, in that order. The counts are numbers of submissions, and some had more than one problem.

Running on a fresh machine

No download step, or the download commented out (3). Put download.file() in script 1, behind file.exists(), so a fresh clone fetches the file itself.
A broken or empty download URL (2). Copy the URL from the assignment page into the parameter block and test it from a fresh clone.
An object that existed only in the R session (2). No line of the scripts creates it, so the code ran only in the session where it was made. Restart R and source run_everything.R before you submit.
Output folders never created (4). Call dir.create("figures", showWarnings = FALSE) before the first file is written there, and the same for data/ and data_clean/.
install.packages() inside a script (1). Delete it. This figure needs base R only.
An empty run_everything.R (1). It needs two source() calls, in order.
The figure written to the wrong path (1). Write figures/hw1_target.png, with the path in the parameter block.
Reading an .rds file uploaded to the repo (1) in place of the one script 1 writes. Read the path script 1 saves to, and leave data_clean/ out of the upload.



The figure

Panels A and B on different date axes (7). Different left or right margins shift one panel, and the 7 January line breaks between them. Give both panels the same mar, the same xlim and xaxs = "i".
Category colours shifted (4). image() got six colours with no breaks or zlim, so orange cells came out red and red cells maroon. Add zlim = c(0.5, 6.5).
Row labels missing, or numbers in place of site names (4). Write the labels with mtext() on side 2, as at lines 179–180 of code/2_plot_figure.R.
Instruments merged into one row per site (3), giving 33 or 40 rows where the target has 42. Build the key from all three columns, Site ID, POC and AQS Parameter Code.
Red line missing from panel B (2). Draw it from panel B with xpd = NA, as above.
Wrong figure size (2). Use width = 183 / 25.4 and height = 247 / 25.4 with units = "in".
Panel A missing from the saved file (1). The PNG got two pages, and a PNG file keeps only the last one. Call layout() once, before the first plot(), so the two plot() calls fill its two slots on one page.
POC brackets lost to a typo (1). Without its hyphen, the arrow <- becomes the comparison <. R evaluates the comparison and discards the result without an error. Put the hyphen back.

Three more differences were common and cost no points.

Panel A keeps the 4 percent padding plot() adds at each end (10), so its lines stop short of the grid’s edges. xaxs = "i" removes it.
Distance labels one kilometre off (many). The assignment page gave about 111 and 92 km per degree and said the target used 111.32 and 92.10. A one-kilometre difference cost nothing.
Percentiles from quantile() (several). It interpolates between readings, so its grey lines differ slightly from sort() and an index.



The code

Values typed into the code that belong in the parameter block, three or more of them (16). The file names, the window and ignition dates, the fire’s coordinates, the km-per-degree constants and the six AQI colours go in misc at the top, as the assignment page asks, and the code refers to them as misc$....
A script with no comments on its working steps (7). Add one comment per step that says what it does and why.
run_everything.R holding copies of the scripts (2). Two source() calls keep each line of code in one file.

title: HW1 solution · How bad was the air?
text:
A mistake in the target
The target as first posted had a flaw of its own. Panel B was drawn with image(x = d$cal, ...), where d$cal holds Dates. image() puts each cell’s edges halfway between neighbouring x values, and it finds that half with 0.5 * diff(x). For Dates, diff() returns a time difference. R rounds a time difference to whole days before it adds it to a Date or subtracts it from one, and half a day rounds to 0. The edges landed on the dates themselves, which gave the cell for 1 December zero width and put each of the other 89 days half a day to the left of its date. A plain number such as the 0.5 in d$start - 0.5 keeps its half day, so the xlim above is unaffected. You can see the difference in any R session:


Console, any R session

x <- as.Date(c("2024-12-01", "2024-12-02"))
x[1] - 0.5 * diff(x)     # "2024-12-01": the half day rounds to zero
as.numeric(x)[1] - 0.5   # 20057.5, half a day before 1 December
unclass(x[1] - 0.5)      # 20057.5: a plain 0.5 keeps the half day

Three graders spotted it. The target was corrected and re-posted before grades went out, and no student lost points over it. The fix passes the dates to image() as plain numbers, which keep their half days.


code/2_plot_figure.R, lines 148–151

    # x as plain numbers: given Dates, image() rounds the half-day cell edges
    # to whole days, which drops 1 December and shifts every day half a day left.
    image(x = as.numeric(d$cal), y = 1:nrows, z = t(band[nrows:1, ]), add = TRUE,
          col = misc$cols, zlim = c(0.5, length(misc$cols) + 0.5))

title: HW1 solution · How bad was the air?
text:
The full code
These are the three files exactly as they run.


code/run_everything.R

# =============================================================
# AEM 6850 - HW1: "How bad was the air?"
# Master file. Runs the whole thing, in order.
#
# Open hw1.Rproj first. It sits at the project root, so the working
# directory is hw1/ and every path below is relative to it.
#
#   source("code/run_everything.R")     from the R console
#   Rscript code/run_everything.R       from a terminal, run in hw1/
#
# 1_get_clean_data.R  downloads the EPA files, writes data_clean/hw1_clean.rds
# 2_plot_figure.R     reads that, writes figures/hw1_target.png
# =============================================================

  rm(list = ls())

  source("code/1_get_clean_data.R")
  source("code/2_plot_figure.R")



code/1_get_clean_data.R

# =============================================================
# AEM 6850 - HW1: "How bad was the air?"
# Script 1 of 2 - get the data and clean it.
#
# Downloads one CSV of EPA daily PM2.5 for the monitors around the January
# 2025 Los Angeles fires, keeps the 90-day window, and puts the monitors in
# order of how far they sit from the fire. Writes one object for the
# plotting script.
#
# Writes: data_clean/hw1_clean.rds
#
# Open hw1.Rproj first. It sits at the project root, so the working
# directory is hw1/ and every path below is relative to it.
#
#   source("code/1_get_clean_data.R")
# =============================================================


# 1). Preliminary ----

  # Packages: none. Base R only.

  # Parameters
  misc <- list()
  misc$url      <- "https://arielortizbobea.github.io/assets/data/epa_pm25_la_fires_2024_2025.csv"
  misc$file     <- "data/epa_pm25_la_fires_2024_2025.csv"
  misc$clean    <- "data_clean/hw1_clean.rds"
  misc$start    <- as.Date("2024-12-01")
  misc$end      <- as.Date("2025-02-28")
  misc$min_days <- 60                  # of the 90; drop instruments that rarely report

  # Where the Eaton fire started, from CAL FIRE's own incident record.
  # The Palisades fire started the same week, 40 km west, but its smoke blew
  # straight out to sea; Eaton is the one whose plume crossed the monitored
  # basin, so distances here are measured from Eaton.
  misc$fire_lat <- 34.203483
  misc$fire_lon <- -118.069155

  # Turning a difference in degrees into a distance in kilometres. A degree
  # of latitude is about 111 km anywhere on Earth. A degree of longitude is
  # shorter, and shorter still the further you are from the equator: at Los
  # Angeles it is about 92 km.
  misc$km_lat <- 111.32
  misc$km_lon <- 92.10

  dir.create("data",       showWarnings = FALSE)
  dir.create("data_clean", showWarnings = FALSE)


# 2). Get the data ----

  # One file, one line. It is a plain CSV on the web, so download.file()
  # fetches it and read.csv() opens it exactly like a local file.
  if (!file.exists(misc$file)) download.file(misc$url, misc$file)

  d <- read.csv(misc$file, colClasses = c("Site.ID" = "character"))

  # Site.ID is a LABEL, not a quantity. Left to itself read.csv() calls the
  # column an integer and the leading zero disappears: 060371103 becomes
  # 60371103, silently. colClasses protects it at read time.


# 3). Clean ----

  names(d)[names(d) == "Daily.Mean.PM2.5.Concentration"] <- "pm25"
  names(d)[names(d) == "Local.Site.Name"]                <- "site"
  names(d)[names(d) == "Daily.AQI.Value"]                <- "aqi"

  d$date <- as.Date(d$Date, format = "%m/%d/%Y")
  d <- d[d$date >= misc$start & d$date <= misc$end, ]

  # A site is a place; a monitor is one instrument at that place, and a busy
  # site runs several. Site plus POC plus parameter names the instrument.
  # That key is unique on any given day, so every instrument can have its own
  # row in the heat map and nothing is counted twice.
  d$monitor <- paste(d$Site.ID, d$POC, d$AQS.Parameter.Code)
  stopifnot(anyDuplicated(paste(d$monitor, d$date)) == 0)

  # How far each monitor sits from the fire. The coordinates come with the
  # file, so no site is named anywhere in this script: the distance decides
  # the order the monitors appear in.
  north <- (d$Site.Latitude  - misc$fire_lat) * misc$km_lat
  east  <- (d$Site.Longitude - misc$fire_lon) * misc$km_lon
  d$km  <- sqrt(north^2 + east^2)

  # One row per monitor, nearest the fire first.
  m <- d[!duplicated(d$monitor), ]
  m <- m[order(m$km), ]

  # Label with the site name, and add the POC only where a site runs more
  # than one instrument, so those rows stay distinguishable. One site in
  # the file, 060839001 in Santa Barbara County, ships with a blank name;
  # it gets its ID instead, so no row is left unlabelled.
  m$label <- m$site
  blank <- m$label == ""
  m$label[blank] <- paste("Site", m$Site.ID[blank])
  many <- m$site %in% m$site[duplicated(m$site)]
  m$label[many] <- paste0(m$site[many], " [", m$POC[many], "]")

  # One column per calendar day. Days a monitor did not report stay NA,
  # which is what makes the gaps visible in the figure.
  cal     <- seq(misc$start, misc$end, by = "day")
  day     <- factor(format(d$date), levels = format(cal))
  grid_pm  <- tapply(d$pm25, list(d$monitor, day), mean)[m$monitor, ]
  grid_aqi <- tapply(d$aqi,  list(d$monitor, day), mean)[m$monitor, ]

  # Some instruments sample one day in three, or one in six. Their rows are
  # mostly gaps, and a wall of grey hides the pattern in the rows that do
  # report every day, so keep only the instruments that report often enough.
  enough   <- apply(!is.na(grid_pm), 1, sum) >= misc$min_days
  grid_pm  <- grid_pm[enough, ]
  grid_aqi <- grid_aqi[enough, ]
  m        <- m[enough, ]

  saveRDS(list(grid_pm  = grid_pm,   # monitor x day, concentrations
               grid_aqi = grid_aqi,  # monitor x day, EPA's own AQI value
               label   = m$label,   # row labels, nearest the fire first
               km      = m$km,      # km from the Eaton fire
               cal     = cal,
               start   = misc$start,
               end     = misc$end),
          misc$clean)

  cat(sprintf("%d monitors at %d sites, reporting %d+ of the 90 days\n",
              nrow(m), length(unique(m$site)), misc$min_days))
  cat(sprintf("%d of %d cells have a reading (%d%%)\n",
              sum(!is.na(grid_pm)), length(grid_pm),
              round(100 * sum(!is.na(grid_pm)) / length(grid_pm))))
  cat(sprintf("nearest %.0f km, farthest %.0f km from the Eaton fire\n",
              min(m$km), max(m$km)))
  cat("Saved:", misc$clean, "\n")

# the end



code/2_plot_figure.R

# =============================================================
# AEM 6850 - HW1: "How bad was the air?"
# Script 2 of 2 - the target figure.
#
# Reads data_clean/hw1_clean.rds, written by 1_get_clean_data.R, and
# produces: figures/hw1_target.png
#
#   A  the network as a whole: the daily average across monitors, with the
#      10th and 90th percentile of monitors on the same day
#   B  every monitor, every day, coloured by EPA's daily AQI category,
#      ordered by distance from the fire
#
# Open hw1.Rproj first. It sits at the project root, so the working
# directory is hw1/ and every path below is relative to it.
#
#   source("code/2_plot_figure.R")
# =============================================================


# 1). Preliminary ----

  # Packages: none. Base R only.

  # Parameters
  misc <- list()
  misc$clean    <- "data_clean/hw1_clean.rds"
  misc$fig      <- "figures/hw1_target.png"
  misc$ignite   <- as.Date("2025-01-07")

  # Color is EPA's Air Quality Index: six categories, six published colors,
  # nothing else. Breaks are the category lower bounds; findInterval() puts
  # each day's AQI into its band.
  misc$breaks <- c(0, 51, 101, 151, 201, 301)
  misc$cols   <- c("#00E400",    # Good
                   "#FFFF00",    # Moderate
                   "#FF7E00",    # Unhealthy for sensitive groups
                   "#FF0000",    # Unhealthy
                   "#8F3F97",    # Very unhealthy
                   "#7E0023")    # Hazardous
  misc$labs   <- c("Good, AQI 0-50",
                   "Moderate, 51-100",
                   "Unhealthy for sensitive groups, 101-150",
                   "Unhealthy, 151-200",
                   "Very unhealthy, 201-300",
                   "Hazardous, 301+")
  misc$no_data <- "white"

  # Figure size and text. One place to change any of it. 183 x 247 mm is a
  # full-page, double-column figure in some journals
  misc$width  <- 183 / 25.4                # 7.20 in
  misc$height <- 247 / 25.4                # 9.72 in
  misc$pt     <- 9
  misc$mar    <- c(2.0, 15.4, 1.4, 3.7)   # shared, so the two x axes line up;
                                          # left fits the longest site name exactly
  misc$cex    <- 1.05                     # one size for every axis label

# Create folder for figure
  dir.create("figures", showWarnings = FALSE)
  
# Read data
  d <- readRDS(misc$clean)

# Small function
# The 10th and 90th percentile of a day's readings. sort() drops the
# monitors that did not report, then one value is picked by position, so
# this needs nothing beyond sorting and indexing.
  pctl <- function(x, p) {
    x <- sort(x)
    if (length(x) == 0) return(NA)
    x[max(1, round(p * length(x)))]
  }


# 2). Compute daily summaries ----

  # Compute summaries
  avg <- apply(d$grid_pm, 2, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
  p10 <- apply(d$grid_pm, 2, pctl, p = 0.10)
  p90 <- apply(d$grid_pm, 2, pctl, p = 0.90)

  # Which color bin every cell falls in. findInterval() turns a number into
  # the position of the band it falls in. NA stays NA.
  band   <- d$grid_aqi
  band[] <- findInterval(d$grid_aqi, misc$breaks)

  # Tick marks on the 1st and 15th of each month, labelled "Dec 1", "Dec 15"...
  ticks <- as.Date(c("2024-12-01", "2024-12-15", "2025-01-01",
                     "2025-01-15", "2025-02-01", "2025-02-15"))
  tlabs <- paste(format(ticks, "%b"), as.numeric(format(ticks, "%d")))
  nrows  <- nrow(d$grid_pm)


# 3). Create the figure ----

  # Header
  png(misc$fig, width = misc$width, height = misc$height,
      units = "in", res = 300, pointsize = misc$pt)
  layout(matrix(1:2, ncol = 1), heights = c(1, 2.6))
  par(oma = c(0.2, 0.2, 0.2, 0.2), mgp = c(2.2, 0.5, 0), tcl = -0.35,
      las = 1, family = "sans", cex.axis = misc$cex)

  # Panel A: the network as a whole -----
  if (T) {
    # Parameters
    ylim <- c(0, 80)
    par(mar = misc$mar)

    # Main plot
    plot(NA, xlim = c(d$start - 0.5, d$end + 0.5), ylim = ylim,
       axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", xaxs = "i")
    lines(d$cal, p90, col = "grey65", lwd = 1)
    lines(d$cal, p10, col = "grey65", lwd = 1)
    lines(d$cal, avg, col = "black",  lwd = 2)

    # Outer
    axis(1, at = ticks, labels = tlabs)
    axis(2, at = seq(0, 80, 20), las=2)
    
    box(bty = "l")

    # Text
    mtext("Fire begins", side=3, at=misc$ignite, col="red", font=2)
    mtext("Daily PM2.5 (ug/m3)", side = 2, line = 3, las = 0, cex = misc$cex)
    mtext("A", side = 3, line = 0.15, adj = 0, at = par("usr")[1], font = 2, cex = misc$cex * 1.3)
    legend("topright", inset = c(0.01, 0.02), bty = "n", cex = misc$cex * 0.92,
           seg.len = 1.8, y.intersp = 1.15,
           legend = c("average across monitors",
                    "10th and 90th percentile"),
         col = c("black", "grey65"),
         lwd = c(2, 1), lty = c(1, 1))
  }
  
  # Panel B: every monitor, every day -----
  if (T) {
  
    # Parameters
    par(mar = misc$mar)
  
    # main plot
    plot(NA, xlim = c(d$start - 0.5, d$end + 0.5), ylim = c(0.5, nrows + 0.5),
       axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")

    # Grey underneath, so a cell with no reading never reads as clean air.
    # rect(d$start - 0.5, 0.5, d$end + 0.5, nrows + 0.5, col = misc$no_data, border = NA)

    # image() draws row 1 at the bottom, so the matrix goes in upside down to
    # put the monitor nearest the fire at the top.
    # x as plain numbers: given Dates, image() rounds the half-day cell edges
    # to whole days, which drops 1 December and shifts every day half a day left.
    image(x = as.numeric(d$cal), y = 1:nrows, z = t(band[nrows:1, ]), add = TRUE,
          col = misc$cols, zlim = c(0.5, length(misc$cols) + 0.5))
  
    # Outer
    axis(1, at = ticks, labels = tlabs)
    box()
  
    # The key, in the lower right corner: one legend() call, a colored box
    # and a label for every AQI category, whether or not it occurs in this
    # window, on a white background so it stays readable over the cells.
      legend("bottomright", inset = 0.01, bg = "white", box.col = "grey45",
           cex = misc$cex * 0.72, y.intersp = 1,
           title = "EPA Air Quality Index (AQI):", title.adj = 0.1,
           legend = c(misc$labs, "No reading"),
           fill   = c(misc$cols, misc$no_data), border = "grey45")

    # One red line for the moment of ignition, running from the top of panel A
    # to the bottom of panel B, through the gap between them. Drawn from B
    # with xpd = NA so it can leave the plot region. par("pin") is the plot
    # region in inches and par("mai") the margins, which is enough to work
    # out where panel A's top edge is in panel B's own y units.
    per_in   <- nrows / par("pin")[2]                        # B's y units per inch
    fig_b_in <- par("pin")[2] + par("mai")[1] + par("mai")[3] # B's figure height
    fig_a_in <- fig_b_in / 2.6                                # from layout heights
    a_plot   <- fig_a_in - par("mai")[1] - par("mai")[3]      # A's plot height
    y_top    <- nrows + 0.5 + per_in * (par("mai")[3] + par("mai")[1] + a_plot)
    lines(c(misc$ignite, misc$ignite), c(0.5, y_top), col = "red", lwd = 1.5, xpd = NA)
  
    # Text
    mtext(rev(d$label), side = 2, at = 1:nrows, las = 1, line = 0.35,
          cex = misc$cex, adj = 1)
    mtext(rev(round(d$km)), side = 4, at = 1:nrows,
          las = 1, line = 0.25, cex = misc$cex, adj = 0, col = "grey45")
    mtext("Distance to the Eaton fire ignition point (km)",
          side = 4, line = 2.4, las = 0, cex = misc$cex)
    mtext("B", side = 3, line = 0.15, adj = 0, at = par("usr")[1],
          font = 2, cex = misc$cex * 1.3)
    
  }
  
  dev.off()
  
# The end

title: Homework
text: Weekly assignments, each a self-contained piece of the semester’s investigation using that week’s tools. Each one posts here after class and is due a week later; the exact dates are in the table.

title: Homework
text:
How it works

Starters live in a private repository per student in the course’s GitHub organization. Access instructions are on Canvas, not here.
Submit by committing to that repository. HW1 took browser uploads; from HW2 on it is git, which session 7 covers. The commit timestamp is the submission time.
Figures are not submitted. The grader runs your code on a fresh machine and grades the figures it draws, so commit the code; uploading the figures is not needed.
Solutions are posted on this site and linked from the table above. Several assignments build on the one before, and a solution can go up while the assignment that extends it is still open. That assignment still starts from your own submission. What I value most is that you understand each change you make to it, including the ones an AI agent makes for you. Each solution is a complete project, in the same folder layout you were asked to produce.
Late work is not accepted, and your lowest homework score is dropped. Documented emergencies: talk to me.
AI tools are permitted by default, with disclosure, except where an assignment says otherwise. HW1 says otherwise.

title: Homework
text:
Rubric
Every homework is graded on the first three dimensions below. HW1, the no-AI assignment, was graded on those three (9 points). From HW2 on, AI is allowed and two dimensions are added, Verification and The note and the history (15 points). An assignment’s page may add requirements of its own, such as a rule for getting the data.
15 points. Five dimensions, three points each. The grader clones your repository into an empty folder, runs code/run_everything.R in a fresh R session, compares what it produces with the target, and reads your code, your note and your commits.

Similarity (3 points)







3
The output is virtually identical to the target. One has to really pay attention to see any difference.


2
The output has one or two clear differences from the target: an element missing, the wrong ordering, a scale or a unit that is not the one specified, values in a table that differ.


1
The output is clearly different from the target: three or more clear differences, or a panel missing.


0
No output, or output of something else.



Similarity is judged on what the output encodes, not on pixel-level matching. A slightly different font size is not a difference. A row missing from a table, or a series missing from a panel, is.


Reproducibility (3 points)







3
The code runs start to finish in a fresh clone, without any edits, and produces the output, getting its data the way the assignment says. Paths are relative to the project root. Nothing depends on objects left over from an earlier session.


2
One minor edit is needed to run it: a stray absolute path, a folder it expected to exist, a library() call for something base R already does. Also here: a rule the assignment sets for getting the data is not followed.


1
Several edits are needed, or it runs with errors, or it does not produce the output.


0
The code does not run.



Two things cost points here every year. Absolute paths: read.csv("/Users/you/Desktop/...") works on your laptop and nowhere else; open the .Rproj and use "data/...". Session leftovers: a script that works because an object is still in your environment from twenty minutes ago is not a script that works. Restart R and source it before you push.


Coding structure (3 points)







3
The code (1) has clear and logical sections, (2) has a clearly identified parameter section that can be modified to produce slightly different versions of the output, (3) is well annotated, and (4) is concise but spacious.


2
The code has at most one of the following: (1) no clear structure, (2) parameters hard-coded within the core of the script, (3) missing key annotations, (4) too dense or too verbose.


1
The code has more than one of those.


0
There is no code, or the code cannot perform the basic steps needed to generate the output.



“A clearly identified parameter section” means the URLs, the file names, the dates, the constants and the colours live together at the top of each script, named, and are used by name below. “Concise” means a step done many times is written once and called.


Verification (3 points)







3
The script states what it expects of its data and stops when the data disagrees, at the places the data can go wrong. At least one check could have failed on a mistake you could actually have made, and your note says for each check what it would have caught.


2
Checking is thin: one place covered and an obvious one left open, or a bound so wide that the right answer and the wrong answer both pass, or the note lists the checks without saying what any of them would catch.


1
Every check is one that cannot fail: a count compared with a number taken from the same run, a test that the line above has already made true.


0
The script makes no check of its own data.



A check earns its point by being able to fail.


The note and the history (3 points)







3
The work arrives in separable commits in a sensible order, each message naming what that commit did. The note explains the choices the code makes and why, says what you checked, and discloses the tools, the uses and what you verified.


2
One of those falls short: the whole assignment in a single commit, messages that say only “update”, a choice or a check in the code that the note does not mention. A push problem you raised on the day is not counted here.


1
Two or more fall short.


0
No note, or no commit of your own. Also here: a note with no AI disclosure block, or an empty one. The block is required even when it says no AI was used.



The note is NOTES.md at the root of your repository. Write it for a reader who knows the assignment and has never seen your code. A good note has three parts.

Your choices. Each decision the assignment left to you, and why you made it: which files you used and which you skipped, how your code finds what it needs in them, what you did with the cases that did not fit.
Your checks. Each check in the script, where it sits, and the mistake it would catch. For example: “code/read_reports.R stops if a yield falls outside 100 to 200 bushels per acre, which would catch a row of tonnage read as the yield.”
AI disclosure. A section of its own naming the tools you used, what you used each one for, and what you checked in what they gave you. If you used none, the section says so.



AI use
Permitted unless an assignment says otherwise, and always disclosed. Undisclosed AI use, and code taken from anyone else without saying whose, are misrepresentation under the syllabus and are treated as integrity violations rather than as grading matters.

The HW1 solution is posted, with the full code and the most common mistakes.
No AI on this one. See the rule near the bottom. It is the only kind of exception the course makes, and it is made on purpose.

title: HW1 · How bad was the air?
text:
What happened
On the morning of 7 January 2025, a wildfire started in the hills above Pacific Palisades, on the coast of Los Angeles, California. That evening a second fire started in Eaton Canyon, above the city of Altadena, 40 km to the east. Both were driven by Santa Ana winds, a dry wind that blows from the desert toward the ocean, gusting that night past 100 km/h. The two fires burned for over three weeks, destroyed thousands of homes, and became two of the most destructive wildfires in California’s history.

Palisades Fire: 23,448 acres, 7 to 31 January.
Eaton Fire: 14,021 acres, 7 to 31 January.

Los Angeles sits in a basin ringed by mountains, and the basin is dense with air quality monitors. The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) publishes what every one of them recorded, every day. This assignment asks a plain question of that record: how bad did the air get, where, and for how long?

title: HW1 · How bad was the air?
text:
What you produce
One figure, rebuilt from the raw data so that it matches the target below as closely as you can.



Target figure


Panel A is the whole network on each day: the average across every monitor reporting, with the 10th and 90th percentile of monitors.
Panel B is every monitor on every day, coloured by EPA’s Air Quality Index category, with the monitors nearest the Eaton Fire at the top and their distance from it down the right edge.
Study the target before you write a line. Two things it shows are worth noticing now: the air was worse in early December than during the fire, and the fire’s effect stops about 60 km out.

title: HW1 · How bad was the air?
text:
What you get
The data. One file, exactly as EPA’s Download Daily Data tool ships it. Nothing has been cleaned or reformatted.

https://arielortizbobea.github.io/assets/data/epa_pm25_la_fires_2024_2025.csv

Daily PM2.5 for every monitor within 150 km of the Eaton Fire, 1 December 2024 to 28 February 2025. 3,995 rows, 1 MB. PM2.5 is fine particulate matter, in micrograms per cubic metre (µg/m³); EPA’s 24-hour health standard is 35. The file also carries EPA’s own Daily AQI Value, the number behind the colour categories you see on the news.
The fire. The Eaton Fire’s ignition point, from CAL FIRE’s incident record:

34.2035 °N, −118.0692 °W

You will measure every monitor’s distance from this point.
The starter. Your private repo in the course GitHub organization contains hw1.Rproj, an empty code/ folder, and this page. Click the green Code button, Download ZIP, unzip it somewhere you keep coursework, and open hw1.Rproj.

title: HW1 · How bad was the air?
text:
The rules the figure follows
To rebuild the figure you need to know exactly what it encodes. None of this is hidden. The pipeline is the assignment; the choices were never the secret.

Window: 1 December 2024 to 28 February 2025, inclusive.
A monitor is an instrument, not a place. A site is a place. Several sites run more than one instrument, each with its own POC number and parameter code. Every instrument gets its own row in panel B. The key Site ID + POC + AQS Parameter Code is unique on any given day, and your script should check that it is.
Keep monitors that reported at least 60 of the 90 days. Some instruments sample one day in three or one in six; their rows would be mostly gaps.
Distance from the fire, in km, from each row’s Site Latitude and Site Longitude. A degree of latitude is about 111 km anywhere on Earth. A degree of longitude is shorter, and shorter the further you are from the equator; at Los Angeles it is about 92 km. Convert each difference into km, then use Pythagoras. The target was drawn with 111.32 and 92.10; with 111 and 92 a few of the km labels come out one kilometre different, which is fine.
Panel B rows are sorted by that distance, nearest at the top. Where a site runs more than one instrument, append the POC in brackets so the rows stay distinguishable. One site in the file ships with a blank name; label it by its ID.
Panel A: for each day, the mean across the monitors that reported, and the 10th and 90th percentile of those same readings.
Colour is EPA’s Air Quality Index: six categories, six colours, from the file’s own Daily AQI Value. Days a monitor did not report are white. The key is drawn with legend() and lists all six categories, whether or not they occur.
One red line marks 7 January, running through both panels.
Output: figures/hw1_target.png, 183 × 247 mm, 300 dpi.

title: HW1 · How bad was the air?
text:
Tips
The colours. EPA publishes the exact colours of the AQI scale in its AQI technical assistance document, Table 2, as RGB triplets. In hex they are:



category
AQI
colour




Good
0 to 50
#00E400


Moderate
51 to 100
#FFFF00


Unhealthy for sensitive groups
101 to 150
#FF7E00


Unhealthy
151 to 200
#FF0000


Very unhealthy
201 to 300
#8F3F97


Hazardous
301 and above
#7E0023



R takes a hex code anywhere it takes a colour name.
read.csv() damages a column. Site ID is a label that happens to be spelled with digits, and read.csv() reads it as a number, so 060371103 becomes 60371103 with no warning. colClasses protects it at read time. Note that colClasses uses R’s name for the column, Site.ID, not the file’s header.
image() draws row 1 at the bottom. If you want the nearest monitor at the top, the matrix goes in upside down. rev() does it.
Percentiles without quantile(). You have not met quantile(). You do not need it: sort() the day’s readings, which also drops the NAs, and pick the value by position.
Grey cells hide the pattern. Paint the panel white with rect() before image() draws over it, so days with no reading show as white rather than as the background colour.
One site has no name. Look at your row labels. If one is blank, find out why, and give it a label that says what it is.
Restart and source before you submit. A script that only works because of what is already in your environment is the most common way to lose points here. Session > Restart R, then source("code/run_everything.R"). It must run top to bottom with no errors.

title: HW1 · How bad was the air?
text:
Rubric
The course rubric, as on the Homework page.
9 points. Three dimensions, three points each. The grader opens your repository in a fresh R session, runs your master script from the top, and compares what it produces with the target.

Replicability (3 points)







3
The code runs start to finish, without any edits, and produces the output. Paths are relative to the project root. Nothing depends on objects left over from an earlier session.


2
The code requires one minor edit to run: a stray absolute path, a folder it expected to exist, a library() call for something base R already does.


1
The code requires several edits to run, or runs with errors, or does not produce the output.


0
The code does not run.



Two things that cost points here every year. Absolute paths: read.csv("/Users/you/Desktop/...") works on your laptop and nowhere else; open the .Rproj and use "data/...". Session leftovers: a script that works because x is still in your environment from twenty minutes ago is not a script that works. Restart R and source it before you upload. Every time.


Similarity (3 points)







3
The output is virtually identical to the target. One has to really pay attention to see any difference.


2
The output is similar but has some clear differences from the target: an element missing, the wrong ordering, a scale that is not the one specified.


1
The output is clearly different from the target.


0
No output.



Similarity is judged on what the output encodes, not on pixel-level matching. A slightly different font size is not a difference. A row missing from a table, or a monitor missing from a panel, is.


Coding (3 points)







3
The code (1) has clear and logical sections, (2) has a clearly identified parameter section that can be modified to produce slightly different versions of the output, (3) is well annotated, and (4) is concise but spacious.


2
The code has at most one of the following: (1) no clear structure, (2) parameters hard-coded within the core of the script, (3) missing key annotations, (4) too dense or too verbose.


1
The code has more than one of those.


0
There is no code, or the code cannot perform the basic steps needed to generate the output.



“A clearly identified parameter section” means the file names, the dates, the constants and the colours live together at the top of each script, named, and are used by name below. A number that means something typed in six places is six chances to change five of them.


AI use
Permitted by default, with a disclosure block, except where an assignment says otherwise. Undisclosed AI use is misrepresentation under the syllabus and is treated as an integrity violation, not as a grading matter.


For this assignment

The output is figures/hw1_target.png, written by code/run_everything.R.
Similarity means: rows in the right order with the right labels, the right colour on the right day, both panels on one x axis with the red line through both. A monitor missing from panel B is a difference.
The parameter section should hold the file names, the dates, the fire’s coordinates, the km-per-degree constants and the six colours.
AI: this is a no-AI assignment. If you used a chatbot or coding assistant on any part of it, say so at the top of run_everything.R. Disclosed use will be discussed, not punished; undisclosed use is an integrity matter.

title: HW3 · Did the May forecast survive the summer?
text:
The question
Every month USDA’s World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) project the U.S. corn yield and the price farmers will receive. The first projection for a crop comes in May and is revised every month until January. In May 2012 USDA projected 166.0 bushels per acre; the drought brought it to 123.4. How did the May forecasts of yield and price hold up from 2000 to 2026, and what did the world price do meanwhile?
crumbs: 3 Did the May forecast survive the summer?

title: HW3 · Did the May forecast survive the summer?
text:
Target



Target figure
crumbs: 3 Did the May forecast survive the summer?

title: HW3 · Did the May forecast survive the summer?
text:
Data

The list of WASDE reports: an API. USDA’s ESMIS archive returns every report since 1973 as JSON, 25 per page, with the URLs of each report’s files: https://esmis.nal.usda.gov/api/v1/release/findByIdentifier/wasde?latest=false&page=0
The reports themselves: downloads, read with regular expressions. Take the .txt file of each report, or the .xml when there is no text. The yield and the price are in the CORN block of the table “U.S. Feed Grain and Corn Supply and Use”.
The world price of corn: a CSV. FRED series PMAIZMTUSDM, dollars per metric ton (one ton is 39.368 bushels): https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=PMAIZMTUSDM

USDA’s robots.txt asks for ten seconds between requests. Save every file you download and never download it twice. Save each report under data/wasde/ plus the part of its URL after release-files/, so …/release-files/3t945q76s/ms35t8930/t435gd264/wasde-08-10-2012.xml goes to data/wasde/3t945q76s/ms35t8930/t435gd264/wasde-08-10-2012.xml.

title: HW3 · Did the May forecast survive the summer?
text:
Figure rules

One line per season, from the May report to the January report, each point at its report’s release date.
Top panel: the yield. Bottom panel: the price projection (the midpoint when USDA gives a range), over the monthly world price in grey.
Colour: warm when the January yield ended below May, cool when above, darker as the gap grows. The price line takes its season’s colour. The season still open is yellow.
An open circle at May, a white dot at January, on a dark background.

Font, exact shades and the key’s layout are never differences.

title: Resources
text: Manuals and guides worth keeping open while you work. Everything below is free online unless the entry says otherwise. None of it is required reading. Use it when you are stuck, or when you want the long version of something a session covered in five minutes.

title: Resources
text:
Coming from Stata
stata2r puts Stata and R side by side for the same task, using the data.table and fixest packages. If you already think in Stata commands, start here: look up the command you know and read across.
Stata Coding Guide, Julian Reif (University of Illinois). Stata first, but most of it is about problems no language solves for you: folder structure, managing packages so a co-author can reproduce your results, automating tables and figures, and what a journal replication package has to contain. The chapter on calling R from Stata is useful in both directions.
R for Stata Users, Robert Muenchen and Joseph Hilbe (Springer, 2010). A book, not free. It defines R terms in Stata vocabulary, and works the same programs through both languages so you can read them against each other. Dated on the tidyverse, still good on the concepts.

title: Resources
text:
Learning R
R for Data Science, Hadley Wickham, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Garrett Grolemund. The standard free reference for the tidyverse. It covers the same ground as sessions 4 and 5 at more length, and keeps going well past them.
Advanced R, Hadley Wickham. Read the Foundations chapters if you want the formal version of session 2: what an object is, what a class is, how vectors and attributes work, and how S3 dispatch decides which summary() you get.
The tidyverse style guide, Hadley Wickham. Naming, spacing, line breaks, pipe formatting. Adopt its conventions or adopt your own, but adopt something and be consistent. Your future co-authors are reading.

title: Resources
text:
Coding guides
Code and Data for the Social Sciences: A Practitioner’s Guide, Matthew Gentzkow and Jesse Shapiro. About thirty pages on directory structure, automation, version control, and abstraction, written for economists by economists. Widely used in the profession, and short enough to read in one sitting. Read it before your first real project, not after.
Data Science for Economists, Grant McDermott (EC 607, University of Oregon). A full graduate course in the open, lecture notes and code: git, data wrangling, APIs, web scraping, spatial analysis, parallel programming, databases. It goes further than this course in several directions, and the material is free to read.
Coding for Economists, Arthur Turrell (Bank of England). Python rather than R, and useful for exactly that reason: the same problems in a different language, so you can see which parts of what you learn here are about data work and which are about R.

title: Resources
text:
Getting unstuck
Before you search, try the help page: ?function_name in the console, or ??keyword if you do not know the name. Session 2 covers both.
When the help page is not enough, paste the exact error message into a search engine. R’s error messages are terse but they are specific, and somebody has almost certainly hit yours. Stack Overflow and Posit Community carry most of the answers.
For AI assistants, wait for sessions 8 and 9. The course has things to say about when to trust them and how to check what they give you, and the habits are easier to build before you have bad ones.

title: 2 · R essentials I
text:
Objectives
By the end of this session you can:

Build vectors and do arithmetic on them.
Say what R does when a vector mixes classes, and why that turns a column of numbers into text.
Handle missing values instead of being surprised by them.
Subset a vector or a data frame with a logical condition.
Say what a factor is, and repair the trap it sets.

title: 2 · R essentials I
section: R is a language and a program
text:
R is a language and a program



R is a language. A grammar for saying what to do with data.
R is also a program. The thing you installed, which reads that grammar and runs it.
RStudio is neither. It is an editor with an R console attached.
Delete RStudio and R still works. Delete R and nothing works.

title: 2 · R essentials I
text:
Objects and calls

Everything that exists is an object. Everything that happens is a function call.
John Chambers, one of R’s designers


x <- c(1, 2, 3)
f <- function(v) v * 2

class(f)        # a function is an object, exactly like a vector

#> [1] "function"

class(`+`)      # so is the plus sign

#> [1] "function"

`+`(x, 1)       # so x + 1 is a call to that object

#> [1] 2 3 4

title: 2 · R essentials I
text:
What “object-oriented” means
Code organised around objects: values that carry their own class, where the class decides what a function does with them.

Polymorphism means that a developer can consider a function’s interface separately from its implementation, making it possible to use the same function form for different types of input.
Hadley Wickham, Advanced R

Plainly: one name, many behaviours. You write summary(x) without knowing what x is. R reads the class and runs the version built for it.

title: 2 · R essentials I
text:
One name, many behaviours

summary(c(1, 2, 3, 100))

#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>    1.00    1.75    2.50   26.50   27.25  100.00

summary(c("a", "b", "a"))

#>    Length  N.unique   N.blank Min.nchar Max.nchar 
#>         3         2         0         1         1


Same call, two results. R read the class and picked the method. That is polymorphism, and it is why you learn summary(), print() and plot() once and they keep working on things you have not met yet.
