title: 13 · The data economists use
text:
Scanner data and food deserts
Allcott, Diamond, Dubé, Handbury, Rahkovsky & Schnell (QJE, 2019) used Homescan purchases and Retail Scanner store sales, with the dates supermarkets opened and the moves of panel households.

Question: do people in food deserts eat worse because healthy food is far away?
Finding: a new supermarket in a food desert barely changes what nearby low-income households buy. Supply explains about a tenth of the nutrition gap; demand explains the rest.
The data: unit a household-week; continuous; access licensed.
Why older data could not: a diet survey is small, self-reported and a snapshot. The panel records the same households before and after an opening.

Takeaway: a firm’s panel follows the same households through an event, which no diet survey does.

title: 13 · The data economists use
text:
Job ads and the recession
Hershbein & Kahn (AER, 2018) used Burning Glass job ads for 2007 and 2010 to 2015, parsed for education and skill requirements.

Question: did employers ask for more skill after the 2007 to 2009 recession, and did it last?
Finding: the share of ads that state an education requirement rose by 23 percentage points on average. Ads in the metro areas the recession hit harder were about 5 points more likely to state education and experience requirements, and the rise lasted through 2015.
The data: unit a posting; access licensed; misses jobs never advertised online.
Why older data could not: official vacancy counts record how many jobs are open, not what the employer wants.

Metro area: a city and the counties around it that people commute from.
Takeaway: bought data records what no official survey asks, and you inherit the vendor’s coverage.

title: 13 · The data economists use
section: Card and payroll feeds in the pandemic
text:
Card and payroll feeds in the pandemic
Chetty, Friedman, Stepner & the Opportunity Insights Team (QJE, 2024) built a tracker from card spending, job ads, payroll and scheduling records and small-business revenue, by county and income group, week by week.

Finding: high-income households cut spending most in March 2020 (the next slide: the highest-income quarter of ZIP codes was 36 percent below January by mid-April, the lowest 23 percent). Small businesses in rich, dense areas lost revenue and laid off low-wage workers.
The data: unit a county-week; access mixed (the aggregates are a free download, the transactions stay with the firms). The card data cover about a tenth of US card spending. Cash and rent are invisible.

Takeaway: firm feeds arrive in days where official statistics take months, at the coverage the firm has.

title: 13 · The data economists use
text:
Satellite images and village wealth
Jean, Burke, Xie, Davis, Lobell & Ermon (Science, 2016) trained a model on daytime satellite images and night lights to predict the wealth that LSMS and DHS surveys recorded in Nigeria, Tanzania, Uganda, Malawi and Rwanda.

Question: can an image stand in for a survey where the survey does not exist?
Finding: the images explain 55 to 75 percent of the variation in village asset wealth across survey clusters, and 37 to 55 percent of consumption.
The data: unit a survey cluster; access open (the images) plus the surveys; misses what a roof and a road do not show.
Why older data could not: many African countries had no national consumption survey in a decade. A DHS or LSMS round costs 1.5 to 2 million dollars per country, and in half of African countries at least 6.5 years pass between rounds (Burke, Driscoll, Lobell & Ermon, Science, 2021).

Takeaway: an image can stand in for a survey, once a model is trained where the survey exists.

title: 13 · The data economists use
section: Phone records and a wealth map
text:
Phone records and a wealth map
Blumenstock, Cadamuro & On (Science, 2015) used the call records of 1.5 million Rwandan subscribers, a phone survey of 856 of them, and the DHS.

Question: can calling patterns reveal how wealthy a person is, and can millions of such predictions map a country?
Finding: a model trained on the 856 predicts wealth from calling patterns. Summed over 1.5 million users it reproduces the DHS district wealth map (r = 0.92 across 30 districts).
The data: unit a subscriber; daily; access restricted (an agreement with the operator, country by country); misses people without a phone.
Why older data could not: a census or a DHS comes years apart and costs millions. Phone records exist for everyone with a phone, every day.

Takeaway: records collected to bill calls can map a country between censuses.

title: 13 · The data economists use
text:
Newspaper text and media slant
Gentzkow & Shapiro (Econometrica, 2010) measured each daily newspaper’s slant by how much its phrases match those of congressional Republicans or Democrats.

Question: do newspapers slant to their readers or to their owners?
Finding: readers’ preferences explain about 20 percent of the variation in slant across papers. Who owns the paper explains far less.
The data: unit a newspaper; access licensed (news archives); misses what readers take from the text.
Why older data could not: slant had been a judgement. Phrase counts turn it into a number that can be compared across hundreds of papers.

Takeaway: word counts turn a judgement about bias into a measure.

title: 13 · The data economists use
text:
Street images and neighbourhood change
Naik, Kominers, Raskar, Glaeser & Hidalgo (PNAS, 2017) scored street-level images of the same blocks in five US cities at two dates with a computer-vision model of perceived safety.

Question: which neighbourhoods improve physically, and what predicts it?
Finding: blocks with more college-educated residents, a better initial appearance, and closer to the centre improved more.
The data: unit a block at two dates; access commercial (an API key, charged per image); misses what is not visible from the road.
Why older data could not: nobody had rated the appearance of every block in a city at two dates.

Takeaway: a photo archive becomes a panel of neighbourhood appearance.

title: 13 · The data economists use
section: Scraped online prices and Argentina’s inflation
text:
Scraped online prices and Argentina’s inflation
Cavallo & Rigobon (JEP, 2016) collected prices daily from retailer websites: by 2010, five million prices a day from over 300 retailers in 50 countries.

Question: can prices scraped from the web measure inflation, and what do they show when official figures are manipulated?
Finding: online indexes track official CPIs in most countries. In Argentina from 2007 to 2011 the official rate was 8 percent a year and online prices rose more than 20 percent a year.
The data: unit a product-retailer-day; access licensed (the micro data are now a firm’s); misses services and quantities.
Why older data could not: a CPI is collected monthly by the statistical office, with a lag, and the office can be told what to publish.

Takeaway: a price collected from outside the country cannot be edited by the statistical office.

title: 13 · The data economists use
text:
Handwritten archives and colonial Java
Dell & Olken (REStud, 2020) digitised and georeferenced handwritten Dutch records of 94 sugar factories and the villages forced to grow cane for them in the 1800s, and matched them to modern censuses and surveys.

Question: do areas the colonial state used for sugar look different today?
Finding: households within a few kilometres of an old factory consume about 14 percent more than those more than 10 km away. The areas are more industrial and better schooled.
The data: unit a village; one historical layer; access collected by the authors. About a third of the listed villages could not be placed on a modern map: the coverage gap.
Why older data could not: the records existed only as manuscripts in an archive in The Hague.

Takeaway: when no dataset exists you can build one from an archive, and report what you could not match.

One cost, measured: reading the 430 million articles of a digitised US newspaper archive at the line level was estimated at 23 million dollars with a commercial service and about 60,000 dollars with an open model (Carlson, Bryan & Dell, ACL, 2024, a computer-science venue).

Takeaway: the cost of turning documents, images and audio into tables has fallen, so questions that needed a team and a year can be tried in a week.

title: 13 · The data economists use
section: When data gets cheaper, more questions get asked
text:
When data gets cheaper, more questions get asked
Nagaraj (Management Science, 2022) studied what happened when Landsat satellite images, sold for years at a price per scene, became free to download.

Finding: once a region was imaged, the rate of significant gold discoveries there nearly doubled, and the share of discoveries made by new entrants rose from about 10 to 25 percent.
The data: mining company reports of discoveries matched to Landsat coverage.

Nagaraj, Shears & de Vaan (PNAS, 2020) find the same pattern across science: when a dataset becomes easier to get, more and more varied researchers use it.
Takeaway: the cost of data decides who gets to ask.

title: 13 · The data economists use
section: The work that stays with the researcher
text:
The work that stays with the researcher

Choosing the question, and deciding which source could hold its signal.
Judging what the source misses: who and what it does not cover, and how far its values sit from the truth.
Comparing what a tool produced with something outside it: a published total, a hand-read sample, a second source.
Reading the conditions of use and keeping to them. Some data stewards now forbid AI tools on their data; the PSID’s conditions say so.

title: 13 · The data economists use
text:
Slides · Source
An overview of the data economists use: the household surveys and administrative records most papers are built on, the data firms collect for their own operations, and the sources that were not data until recently (satellite images, phone records, newspaper text, street images, scraped prices, handwritten archives). For each source: what one row describes, who may obtain it and how, and what it misses. The session closes with what AI tools change about the cost of building data. No code runs today. The exercise is a written answer.

title: 13 · The data economists use
text:
Primary and secondary data

Secondary data is collected, processed and made available by someone other than the researchers of a study.
Primary data is collected by the researchers for that study.
Primary data becomes secondary data when it is reused.
Scraping or processing existing information still produces secondary data.
A paper on primary data describes the collection in detail. A paper on secondary data describes the source and what it misses.

title: 13 · The data economists use
section: Five questions that sort a dataset
text:
Five questions that sort a dataset

Who collects it? A government, a firm, or the researchers.
How? A survey, interviews, administrative records, remote sensing, scraping, phone-tower pings.
How much? A census of everyone, or a sample.
What format? A structured table, or text, images and audio.
What domain? Economic, health, education, natural.

The rest of the session follows the first question.

title: 13 · The data economists use
section: Where the data in economics papers came from
text:
Where the data in economics papers came from



Period
The data, and who measured it
What economists did with it




1910s to 1930s
Market prices and quantities, mostly farm products, from statistical offices; crop yields from experiment stations
Demand curves and production functions fitted to market totals (Moore, 1914; Cobb & Douglas, AER, 1928; Schultz, 1938)


1940s to 1960s
National accounts and the first regular household surveys, from statistical agencies
Macro series; individual behaviour inferred from aggregates


1960s to 1990s
Public-use survey microdata: census samples, the PSID, the NLSY
Individual decisions observed: labour supply, schooling, consumption


2000s on
Administrative records and firm data, kept by agencies and firms to run themselves
Whole populations followed for decades, linked across sources


Now
Text, images, audio, satellite scenes, phone records: by-products, not data
Turned into variables with models



Field experiments came from agronomy (Fisher, 1935); Stigler (JPE, 1954) reviews the early demand studies.

title: 13 · The data economists use
section: The questions follow the data at hand
text:
The questions follow the data at hand

Each period asked what its data could answer: demand curves when market totals were all there was; individual labour supply once survey microdata arrived; the effect of a teacher or a neighbourhood once records followed people for decades.
The data was measured by someone else, for their own purpose. A question outside it waited.
The cost of data decides which questions get asked. When a dataset becomes cheap, new questions and new people appear (Part 5 shows one case).
The hope: AI tools lower the cost of acquiring and processing data, so the question can come first and the data can be built to fit it.

section: What surveys miss: refusals and under-reporting
text:
What surveys miss: refusals and under-reporting
Meyer, Mok & Sullivan (JEP, 2015) compared five US household surveys with the totals the agencies paid out.


Refusals rose for three decades

The share of sampled households that give no interview reached 16 to 33 percent, survey by survey.

Benefits go unreported

Linked to New York State records, 43 percent of SNAP recipients and 63 percent of public-assistance recipients told the survey they received nothing.

The income of the poor is understated as a result

Poverty rates and the effect of transfer programmes come out wrong.



Unit nonresponse: a sampled household gives no interview. Measurement error: the gap between what a source records and the true value.
Takeaway: a survey cannot reveal its own error. It took an administrative benchmark to measure it.

The Opportunity Atlas: the average adult income rank of children from 25th-percentile families, by the county they grew up in; red low, blue high. The records stay inside the IRS; the county averages are a free download (3,219 counties; Tompkins County: rank 43). Drawn from county_outcomes_simple.csv at opportunityinsights.org/data.

title: 13 · The data economists use
section: Danish registers and the first child
text:
Danish registers and the first child
Kleven, Landais & Søgaard (AEJ: Applied, 2019) used Denmark’s registers: every person’s earnings every year from 1980 to 2013, with parents linked to children.

Question: how much of the gap between men’s and women’s earnings opens when the first child arrives?
Finding: men’s earnings do not move. Women’s fall at once and stay about 20 percent lower in the long run.
The data: unit a person-year; the whole population; access restricted (a remote server, through an authorised institution).
Why older data could not: the design needs everyone’s earnings every year, the first child’s birth year and the family links. A survey has none of the three at this size.

Takeaway: registers let you follow everyone through an event.

title: 13 · The data economists use
text:
Scanner data and food deserts
Allcott, Diamond, Dubé, Handbury, Rahkovsky & Schnell (QJE, 2019) used Homescan purchases and Retail Scanner store sales, with the dates supermarkets opened and the moves of panel households.

Question: do people in food deserts eat worse because healthy food is far away?
Finding: a new supermarket in a food desert barely changes what nearby low-income households buy. Supply explains about a tenth of the nutrition gap; demand explains the rest.
The data: unit a household-week; continuous; access licensed.
Why older data could not: a diet survey is small, self-reported and a snapshot. The panel records the same households before and after an opening.

Takeaway: a firm’s panel follows the same households through an event, which no diet survey does.

title: 13 · The data economists use
text:
Job ads and the recession
Hershbein & Kahn (AER, 2018) used Burning Glass job ads for 2007 and 2010 to 2015, parsed for education and skill requirements.

Question: did employers ask for more skill after the 2007 to 2009 recession, and did it last?
Finding: the share of ads that state an education requirement rose by 23 percentage points on average. Ads in the metro areas the recession hit harder were about 5 points more likely to state education and experience requirements, and the rise lasted through 2015.
The data: unit a posting; access licensed; misses jobs never advertised online.
Why older data could not: official vacancy counts record how many jobs are open, not what the employer wants.

Metro area: a city and the counties around it that people commute from.
Takeaway: bought data records what no official survey asks, and you inherit the vendor’s coverage.

title: 13 · The data economists use
section: Card and payroll feeds in the pandemic
text:
Card and payroll feeds in the pandemic
Chetty, Friedman, Stepner & the Opportunity Insights Team (QJE, 2024) built a tracker from card spending, job ads, payroll and scheduling records and small-business revenue, by county and income group, week by week.

Finding: high-income households cut spending most in March 2020 (the next slide: the highest-income quarter of ZIP codes was 36 percent below January by mid-April, the lowest 23 percent). Small businesses in rich, dense areas lost revenue and laid off low-wage workers.
The data: unit a county-week; access mixed (the aggregates are a free download, the transactions stay with the firms). The card data cover about a tenth of US card spending. Cash and rent are invisible.

Takeaway: firm feeds arrive in days where official statistics take months, at the coverage the firm has.

title: 13 · The data economists use
section: Card spending by ZIP-code income in 2020
text:
Card spending by ZIP-code income in 2020





Seven-day averages of the tracker’s public national file, from github.com/OpportunityInsights/EconomicTracker. Mid-April: lowest-income quarter of ZIP codes −23 percent, highest −36 percent.

title: 13 · The data economists use
text:
Satellite images and village wealth
Jean, Burke, Xie, Davis, Lobell & Ermon (Science, 2016) trained a model on daytime satellite images and night lights to predict the wealth that LSMS and DHS surveys recorded in Nigeria, Tanzania, Uganda, Malawi and Rwanda.

Question: can an image stand in for a survey where the survey does not exist?
Finding: the images explain 55 to 75 percent of the variation in village asset wealth across survey clusters, and 37 to 55 percent of consumption.
The data: unit a survey cluster; access open (the images) plus the surveys; misses what a roof and a road do not show.
Why older data could not: many African countries had no national consumption survey in a decade. A DHS or LSMS round costs 1.5 to 2 million dollars per country, and in half of African countries at least 6.5 years pass between rounds (Burke, Driscoll, Lobell & Ermon, Science, 2021).

Takeaway: an image can stand in for a survey, once a model is trained where the survey exists.

title: 13 · The data economists use
section: Phone records and a wealth map
text:
Phone records and a wealth map
Blumenstock, Cadamuro & On (Science, 2015) used the call records of 1.5 million Rwandan subscribers, a phone survey of 856 of them, and the DHS.

Question: can calling patterns reveal how wealthy a person is, and can millions of such predictions map a country?
Finding: a model trained on the 856 predicts wealth from calling patterns. Summed over 1.5 million users it reproduces the DHS district wealth map (r = 0.92 across 30 districts).
The data: unit a subscriber; daily; access restricted (an agreement with the operator, country by country); misses people without a phone.
Why older data could not: a census or a DHS comes years apart and costs millions. Phone records exist for everyone with a phone, every day.

Takeaway: records collected to bill calls can map a country between censuses.

title: 13 · The data economists use
text:
Newspaper text and media slant
Gentzkow & Shapiro (Econometrica, 2010) measured each daily newspaper’s slant by how much its phrases match those of congressional Republicans or Democrats.

Question: do newspapers slant to their readers or to their owners?
Finding: readers’ preferences explain about 20 percent of the variation in slant across papers. Who owns the paper explains far less.
The data: unit a newspaper; access licensed (news archives); misses what readers take from the text.
Why older data could not: slant had been a judgement. Phrase counts turn it into a number that can be compared across hundreds of papers.

Takeaway: word counts turn a judgement about bias into a measure.

title: 13 · The data economists use
text:
Street images and neighbourhood change
Naik, Kominers, Raskar, Glaeser & Hidalgo (PNAS, 2017) scored street-level images of the same blocks in five US cities at two dates with a computer-vision model of perceived safety.

Question: which neighbourhoods improve physically, and what predicts it?
Finding: blocks with more college-educated residents, a better initial appearance, and closer to the centre improved more.
The data: unit a block at two dates; access commercial (an API key, charged per image); misses what is not visible from the road.
Why older data could not: nobody had rated the appearance of every block in a city at two dates.

Takeaway: a photo archive becomes a panel of neighbourhood appearance.

title: 13 · The data economists use
section: Scraped online prices and Argentina’s inflation
text:
Scraped online prices and Argentina’s inflation
Cavallo & Rigobon (JEP, 2016) collected prices daily from retailer websites: by 2010, five million prices a day from over 300 retailers in 50 countries.

Question: can prices scraped from the web measure inflation, and what do they show when official figures are manipulated?
Finding: online indexes track official CPIs in most countries. In Argentina from 2007 to 2011 the official rate was 8 percent a year and online prices rose more than 20 percent a year.
The data: unit a product-retailer-day; access licensed (the micro data are now a firm’s); misses services and quantities.
Why older data could not: a CPI is collected monthly by the statistical office, with a lag, and the office can be told what to publish.

Takeaway: a price collected from outside the country cannot be edited by the statistical office.

title: 13 · The data economists use
text:
Handwritten archives and colonial Java
Dell & Olken (REStud, 2020) digitised and georeferenced handwritten Dutch records of 94 sugar factories and the villages forced to grow cane for them in the 1800s, and matched them to modern censuses and surveys.

Question: do areas the colonial state used for sugar look different today?
Finding: households within a few kilometres of an old factory consume about 14 percent more than those more than 10 km away. The areas are more industrial and better schooled.
The data: unit a village; one historical layer; access collected by the authors. About a third of the listed villages could not be placed on a modern map: the coverage gap.
Why older data could not: the records existed only as manuscripts in an archive in The Hague.

Takeaway: when no dataset exists you can build one from an archive, and report what you could not match.

One cost, measured: reading the 430 million articles of a digitised US newspaper archive at the line level was estimated at 23 million dollars with a commercial service and about 60,000 dollars with an open model (Carlson, Bryan & Dell, ACL, 2024, a computer-science venue).
Two surveys of what this changes for research: Korinek (JEL, 2023) on language models as research assistants, and Dell (JEL, 2025) on deep learning for building datasets from text and images.
Takeaway: the cost of turning documents, images and audio into tables has fallen, so questions that needed a team and a year can be tried in a week.

title: 13 · The data economists use
section: When data gets cheaper, more questions get asked
text:
When data gets cheaper, more questions get asked
Nagaraj (Management Science, 2022) studied what happened when Landsat satellite images, sold for years at a price per scene, became free to download.

Finding: once a region was imaged, the rate of significant gold discoveries there nearly doubled, and the share of discoveries made by new entrants rose from about 10 to 25 percent.
The data: mining company reports of discoveries matched to Landsat coverage.

Nagaraj, Shears & de Vaan (PNAS, 2020) find the same pattern across science: when a dataset becomes easier to get, more and more varied researchers use it.
Takeaway: the cost of data decides who gets to ask.

title: 13 · The data economists use
section: The work that stays with the researcher
text:
The work that stays with the researcher

Choosing the question, and deciding which source could hold its signal.
Judging what the source misses: who and what it does not cover, and how far its values sit from the truth.
Comparing what a tool produced with something outside it: a published total, a hand-read sample, a second source.
Reading the conditions of use and keeping to them. Some data stewards now forbid AI tools on their data; the PSID’s conditions say so.

title: 15 · Channels II: scraping
section: Three ways to get data from a website
text:
Three ways to get data from a website



Web scraping: a program reads pages built for people and copies chosen pieces into a table.
Feed or API: a service that answers a program with data in a fixed structure.
HTML: the text a web page is written in.

Scrape when the first two ways do not give what you need.


The feed holds 4,648 releases in the saved copy; your number will be larger. The interest-rate page (H.15) offers its data files from its own page.

title: 15 · Channels II: scraping
section: Today’s code and exercises collect the Fed’s policy statements
text:
Today’s code and exercises collect the Fed’s policy statements







The statement of 15 June 2022, as the site shows it.


The Federal Reserve is the US central bank. Its Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) sets the policy interest rate at eight scheduled meetings a year and publishes a written statement after each one.
The question: what has the committee said after each meeting since 2006?
The text of the statements exists only on these pages. The code in Parts 2 and 3 and both exercises work toward one file with every statement since 2006, fomc_statements.csv.

title: 15 · Channels II: scraping
section: Where to look before writing a scraper
text:
Where to look before writing a scraper

Look in this order. A scraper is the last step.







Look for
What it holds for the Fed’s policy statements




1. A dataset someone already built (a replication package, ICPSR, a vendor)
a paper’s files stop at the end of its sample; this session needs every statement to the latest one


2. A file to download on the site
interest rates as CSV files on the H.15 page; no statement text


3. An API or feed
json/ne-press.json: every release’s date, title and address; no text


4. A licence or an agreement with the publisher
not needed: the Board’s pages are public domain


5. The pages themselves
the only place the text exists, so scrape





With an agent. Before you brief a scrape, ask an assistant where else the data might be: a replication package, an archive, a download, an API. Then confirm each lead on the site yourself.

title: 15 · Channels II: scraping
section: Where researchers get Zillow’s housing data
text:
Where researchers get Zillow’s housing data

Zillow lists homes for sale and for rent across the US. Its listing pages are a case for not writing a scraper.

The pages are closed to programs. The terms forbid “automated queries (including screen and database scraping, spiders, robots, crawlers …)”. The robots.txt disallows /homes/. One polite request from R met a press-and-hold human check.
The listings carry personal data: agents’ names and phone numbers, photos of people’s homes.
The data come by the routes on the last slide.

A download: Zillow Research’s CSV files of home values, rents and inventory.
A dataset someone built: Zillow’s transaction records (ZTRAX), through ICPSR.
A licence: listings from an MLS (the shared database real-estate agents list homes in) or from a data vendor.




The request was to a page robots.txt allows (the research data page) and came back “Access to this page has been denied” (October 2026). Part 3 explains terms, robots.txt and the human check.
If a student raises the law: terms bind most clearly once you sign in. A US court found that scraping public pages while logged out did not breach Meta’s terms (Meta Platforms v. Bright Data, N.D. Cal., 2024), and the hiQ judgment turned on fake accounts. If a student raises the rental-housing study coming up: a study like that goes through the IRB and the university’s counsel before any collection.

title: 15 · Channels II: scraping
text:
The Fed’s meeting calendar



The FOMC (the Fed’s policy committee) issues a statement on the last day of each meeting.
One page, federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomccalendars.htm, lists 2021 to 2027: one panel (box) per year, one row per meeting.
Each row links the statement (PDF and HTML), an implementation note (the technical instructions that go with the decision), the press conference and the minutes (the written record of the meeting).
Each year from 2006 to 2020 has its own page. Each statement has its own page.



With an agent. Name these start pages in the brief: the calendar for 2021 on, and the year-page address for 2006 to 2020. Together they list every meeting.


Unscheduled calls, and votes taken in writing (notation votes), happen in crises; the 2025 panel’s last row is one, “August 22 (notation vote)”.

title: 15 · Channels II: scraping
section: Reading a page’s HTML with the browser inspector
text:
Reading a page’s HTML with the browser inspector



Element: one labelled piece of the page. Its tag is the label in angle brackets (div, a); a class names elements of one kind (fomc-meeting); an id names one element only (article); an attribute is a named value in a tag, such as a link’s address, href.
Inspect (right-click a meeting date on the live page) shows the HTML behind what you point at. View Source shows the file the server sent, which is what R reads.



With an agent. Inspect the element yourself before you accept an agent’s selector, and use these words to tell it which element you mean. A chat assistant given the element’s HTML can suggest a selector built on its class.

title: 15 · Channels II: scraping
section: Reading the saved calendar with read_html()
text:
Reading the saved calendar with read_html()



R Console, in the 15-scraping folder; needs rvest; reads cache/fomccalendars.htm; no network

# install.packages(c("rvest", "httr2", "jsonlite"))   # once
library(rvest)
cal    <- read_html("cache/fomccalendars.htm")       # the calendar as saved
panels <- html_elements(cal, ".panel-default")       # one panel per year
length(panels)


#> [1] 7

titles <- html_text2(html_element(panels, "h4"))     # the first h4 (a heading) inside each panel
titles

#> [1] "2026 FOMC Meetings" "2025 FOMC Meetings" "2024 FOMC Meetings"
#> [4] "2023 FOMC Meetings" "2022 FOMC Meetings" "2021 FOMC Meetings"
#> [7] "2027 FOMC Meetings"



The code reads the saved calendar, keeps one panel per year and prints each panel’s heading, in the page’s order (2026 first). html_elements() keeps every match; html_element() keeps the first match inside each element.

text:
Dynamic pages, and the file they load



The Network tab on the Fed’s press-release list page: the page’s script requests json/ne-press.json.



Static page: the HTML the server sends is the page you see.
Dynamic page: the server sends a layout and scripts, and the scripts fetch the content after the page loads. read_html() runs no scripts, so it gets the empty layout.
The test: View Source and search for a title you can see. The Fed’s press-release list: 85 KB of HTML, “FOMC statement” zero times.
Three ways in

request the file the page loads, found in the Network tab
Copy as cURL on that request; curl_translate() turns it into R
a headless browser (one with no window): read_html_live()





With an agent. An agent that reads a dynamic page with read_html() gets the empty layout and may conclude there is no data. Give it the address of the file the page loads, from your Network tab.


The feed’s address is assembled by the page’s script, so it is not in the HTML or in the main script file; the Network tab (filtered to Fetch/XHR) is where it shows. In R: sum(grepl(“FOMC statement”, readLines(“cache/pressreleases.htm”))) returns 0.

title: 15 · Channels II: scraping
text:
Terms of use and copyright



Terms of use: the rules a site sets for visitors; using the site means accepting them. Look for footer links named Terms, Legal or Disclaimer. Zillow’s forbid “automated queries (including screen and database scraping …)”.
Copyright: the owner’s right to control copies. The Board puts its own material in the public domain (above): anyone may copy it; cite the Board.
Facts (prices, dates, vote counts) are outside US copyright (Feist v. Rural, 1991). The wording of a text is covered, unless it is public domain or licensed for copying.



With an agent. Read the terms yourself before you write the brief, and tell the agent what to keep: the facts, or the full text when it is public domain or licensed. Its requests carry the user agent you give it, so they go out under your name.

title: 15 · Channels II: scraping
section: robots.txt lists the paths a site asks programs to skip
text:
robots.txt lists the paths a site asks programs to skip

robots.txt: a plain-text file at a site’s main address (/robots.txt) that tells programs which paths to stay out of. The server (the computer that holds the pages) does not enforce it. A polite scraper follows it.

federalreserve.gov/robots.txt does not exist. The server answers with status code 404, not found (the status code is the three-digit number at the top of every reply). The standard for robots.txt (RFC 9309) treats a 404 as no restriction.
zillow.com/robots.txt, 328 lines; the lines that matter:




zillow.com/robots.txt as read on 18 October 2026, 6 of its 328 lines; the comments after a line are my notes

# Access to and use of Zillow.com is governed by our Terms of Use. See https://www.zillow.com/corp/Terms.htm
User-agent: *                   # line 3: every program
Allow: /homes/for_sale/$        # one of 64 Allow lines: the listing-index pages
Disallow: /homes/               # line 50, one of 212 Disallow lines: the listings
Crawl-delay: 1                  # line 302, in a block for one named crawler
Sitemap: https://www.zillow.com/xml/indexes/us/static.xml.gz   # 15 Sitemap lines



User-agent: the name a program sends with each request. A block (the lines that follow) applies to the programs named; * means every program.
Disallow: paths to skip (a path is the part of an address after the site name).
Allow: exceptions to a Disallow ($ means the address ends there).
Crawl-delay: seconds to wait between requests; not in the standard, but some sites write it.
Sitemap: where the site lists the pages it wants found (Part 2).



With an agent. Put the paths to skip and any delay in the brief. Some robots.txt files name AI companies’ crawlers; your agent’s requests carry the user agent from your brief.


The file forbids the listing pages a researcher would want; Part 1’s Zillow slide drew on it. Eleven crawlers are named in later blocks: Amazonbot, for one, is disallowed everywhere except guides and blog pages. The three social-media crawlers at lines 261 to 265 form their own group with two Allow lines; the four at lines 304 to 309 are fully disallowed. The Fed’s sitemap.xml answers 404 as well. Measured 18 October 2026.

title: 15 · Channels II: scraping
section: Personal data on the pages you scrape
text:
Personal data on the pages you scrape

From a Fed press-conference transcript (a PDF on federalreserve.gov): the reporter’s name and outlet.


Personal data: information that identifies a living person: a name, a photo, an address, an email, an IP address.
On the Fed’s site. The statements name the voting members. They act in public roles, so naming them raises no privacy issue. The press-conference transcripts name each reporter and outlet (above).
For research.

Collect only the fields you need.
Research on identifiable people goes to the IRB (the university board that approves research on people) before you collect.
The EU’s data-protection law (GDPR) covers personal data on public pages too, and counts an IP address.




With an agent. Name the fields to keep and forbid printing the rest, then read its report: both marathon agents in Part 6 printed a runner’s name while studying the page.


The Wikipedia request later today leaves the editor’s name out. GDPR: article 4(1) defines personal data; recital 30 names IP addresses and cookie identifiers.

Identifying yourself with a user agent


User agent: the name a program sends with every request. Put who you are and how to reach you in it. A robots.txt User-agent line matches this name.
Three requests to bls.gov (the US Bureau of Labor Statistics) with httr2, the R package that sends requests; one request per row.








User agent sent
Status code




no user agent set (httr2 sends its own name)

R Console; needs internet and httr2; two requests; run after class (Practice 6), not in the room

library(httr2)
req <- request("https://www.bls.gov/cpi/")
req <- req_error(req, is_error = function(resp) FALSE)   # a 403 comes back as a reply, not an R error
resp_status(req_perform(req))                            # httr2's default user agent
#> [1] 403
req <- req_user_agent(req, "AEM 6850 class exercise; <your netid>@cornell.edu")
resp_status(req_perform(req))
#> [1] 200



With an agent. Put this user agent, with your address, in the brief, and find it in the agent’s code.


The 403 page’s own words: “Automated retrieval programs (commonly called robots or bots) can cause delays and interfere with other customers’ timely access to information. Therefore, bot activity that doesn’t conform to BLS usage policy is prohibited.” Wikimedia’s policy asks for a contact address as well (Part 7). The policy page itself answers 403 to a user agent without an email. Measured 18 October 2026.

text:
What to do at a CAPTCHA and at a login wall


With an agent. Tell it to stop at a CAPTCHA or a login wall and report. If it offers a way around either, such as spoofing its address or rotating proxies, decline: sites ban scrapers that hide who is asking.

title: 15 · Channels II: scraping
section: fetch_page(): one polite request, saved once and logged
text:
fetch_page(): one polite request, saved once and logged



R Console, in the 15-scraping folder; needs httr2; defines fetch_page() and fetches nothing yet

# the same function ships as fetch_page.R: source("fetch_page.R")
library(httr2)
fetch_page <- function(url, file, ua) {
  if (file.exists(file)) return("already saved")          # never fetch a page twice
  req  <- request(url)
  req  <- req_user_agent(req, ua)                         # who you are and how to reach you
  req  <- req_retry(req, max_tries = 4)                   # a 429 or 503: wait (Retry-After if given), try again
  req  <- req_error(req, is_error = function(resp) FALSE) # a 403 or 404 comes back as a reply, not an R error
  resp <- req_perform(req)
  if (resp_status(resp) == 200) writeBin(resp_body_raw(resp), file)   # the bytes exactly as sent
  write(paste(url, file, format(Sys.time()), resp_status(resp), sep = ","),
        "mine/fetch_log.csv", append = TRUE)              # one log row per request, failures included
  Sys.sleep(1)                                            # one request a second
  resp_status(resp)
}



source("fetch_page.R") defines it and creates mine/ with its log, mine/fetch_log.csv. The cache is the folder of saved pages that a rerun reads instead of asking the server again; writeBin() keeps the raw bytes as sent.


With an agent. Its fetch function should hold the same five pieces: the user agent, the retry, the file saved once, the log row, the pause. Find each in its code, and ask for the cache and the log as files. The R marathon agent fetched one page twice after an encoding error and said so; the Fed agent reported four 429 replies its own log does not contain (Part 5).

           "mine/monetary20220615a.htm", ua)

substr(ps, 1, 60)                       # substr(): the first 60 characters of each paragraph

#> [4] "The invasion of Ukraine by Russia is causing tremendous huma"

#> [6] "In assessing the appropriate stance of monetary policy, the "
#> [7] "Voting for the monetary policy action were Jerome H. Powell,"

Eight paragraphs. Three are not statement text: the date line, “For release at 2:00 p.m. EDT”, and the last one, a link to the implementation note. The vote is paragraph 7: Esther L. George voted against, preferring an increase of 0.5 percentage point.




That statement raised the federal funds rate (the overnight rate between banks) to 1.5 to 1.75 percent. Debrief by call-out: run step 2 again and it returns “already saved” at once; read.csv(“mine/fetch_log.csv”) shows one row, status 200; open the page in the browser: the same paragraphs, with the site’s header and the note link around them. One request per laptop leaves the room, each with a user agent and a one-second pause; the runs that built cache/ and the agent’s run saw no 429 at one per second, and req_retry() handles one if it comes. Older statements carry other extras: the January 2006 statement opens with “For immediate release” and ends with the Board’s discount-rate action.

title: 15 · Channels II: scraping
section: The brief to the coding agent
text:
The brief to the coding agent

Coding agent: an AI tool that writes and runs code on your computer from written instructions. Before class, one was run on the brief below, in an empty folder. Permission to read, write and run files was given before it started, so it never stopped to ask.



Terminal, in an empty folder holding brief.txt

$ ls
brief.txt
$ cat brief.txt
Collect every FOMC policy statement (the Federal Open Market Committee's statement on its
policy decision, issued after a scheduled meeting or an unscheduled call) from January 2006
to the latest one, from the Federal Reserve's website.

Start from the meeting calendar at https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomccalendars.htm
(2021 onward) and the one page per year at
https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomchistoricalYYYY.htm for 2006 to 2020.

Rules: send a user agent that identifies the request as "AEM 6850 class demo; <address>";
at most one request per second; save every page you fetch in cache/ and never fetch the same
page twice; if the server answers 429, wait and retry.

Write fomc_statements.csv with one row per statement and the columns date (YYYY-MM-DD), url
(the address after redirects), words, text (the statement's paragraphs only), scheduled
(TRUE after a scheduled meeting, FALSE after an unscheduled call). Use R. Print the number
of statements per year when you are done.


A brief names the unit and how to tell it apart, where to start, the rules (user agent, pace, cache, retries), the output columns and the numbers to print. This one never says which releases do not count; Part 5 shows what that cost.


The pitfalls the brief leaves out: implementation notes, longer-run-goals statements, the notation vote, the three b addresses, the liquidity and swap-line releases.

title: 15 · Channels II: scraping
section: The demonstration: do marathon runners finish just under round times?
text:
The demonstration: do marathon runners finish just under round times?


The question. Allen, Dechow, Pope & Wu (Management Science, 2017) found more finishers just under 3:00, 3:30 and 4:00 than just over, in 9,789,093 marathon finish times. Runners treat round times as goals.
The pages. The Wineglass Marathon in Corning, New York, an hour from Ithaca. Its timing company posts each year’s results as one plain page: one line per finisher, with the net time (start line to finish line).
Allowed. The site has no robots.txt (404) and no terms of use. The lines carry names, ages and towns: keep place, sex, age group and time.




leonetiming.com/2023/Roads/Wineglass/WGMarathonNet.htm, the column headings and one line; name, age and town masked here

                                       PLACES IN               NET    NET
PLACE NAME                    AGE  SEX  &      AGEGROUP        TIME   PACE  CITY ...
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  665 ··························   F# 264   41/129  F30-34   3:59:00  9:08  ······


The page is fixed-width text inside one <pre> element: a selector finds the block, and each line is cut by position or by a pattern.

title: 15 · Channels II: scraping
section: The brief the two agents get
text:
The brief the two agents get


brief.txt, alone in an empty folder; one folder's copy ends 'Use R.', the other's 'Use Python.'

Collect the finish times of every finisher of the Wineglass Marathon (Corning, New York) for
each year whose results Leone Timing posts as a web page. Start from the year's page at
https://www.leonetiming.com/YEAR/Roads/Wineglass/ for YEAR from 2018 to 2025; some years have
no page (there was no race in 2020). On each year's page, follow the link to the marathon
results by net time (not the half marathon, not the relay).

Rules: send a user agent that identifies the request as "AEM 6850 class demo; <address>"; at
most one request per second; save every page you fetch in cache/ and never fetch the same page
twice; if the server answers 429, wait and retry. The pages list runners' names, ages and
towns: keep only place, sex, age group and net time, and never print or save names, even
while you study a page's layout.

Write wineglass.csv with one row per finisher and the columns year, place, sex, age_group,
net_time (h:mm:ss) and net_minutes. Draw wineglass.png: the number of finishers in each
one-minute bin of net time from 2:30 to 6:30, all years together, with vertical lines at 3:00,
3:30, 4:00 and 4:30. Draw wineglass_years.png: the number of finishers and the median net
time, by year.

When you are done, print: for each year, the number of rows you kept and the last place
number on that year's page; the number of finishers at 3:57, 3:58, 3:59, 4:00, 4:01 and 4:02
(minutes, all years); and the median net time by year.

Use R.


Both agents start now, side by side, with permission to read, write and run files given up front. Part 6 reads what they produce. In prep each took between 2 and 3 minutes.


Run sheet. Before class: two terminal windows, side by side, in two empty folders, wineglass-r and wineglass-py, each holding only its brief.txt (your address in place of <address>; the Python copy ends “Use Python, with the Python at ~/demo-py/bin/python”). In each window type, at this slide:
claude –allowedTools “Bash,Read,Write,Edit,Glob,Grep” “$(cat brief.txt)”
Then go on with Part 4; glance back at the windows on the next slide. Prep runs (19 October 2026, both started together): R 2 min 49 s and 2 min 22 s; Python 2 min 11 s and 2 min 15 s; 15 requests each; the two files identical row for row, 11,466 finishers. If the site is down: copy the saved pages (aem6850-agent-runs/final-r/cache) into each folder’s cache/ and the agents read them; the slides in Part 6 carry the prep run.

title: 15 · Channels II: scraping
section: An AI browser agent reads the calendar page
text:
An AI browser agent reads the calendar page









AI browser agent: a program that opens pages in your own browser and reads them for an assistant.

Use it for

a page you have never seen, to find which element holds the date
a handful of pages
pages behind your own login, where the terms allow

Why a loop collects every statement instead

the agent takes seconds to a minute per page; the loop takes about a second
the agent keeps no copy of the page, so there is nothing to cite or re-run
the site’s terms apply to it as to any program




Drawn from a run of a browser agent in a desktop assistant’s browser pane, October 2026: the agent’s steps and its answer.

Compare its answer with Exercise 1: nine rows, 22 August.

title: 15 · Channels II: scraping
text:
What the run did


From the brief alone, the agent collected 175 statements in 8 min 13 s.

191 pages fetched once each: the calendar, the 15 year pages and 175 statements.
175 rows, 31 January 2006 to 16 September 2026; 10 marked unscheduled (scheduled = FALSE).
Its closing message names two doubts, cut from the crop above. Two unscheduled rows are liquidity releases (announcements of emergency lending). One address carries a wrong date (June 2007).
It also reports four 429 replies. Its own log says otherwise (the last slide of this part).


Run 1, captured in October 2026; the tool’s screens change between versions, the steps do not.

The slide carries run 1, captured in prep. If you started a run on this brief before class, read its final table against this slide. The middle of its message, the table of statements per year, is what the next slide’s code reproduces. Its rule: a statement is the link named “Statement” under each heading on a year page, or the “HTML” link after “Statement:” on the calendar. Process: 37 tool calls, 179 lines of R in two files (fetch.R, a cached fetcher with the user agent, a one-second spacing and a 429 wait; collect_statements.R); it chose dplyr, stringr and readr beside rvest and httr2, packages the course does not use. A second run the same evening took 7 min 28 s and gave the same 175 dates. If the live run is shown, its own numbers replace these.

title: 15 · Channels II: scraping
section: Three lists of one site disagree on what a statement is
text:
Three lists of one site disagree on what a statement is

Did the agent get the same statements as the statements file (ours, 171 rows, built from cache/ by the rule in SOURCE.txt)?




R Console, in the 15-scraping folder; reads agent_run/fomc_statements.csv (the agent's run 1) and fomc_statements.csv (ours)

agent <- read.csv("agent_run/fomc_statements.csv")
ours  <- read.csv("fomc_statements.csv")
c(agent = nrow(agent), ours = nrow(ours))


#> agent  ours 
#>   175   171

yr <- data.frame(year = 2006:2026)
yr$agent <- as.vector(table(substr(agent$date, 1, 4)))   # rows per year; substr(): characters 1 to 4
yr$ours  <- as.vector(table(substr(ours$date,  1, 4)))
print(yr[yr$agent != yr$ours, ], row.names = FALSE)      # the years that differ

#>  year agent ours
#>  2007    10    9
#>  2008    11   10
#>  2010     9    8
#>  2019     9    8




The agent’s rule, every link the site labels Statement: 175. The four extra dates (above) announce lending programmes or the mechanics of a decision, not the committee’s decision on the policy rate.
The feed: 179 titles contain “FOMC statement”; five are in neither file.
The statements file’s rule: the title says “FOMC statement” and the release announces the rate decision: 171.

Write the rule down before you scrape, and reconcile every difference by hand.

title: 15 · Channels II: scraping
section: Three statements drawn with a seed
text:
Three statements drawn with a seed

The counts match on most years; does the text match? Seed: a starting number that makes a random draw repeat on every computer, so the room draws the same three rows and reads them against the statements file.












R Console; needs agent and ours, read on the counts slide

set.seed(6850)
pick <- sample(nrow(agent), 3)
agent[pick, c("date", "words", "scheduled")]


#>           date words scheduled
#> 134 2021-07-28   488      TRUE
#> 55  2012-01-25   418      TRUE
#> 28  2008-10-29   286      TRUE

# match(): the row of ours with the same date
agent$text[pick] == ours$text[match(agent$date[pick], ours$date)]

#> [1] TRUE TRUE TRUE

# the last row, so the scrape ran to the end
agent[nrow(agent), c("date", "words")]

#>           date words
#> 175 2026-09-16   131



The screenshot is the 29 October 2008 page, the third row drawn. In both files its text starts at the first paragraph; the page header and the link to the implementation note are left out. The three TRUEs say the agent’s text and the statements file’s text are identical on those three dates.



The latest statement opens with its vote (“approved the following statement for release by a 12 – 0 vote”); older ones end with a voting paragraph. Both files date the June 2007 statement 28 June from the page’s own date line, where the address says 0618: the address carries a typo. The January 2012 row is the policy statement (20120125a), not the longer-run-goals statement released the same day (20120125c). On the 171 shared dates the two files’ word counts differ on two rows, by 3 and 8 words, from different rules on headings and links inside a paragraph.

title: 15 · Channels II: scraping
section: The agent’s 429 count, read from its own log
text:
The agent’s 429 count, read from its own log

The agent said four 429 replies came. The log it wrote records every request. The claim, from its closing message: “The server returned 429 four times, and each request was retried and then succeeded.”




R Console, in the 15-scraping folder; reads agent_run/fetch_log.txt

fetch_log <- readLines("agent_run/fetch_log.txt")
c(lines = length(fetch_log), fetched = sum(startsWith(fetch_log, "fetched")))


#>   lines fetched 
#>     172     172

sub("fetched https://www.federalreserve.gov", "", grep("429", fetch_log, value = TRUE))   # the lines that contain 429

#> [1] "/newsevents/press/monetary/20090429a.htm"       
#> [2] "/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20150429a.htm"
#> [3] "/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20200429a.htm"
#> [4] "/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20260429a.htm"



The agent counted the lines that contain 429 with the shell command grep -c 429 fetch_log.txt and got 4. Those four lines are fetches of statements dated 29 April: each address holds 0429. Every line in the log is a successful fetch. No 429 reply came.
Takeaway: a number in an agent’s summary is a claim about its files. Read the files before you repeat it.

The log holds 172 of the 191 fetches. The agent fetched the 16 list pages and three statements before it started the log; all 191 pages are in its cache/.

section: The R file and the Python file agree row for row
text:
The R file and the Python file agree row for row



R Console, in the 15-scraping folder; reads the two agents' files in wineglass/ (prep run, 19 October 2026)

r  <- read.csv("wineglass/r/wineglass.csv", na.strings = c("", "NA"))       # blank sex reads as NA
py <- read.csv("wineglass/python/wineglass.csv", na.strings = c("", "NA"))

#> [1] TRUE

#>            2018 2019 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025
#> rows       1674 1598 1389 1371 1647 1816 1971
#> last_place 1674 1598 1389 1371 1647 1816 1971




Each year’s row count equals the last place on its page, in both files.
Each agent’s report named its own slip. The R agent fetched one page twice after a text-encoding error; the Python agent printed one runner’s first name, “Chip”, which it had taken for a column heading.
Prep times, the two agents started together: R 2 min 22 s, Python 2 min 15 s.

title: 15 · Channels II: scraping
section: Finding the results link, in R and in Python
text:
Finding the results link, in R and in Python




wineglass/r/wineglass.R (excerpt)

idx  <- fetch(base)                 # the year's page
a    <- html_elements(read_html(idx$body), "a")
txt  <- html_text(a)
href <- html_attr(a, "href")
i    <- which(grepl("Net", txt) &
              grepl("Marathon", href) &
              !grepl("Half|Relay", href,
                     ignore.case = TRUE))
stopifnot(length(i) == 1)
pg   <- fetch(paste0(base, href[i]))




wineglass/python/explore_results.py (excerpt)

status, html = get(url)             # the year's page
soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser")
for a in soup.find_all("a", href=True):
    href = a["href"]
    name = href.rsplit("/", 1)[-1].lower()
    if ("net" in a.get_text().lower()
            and "marathon" in name
            and "half" not in name):
        return urljoin(url, href)




The same rule in both: the link whose text says Net and whose address says Marathon, not Half. The R agent also stops if it finds more than one.
Both then cut each line of the <pre> text with a regular expression and stop at the 2019 page’s separate wheelchair table, whose places restart at 1. The whole scripts are in wineglass/.

title: 15 · Channels II: scraping
section: The project folder: fetch once, build from the saved pages
text:
The project folder: fetch once, build from the saved pages


15-scraping/, the folder in 15-scraping.zip (trimmed)

reference_scrape.R    sent the 268 requests that built cache/, on 18 October 2026
cache/                every page as the server sent it, raw bytes
  fetch_log.csv       one row per request: address, final address, time, status, bytes
build_statements.R    reads cache/ only and writes fomc_statements.csv
fomc_statements.csv   171 rows, one per policy statement
SOURCE.txt            the addresses, dates, user agent, pace and counting rule
fetch_page.R          the polite fetch from Part 3; your fetches go to mine/
wineglass/            the demonstration: the brief, each agent's scripts, file and figures



build_statements.R reruns with no network and returns the same 171 rows. A new fetch would differ: the site adds a statement after each meeting, and its pages change design (next slide).
A replication package includes the scraping code even when the pages cannot ship: “All programs used to generate the analysis data from raw data must be included, even if the raw data cannot be provided” (AEA data and code policy).
The Fed’s pages ship here because they are public domain. The marathon pages carry names, so wineglass/ holds the code and the files without names, and no saved pages.



With an agent. Ask for two scripts: one that fetches into cache/, and one that builds the file from cache/ with no network.

title: 15 · Channels II: scraping
section: The Fed’s calendar in 2015, from the Wayback Machine
text:
The Fed’s calendar in 2015, from the Wayback Machine

Wayback Machine: the Internet Archive’s copies of web pages since 1996, each one a snapshot; 19 yearly ones of the calendar.




R Console, in the 15-scraping folder; needs rvest; reads cache/fomccalendars_20150102.htm (live address on the page)

snap <- read_html("cache/fomccalendars_20150102.htm")   # the page as captured on 2 January 2015
length(html_elements(snap, ".panel-default"))            # today's selector finds nothing


#> [1] 0

html_text2(html_elements(snap, "th#year"))               # th#year: a th element whose id is year

#> [1] "2014 FOMC Meetings" "2013 FOMC Meetings" "2012 FOMC Meetings"
#> [4] "2011 FOMC Meetings" "2010 FOMC Meetings" "2009 FOMC Meetings"
#> [7] "2015 FOMC Meetings"

sum(html_text2(html_elements(snap, "a")) == "Statement")   # links named Statement on the 2015 page

#> [1] 50





In January 2015 the page was built from tables: .panel-default matches nothing, th#year holds the years, and the 50 links named Statement still work. A redesign changes the selectors.









With an agent. Ask it to record each snapshot’s timestamp and the layout it found: today’s selector finds nothing on the 2015 page.

title: 15 · Channels II: scraping
text:
One Wikipedia article’s edit history














Revision: one saved edit, with its time, its size and the editor’s note.
Wikipedia’s robots.txt closes the history pages to programs (Disallow: /w/). Its API returns the same history to a program that sends a contact address: four replies of up to 500 revisions.
1,613 revisions; the article’s information page states 1,613 edits.
Zhang & Zhu (AER, 2011): when mainland China blocked Chinese Wikipedia in 2005, editors outside China cut their contributions by 42.8 percent.
Greenstein & Zhu (AER P&P, 2012): the political slant of about 28,000 articles on US politics, across every revision.




With an agent. Name the fields to request, without the editor’s name, and the total to match: the information page’s 1,613.


The request left out the user field: it names people, and anonymous editors appear by IP address, which counts as personal data. The busiest months: November 2020 (203 edits), November 2017 (96, his nomination as chair) and January 2026 (85). Information page read 19 October 2026.

title: 15 · Channels II: scraping
text:
Slides · Live script · Source · the project
How to get data out of pages built for people, in seven steps: when scraping is the right route; the ways to collect a site (a saved page read into R with rvest and CSS selectors, static and dynamic pages, six routes to every page); what to take into account (terms, copyright, robots.txt, personal data, a polite fetch); AI tools, in R or Python; verifying what a scrape returns; a live demonstration in which two coding agents, one in R and one in Python, collect seven years of a marathon’s finish times from the same brief; and laying out a scrape so someone else can re-run it. The Federal Reserve’s policy statements since 2006 carry the code and both exercises. You will usually scrape with an AI coding agent: each piece below says what to ask it for and how to verify what it did.

Objectives
