title: 19 · Audio I: speech to text
text: Materials for this session are not published yet. They appear here before class.

title: 19 · Audio I: speech to text
text:
Objectives
By the end of this session you can:

Transcribe a recording with a speech-to-text model, a program that listens to a recording and writes out the words it hears, and keep the timestamps for each word.
Label who is speaking and join the speaker labels to the words by time.
Build an utterance table with one row per utterance (one unbroken turn by one speaker): speaker, text, start and end.
Save the raw model output so the table rebuilds without transcribing again.
Transcribe a short clip by hand and compute the word-error rate of the model’s transcript against it.

title: 19 · Audio I: speech to text
text:
What we cover

What recorded speech, once written down, has measured in economics. Hassan et al. (QJE, 2019) measured each firm’s political risk as the share of its earnings calls (the quarterly calls where managers present results and answer analysts’ questions) spent on political risks. Hansen, McMahon & Prat (QJE, 2018) measured how members of the Federal Reserve committee that sets US interest rates changed the way they deliberated once they knew their meeting transcripts would be published. Sautner et al. (JF, 2023) measured firms’ exposure to climate change from the attention it gets on earnings calls. All three work from transcripts typed by professionals; a speech-to-text model produces that text for recordings that come without one.
Where recordings come from, and the terms attached to public archives and licensed collections. The running example: Federal Reserve press conferences, whose official transcripts are the reference for measuring the model’s errors.
Speech-to-text models return the transcript, the word-for-word record of what was said, with a timestamp (seconds from the start of the recording) for the start and end of each word or segment, a stretch of speech returned as one piece. You can run one locally, on your own computer so the audio never leaves your machine, or send the audio to a provider’s API.
Speaker diarization is a separate step that marks which voice is talking when, labelling them Speaker 1, Speaker 2 and so on. You join those labels to the words by their timestamps.
The utterance table is the deliverable. The raw model output sits next to it, saved exactly as it came back, so every cleaning step can be rerun from it.
Word-error rate (WER) counts substitutions (wrong words), deletions (missing words) and insertions (extra words), and divides by the number of words in a reference transcript, a careful hand transcript of a short clip. To verify a transcript, write the reference before you read the model’s version, compute the rate, and listen again to the passages where it is worst. Errors tend to cluster on names, numbers and overlapping speech.
Running the models yourself needs Python and a few large installs. A setup guide comes with the session materials, and the model output is provided too, so every step also runs in R alone.

title: 21 · Photographs I: pixels & vision models
text: Materials for this session are not published yet. They appear here before class.

title: 21 · Photographs I: pixels & vision models
text:
Objectives
By the end of this session you can:

Read a photo into R as a grid of numbers and pull out the pixels (the tiny squares that each hold one colour) of one region, such as the patch of sky.
Compute pixel features, numbers built from the pixels, by hand, such as sky colour and contrast.
Score haze with a vision model, an AI model that takes an image and returns text or numbers about it, through its provider’s API.
Relate each score to PM2.5 (the weight of airborne particles 2.5 micrometres across or smaller in each cubic metre of air) with cor() and a short lm() and predict() step.
Compare both methods against the monitor on held-out photos and say which predicts PM2.5 better, and by how much.

title: 21 · Photographs I: pixels & vision models
text:
What we cover

What photographs have measured in economics. Ludwig & Mullainathan (QJE, 2024) trained an algorithm on only the pixels of defendants’ mug shots and found it accounts for up to half of the predictable variation in judges’ jailing decisions. Obaid & Pukthuanthong (JFE, 2022) classified news photos by sentiment to build a daily pessimism index that predicts reversals in market returns and trading volume. Aubry et al. (JF, 2023) predicted art auction prices from images of the works and their other characteristics, and compared the predictions with the auction houses’ own estimates. Here the same idea is applied to air quality.
The data: 365 daily sky photos, one per day for a year, matched to same-day PM2.5 readings from a monitor. The monitor is the ground truth, the trusted measurement every score is verified against.
A photo is an image array, a grid with one layer per colour, so each pixel has RGB values: its amounts of red, green and blue light.
The baseline you build yourself: average the sky’s pixels for colour, take their variance for contrast (how much brightness varies; haze makes a scene flatter and greyer), and you have a haze score in about thirty lines of plain R.
The model route: a vision model gets each photo and a scoring rule, written instructions on what to judge and on what scale, and returns structured output, one number per photo in a fixed format that code reads directly. Every raw response is saved.
From score to PM2.5: cor() for the correlation, how closely the two move together on a scale from -1 to 1, then lm() fitted on the training photos and predict() on the held-out ones, explained step by step.
Holding out photos: split the days into a training set and a held-out set with a seed, so the split repeats exactly. All tuning, such as choosing the sky region or rewording the prompt, uses the training photos; the held-out photos stay untouched until the final comparison.
Both scores compared against the monitor on the same held-out photos, with the prediction error of each method (the average gap between predicted and measured PM2.5) and the gap between them.
An out-of-sample test: webcam images from a wildfire smoke event that neither method saw while it was being built.

title: 23 · Spatial I: vector
text: Materials for this session are not published yet. They appear here before class.

title: 23 · Spatial I: vector
text:
Objectives
By the end of this session you can:

Load and inspect vector data with sf: geometries, attributes and the coordinate reference system.
Confirm the coordinate reference system of every layer and choose a projection for what you will measure.
Run a spatial join and compare the row count before and after.
Flag the homes inside a fire perimeter and measure how far every other home lies from it.
Compare an area computed with st_area() against the published value.

title: 23 · Spatial I: vector
text:
What we cover

Published work built on vector data, map features stored as points, lines or polygons (closed shapes such as a county or a burned area), each paired with a row of information in a table. Black (QJE, 1999) compared house prices on either side of school attendance-zone boundaries in Massachusetts to measure what parents pay for higher test scores. Aaronson, Hartley & Mazumder (AEJ: Policy, 2021) compared neighbourhoods on either side of the lines drawn on the 1930s redlining maps and traced long-run effects on home ownership, house values, rents and segregation. Both use a boundary discontinuity design, which compares places on either side of a border, close enough to share surroundings and subject to different rules. Currie et al. (AER, 2015) measured house prices and infant health by distance from 1,600 industrial plants that opened or closed, and found the effects within about a mile of a plant.
An sf object is a data frame with a geometry column (the coordinates that place each feature and give it its shape) beside its attributes (values such as a county’s name or a home’s sale price), so filtering and joining work as they do on any table. Shapefiles and GeoPackages, the common file formats, store the two together.
The coordinate reference system (CRS), the rule linking a file’s numbers to places on Earth, read from the file and confirmed against the documentation and a basemap of a place you know. Measuring needs a projection, a method for flattening the curved Earth that stretches distances, areas or shapes somewhere. Areas need an equal-area projection, which keeps every region’s area correct; distances need a local projected system in metres.
Spatial joins, which match rows from two layers by location, such as attaching to each home the county it sits in. Compare the row count before and after, since a point on a shared border can match two polygons and duplicate a row.
Areas: st_area() against the Census Bureau’s published land area (ALAND). Reconcile one county’s two values and explain the gap.
Application: a fire perimeter and the homes around it. A point in polygon test (which shape, if any, contains each point) flags the homes inside the burned area. Distances run from each home to the nearest edge; verify that every home inside shows zero.

title: 25 · LiDAR & drone imagery
text: Materials for this session are not published yet. They appear here before class.

title: 25 · LiDAR & drone imagery
text:
Objectives
By the end of this session you can:

Explain what LiDAR measures and how a cloud of laser returns becomes an elevation raster.
Build a terrain model, a surface model and a canopy-height raster from public LiDAR data with lidR and terra.
Compute slope from an elevation raster and summarise it over polygons.
Read a drone orthomosaic into R and line it up with other layers.
Say what plane and drone data resolve that satellite imagery cannot, and what they give up in area covered and visits repeated.

title: 25 · LiDAR & drone imagery
text:
What we cover

Published work built on elevation and aerial imagery. Henderson, Regan & Venables (REStud, 2021) traced every Nairobi building from aerial photographs for 2003 and 2015, measured 2015 building heights with LiDAR, and tracked demolition, rebuilding and the conversion of slums. Saiz (QJE, 2010) measured the land too steep or wet to build on around US metro areas from elevation and water data, and showed that it limits housing supply. Duflo & Pande (QJE, 2007) computed slope across each Indian district and along its rivers from a global elevation grid, and used river gradient to estimate how large dams affect farm output and poverty.
How LiDAR works: a laser scanner on a plane times each reflected pulse and turns it into a distance. The result is a point cloud, millions of points with a location and a height, classified as ground, vegetation or buildings. Each echo is a return; the first often comes from treetops or roofs and the last from the ground, and pulses that slip between leaves give the terrain under a forest canopy. Points come as LAS files, or LAZ when compressed.
From points to rasters: a digital terrain model (DTM, often called a DEM), the bare ground’s height, from ground returns; a digital surface model, the height of whatever stands on top, from first returns; and canopy height as the difference, cell by cell. Both models must share a vertical datum, the zero level of all heights. Compare one LiDAR height with a building of known height.
Slope, how steeply the ground rises, computed from height differences between neighbouring cells and averaged over polygons.
Where to get it: public LiDAR collections cover much of the United States, along with the elevation rasters derived from them.
Drone imagery: photos with a ground sample distance (the ground width one pixel covers) of a few centimetres, stitched into an orthomosaic, one image with true map distances everywhere. It shows single trees, crop rows and roof damage that a satellite pixel averages together. Georeferencing pins it to the map at ground control points, spots with surveyed positions. Overlay a basemap to verify a road lines up.
Application: what each home can see, such as a lake or a new wind turbine, computed from the surface model and set beside sale prices; and buildings that changed between two LiDAR flights of the same area.

This page is written for self-study: every step runs from the code shown, on data downloaded within the page.

title: 27 · Satellite II: Earth Engine
text: Materials for this session are not published yet. They appear here before class.

title: 27 · Satellite II: Earth Engine
text:
Objectives
By the end of this session you can:

Say when to send the computation to the data instead of downloading the data to your machine.
Find a dataset in the catalog and read its documentation.
Filter an image collection by date, place and cloud cover.
Reduce a collection over your own polygons and load the table in R.
Estimate golf-course water use from evapotranspiration data and compare it with the water budgets an agency publishes.

title: 27 · Satellite II: Earth Engine
text:
What we cover

Satellite archives in economics:

Burgess et al. (QJE, 2012) built yearly deforestation data for Indonesia from satellite imagery and found that splitting districts raised deforestation.
Assunção, Gandour & Rocha (AEJ: Applied, 2023) used Brazil’s satellite deforestation alerts, with clouds that block detection as a source of variation in enforcement, to show that monitoring curbs clearing in the Amazon.
Garg, Jagnani & Pullabhotla (AEJ: Policy, 2024) counted satellite fire detections within 10 km of about 11,000 Indian villages and found that new rural roads raised crop burning and downwind infant mortality.

Sending the computation to the data. Some questions need more pixels than your disk holds, such as a decade of images over a continent. Google Earth Engine, a Google service that holds satellite archives, runs your code on the computers that store the data (server-side computation), and only the result comes back.
The data catalog, the searchable list of datasets the service holds: Landsat, Sentinel, MODIS and derived products. Reading a documentation page for units, cloud masks and the scale factor, the number you multiply stored values by to get real units.
Filtering an image collection (a stack of images of one kind, such as every Landsat image of a region) by date range, bounding box and cloud cover. Print the number of images left and compare it with the count you expect from how often the satellite passes over.
Server-side thinking. A loop that works in R hangs in Earth Engine, because the work runs on remote machines. You map a function over the collection (apply it to every image) and then apply a reducer, which collapses many values into one, such as a mean. Each call takes a scale, the pixel size in metres at which the calculation runs.
reduceRegions(). Zonal statistics over your own polygons (closed shapes on a map, such as fields or counties) summarise the pixel values inside each one, such as mean rainfall per county or greenness per field. Export the table as a file, load it in R as a data frame, and verify it by reducing one small polygon with terra and comparing the two numbers.
Derived products and where each is weakest: land-cover maps, and evapotranspiration (water leaving the land as vapour, from soil evaporation plus water released by plants) from OpenET, a public dataset estimated from satellite images at 30-metre pixels across the contiguous US.
Application: golf-course water use under drought restrictions. When a drought brings limits on outdoor watering, do golf courses cut back? Golf-course polygons combined with OpenET evapotranspiration. Compare each course with the land around it to see whether it is watered, then convert the difference to consumptive use (water that evaporates or is taken up by plants and does not return to rivers or aquifers) in acre-feet per year (an acre-foot covers one acre one foot deep). Reconcile each estimate with the water budget, the yearly amount a regional agency says the course needs or may use.
When to stay local. Small areas, one scene, or work you must rerun exactly. Cache the exported table and commit it.
Access: register for noncommercial Earth Engine use at least a week before class, since approval can take a few days. A setup guide with a first test script comes with the session materials.

title: Syllabus
text:
Course
AEM 6850 — Empirical Methods for Applied Economists
Fall 2026. Tuesdays and Thursdays, 8:40–9:55 am. First meeting: August 25. Last meeting: December 3. Location: Malott Hall, Room 406.
Instructor. Prof. Ariel Ortiz-Bobea. Office: 450B Warren Hall. Email: ao332@cornell.edu. Office hours: set in week 1, once I’ve seen the class’s schedule constraints — times posted on Canvas.
Credits. 3. Prerequisites: none. No prior programming, no econometrics. You need a laptop you can bring to every class.

title: Syllabus
text:
What this course is
Every empirical project begins with data someone had to find, fetch, clean, check, and shape. Methods courses assume that work is already done. This course teaches it — across every kind of raw material an economist now meets:
messy tables · text · documents (PDFs & scans) · images · audio · maps & rasters
Two things make the 2026 version of this course different from what you may expect:

AI is ambient. Modern AI tools write competent first-draft code and can read text, documents, images, and audio at scale. We use them openly, from early in the semester, the way you will use them in your research career.
Verification is the graded skill. Precisely because models write the first draft, the human contribution shifts to knowing whether the result is right: predicting what code should produce, checking data against the world, and documenting the evidence. “It runs” is not “it’s right.” That posture — not any one package — is the course.

The semester runs in two parts. Part I (weeks 1–6): foundations — R, version control, AI tools, data wrangling, verification strategy, reproducible projects, graphics. Part II (weeks 7–15): applications — one unconventional data family per session, each walked through the same pipeline: what economic questions it answers → what’s out there → acquire → process → verify.
Homework is a single running investigation of a real, recent event — this year, the January 2025 Los Angeles wildfires — examined through a new data family each week: air-quality readings, damage inspections, parcel and demographic records, official PDFs, news text, press-conference audio, satellite imagery, wind fields. By the end you will have touched every family and built one coherent piece of empirical work, including its climate-justice dimension: who was in the path, and who bears the damage.

title: Syllabus
section: What you will be able to do
text:
What you will be able to do
By December, you can:

Acquire data from files, APIs, web pages, and licensed platforms — politely, reproducibly, with credentials handled correctly.
Process any of the six data families into analysis-ready tables in R.
Verify systematically: match every failure family (vanishing rows, silent type conversion, impossible values, unreconciled totals) to the technique that catches it, and validate model-constructed variables with gold sets and error analysis.
Visualize for diagnosis and for publication.
Reproduce: any of your projects re-runs end-to-end on a fresh machine from its repository.
Delegate to AI tools honestly and safely — scope a task, predict the output, check the diff, disclose the use.

title: Syllabus

How the course works
The website is the course. Every lecture is a manual page you can read before class and revisit any time, paired with slides that mirror it section-for-section and a runnable R script for following along live. If you put in the time, everything is learnable from the site. Materials stay up permanently, archived by year.
A typical week.

Tuesday & Thursday, 8:40: a short Poll Everywhere quiz on the previous session opens most classes (from week 2). Then lecture + live coding + in-class exercises.
Thursday after class: homework posts. Due the following Thursday, 8:40 am, committed to your private course repository on GitHub.

Submission from day one. In the first class you’ll get a private repository in the course’s GitHub organization — no git knowledge needed (the browser handles it). We switch to proper version control in week 3, when you’ll discover you’ve been using it all along.

title: Syllabus
text:
Homework
Thirteen weekly assignments, each a self-contained piece of the semester’s investigation using that week’s tools. Every assignment states its goal precisely and includes reference checkpoints — published totals, documented counts, known facts — so you can know you’re right before submitting. Several assignments are match-the-target: the finished table, figure, or map ships with the assignment, and your job is to rebuild it exactly from raw data.
Mechanics.

Posted Thursday after class; due the following Thursday 8:40 am. HW13 spans Thanksgiving and gets two weeks.
Submitted by committing to your private course repository (browser upload for HW1–3; git from HW4).
Every assignment ships a starter, and every week’s starter includes a known-good checkpoint of the running project — falling behind one week never snowballs.
Late work: homework is not accepted late, and your lowest homework score is dropped. The weekly checkpoint means you can always rejoin cleanly. Documented emergencies: talk to me.

What’s graded (every week, same four dimensions):







Dimension
Question it asks




Reproduces
Does it re-run from a fresh copy on another machine?


Correct
Do your outputs match the stated checkpoints?


Verified
Does your work check itself — predictions, assertions, reconciliations, a diagnostic plot read in one sentence?


Craft
Structure, clarity, commit history, complete disclosure



Weights shift across the semester: early assignments weight Correct most (HW1: 15 / 60 / 15 / 10); by the second half Verified dominates — as AI writes more of your code, the checking becomes your contribution. Each assignment states its weights.
Assignment starters and submissions live in private repositories in the course’s GitHub organization; sign-up and access instructions are posted on Canvas only.

title: Syllabus
text:
Quizzes & attendance
Short Poll Everywhere quizzes at 8:40 in most classes from week 2, typically two per week: 2–4 questions on the previous session — prediction (“how many rows come out?”), spotting (“this runs clean; what’s wrong?”), judgment (“which check catches this?”). They test understanding you can’t look up, they’re auto-graded to Canvas, and they double as attendance.

Your lowest two quiz scores are dropped; this is the absence buffer.
I am flexible about absences when you are transparent with me. Tell me before class when life happens; the dropped scores and the website exist so that missing a class is recoverable.
Quizzes are answered in the room, on your own device, through your own Cornell account. Answering for someone else, or having someone answer for you, is academic misconduct — see below.

title: Syllabus
text:
AI policy
This course assumes you will use AI tools — that’s part of what it teaches. The rules:

Permitted by default. Chatbots, coding assistants, and agents are allowed on all homework unless a specific exercise says otherwise. The early weeks are deliberately structured so working by hand teaches you the vocabulary you’ll later verify in.
Disclosure is mandatory. Every submission includes a short disclosure block: which tools, for what, and what you checked. Disclosed AI use is never penalized. Undisclosed AI use is misrepresentation and is treated as an integrity violation.
No-AI zones. In-class quizzes and designated in-class exercises (announced as such) are your own unassisted work.
You own every number. “The model did it” is not a defense. If it’s in your submission, you are asserting you checked it.
Protect data and people. Never paste licensed data, other students’ work, or personal information into external tools. Licensed datasets (e.g., parcel records) stay inside the private course infrastructure.

title: Syllabus
text:
Academic integrity
Cornell’s Code of Academic Integrity applies. In this course specifically: collaboration on ideas is welcome; submitted work must be your own (with AI use disclosed); quiz impersonation and credential sharing are treated as serious violations; and honest disclosure of a shortcut you took will always be treated more generously than its discovery. I am flexible with people and inflexible with deception.

title: Syllabus
text:
Materials & costs
Everything is free.

Software: R and RStudio (installed in class 1), git and a GitHub account, a Cornell Poll Everywhere account. AI tools at free tiers suffice; course API keys are provided where needed.
No textbook. The course website is the text. Optional references, all free online: R for Data Science (2e), Healy’s Data Visualization, Happy Git with R.

title: Syllabus
text:
Accessibility & support
Students with disabilities: I want this course to work for you. Please share your SDS accommodation letter early, and talk to me — the course’s multiple formats (readable manual, slides, scripts, recorded material where available) exist so there are several ways in. Wellness: if life goes sideways during the semester, tell me early; late-semester rescue is much harder than mid-semester adjustment. Cornell Health and cares.cornell.edu are there for bigger things.
